  • These days I think the original The Hunger Games movie is pretty great, and I’ve rewatched it so many times.
  • Caesar asks Peeta how his 'new leg' is working out.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I can’t believe the release of Sunrise on the Reaping means I’ve been going to the theaters for The Hunger Games movies for nearly fifteen years! I’ll never forget when I went to see one of my favorite novels at the time become a book-to-screen adaptation back in 2012. I just rewatched the franchise and recalled one gripe I had about the movie when I first saw it that I actually understand now as an adult.

These days I think the original The Hunger Games movie is pretty great, and I’ve rewatched it so many times. I remember when I went to see it back then, I thought it was a faithful adaptation, but I was bummed that they decided to take out the fact that Peeta loses his leg in The Hunger Games. Check out this excerpt from the end of the first book:.

Caesar asks Peeta how his 'new leg' is working out. 'New leg?' I say, and I can't help reaching out and pulling up the bottom of Peeta's pants. 'Oh, no,' I whisper,' taking in the metal-and-plastic device that has replaced his flesh.

In the movie, Peeta gets injured like in the book, but Katniss nurses him back to health, and he completely recovers by the end. Yet, in the source material, Peeta is practically bleeding out right before they become the final people in the arena. Katniss is desperate to help him, and she suggests they both have poisonous berries so she can save them both. When they reunite for the post-victory interview with Caesar Flickerman, she learns that his leg had to be amputated right after they left the arena.

Sources indicate that I think when The Hunger Games movie came out, I thought the movie was censoring an crucial aspect of the story. Peeta’s major injury really had me on the edge of my seat while I was reading the book, so it was sort of anticlimactic for the movie to completely skip it.

It has been revealed that however, it just dawned on me during my recent rewatch (with my Hulu subscription) that I haven’t thought about this change to The Hunger Games in a really long time. I guess, ultimately, it didn’t really matter that Peeta only has one leg in the scope of the whole series, and it probably would have caused some extra special effects headaches for the filmmaking team.

Sources indicate that there’s something else. Ultimately, I’m realizing that both Peeta and Katniss have so many horrific things happen to them throughout the series that maybe it was OK for the movies to skip Peeta losing a leg. I mean, what happens to Peeta in Mockingjay alone is just heartbreaking. The guy loses his entire family, he’s captured by the Capitol and starved. And then, his brain is altered so he thinks Katniss is his enemy. That’s some really rough stuff.

Now, I think overall The Hunger Games movie series did a great job of adapting the maturity of the book series, but now I’m OK with the films taking out a few extra traumatic things like Peeta’s amputated leg.

I've given up all chance at inner peace. I've made my mind a sunless space. I share my dreams with spoilers for "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.".

In a recent development, the "Hunger Games" films have always been dark and violent. Yet, somehow, "Sunrise on the Reaping" manages to take the cake, becoming easily the bleakest movie in the franchise yet (even as it tones down certain elements from the book it's adapting). Not only is it filled with brutal deaths, but there's a general sense of meanness and cruelty that surpasses anything the rulers of the Capitol did during the previous films.

Unfolding between 2023's "The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes" and the original "Hunger Games" movies, "Sunrise on the Reaping" finds Panem's President Snow (here portrayed by Ralph Fiennes) operating at the height of his ruthlessness. Indeed, where "The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes" shows how the tyrant rose to power and the first four "Hunger Games" films expose the cracks in his system, this upcoming movie picks up at a point when the Capitol's government and Snow are seemingly invincible. As such, there's a feeling of hopelessness that permeates the story, suggesting that no matter how much people try to fight back, it won't do any good. (Don't worry, "Sunrise on the Reaping" is also a very good movie.).

According to recent reports, in many ways, "Sunrise on the Reaping" is to the "Hunger Games" films what the much-celebrated "Andor" is to the "Star Wars" franchise, i.e. a devastating tale of loss and sacrifice about people who don't know if they'll ever get to see victory or freedom. And nowhere is this better portrayed than with Plutarch Heavensbee (Jesse Plemons), a rebel in disguise who very much brings to mind Stellan Skarsgård's Luthen Rael from "Andor.".

When we first meet the older Plutarch Heavensbee (Philip Seymour Hoffman) as a gamemaker in "The Hunger Games: Catching Fire," he seems to be just another Capitol drone who comes up with sadistic ways to kill tributes. Yet, it turns out he's actually the leader of a rebel movement in the Districts and planning to free the tributes from the arena in that film. Then, in the "Mockingjay" movies, he serves as the head of propaganda for the rebellion.

Similarly, in "Sunrise on the Reaping," the younger Plutarch initially appears to be a television director who's all about attracting viewers. He has some compassion, naturally, yet he seems to care way more about serving the games and, in doing so, advancing his own station. But it quickly becomes clear that Plutarch is not only interested in keeping the movie's protagonist, Joseph Zada's Haymitch Abernathy, alive, he also sees the young man as an opportunity to genuinely hurt the Capitol.

According to recent reports, that's right, even 25 years before the events of "Catching Fire," Plutarch was already a rebel at heart subtly working against President Snow's tyrannical government. After all, it's Plutarch who helps save Haymith by feeding him information before the games. At the same time, he, very un-heroically, uses the games to benefit his cause and is willing to throw others under the bus.

In this way, Plutarch is a whole lot like Luthen, a character who aids what eventually becomes the Rebellion while working behind enemy lines in "Andor." Both men recognize they're no one's idea of a hero, but they refuse to get out of the game. Instead, they burn their own lives for a day they know they'll probably never see.

The thing that makes Plutarch so interesting, particularly in "Sunrise on the Reaping," is how much he oscillates between making propaganda for the Capitol and building a rebellion. It was one thing when we found out Plutarch was a rebel at the end of "Catching Fire," but it's another to see him here, 25 years earlier, equally invested in taking down the Capitol and willing to live a double life, every day a performance.

It has been revealed that in many ways, he's even closer to the danger than Luthen Rael is in "Andor," as Plutarch directly deals with and personally knows President Snow. His role in the film echoes the the cloak-and-dagger thrills of "Andor," most notably the joys of watching the quiet yet extraordinary work of rebels whose names will be forgotten by history, as opposed to the hotshot heroes who fight in the open. When Haymitch turns to with despair and hopelessness, Plutarch reminds him that their efforts matter and nothing is inevitable, not even the Capitol. Like Luthen, Plutarch is a man armed with an unwillingness to yield and an eagerness to fight.

According to recent reports, indeed, Plutarch even has a speech toward the end of the film that echoes Luthen's epic speech from "Andor" Season 1, where he acknowledges he's not anyone's idea of a hero and knows it's likely he won't live to see the rebellion succeed. Plutarch recognizes that his mission failed in "Sunrise on the Reaping," but knows Haymitch has it in him to inspire others to rebel and that, one day, he will light the fire that can bring down tyranny. In the end, Plutarch's not a hero, either, but his investment in the rebellion is epic.

You can currently catch "Sunrise on the Reaping" in theaters.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Princess Kate Middleton has opened up in rare and deeply personal ways since announcing her cancer diagnosis, revealing what it was like for her to live through a serious illness.

Industry observers note that the Princess of Wales revealed in February 2024 that she was diagnosed with an undisclosed form of cancer, for which she completed a preventative round of chemotherapy. Kate revealed in January 2025 that she was in remission, since using her platform to speak about the emotional, physical and spiritual toll of a cancer diagnosis, treatment and ongoing recovery.

Scroll below for her most candid reflections on recovery:.

In an Instagram post shared January 14, 2025, Kate confirmed she was officially in remission.

Sources indicate that “It is a relief to now be in remission,” she wrote at the time. “And I remain focussed on recovery. As anyone who has experienced a cancer diagnosis will know, it takes time to adjust to a new normal.”.

Visiting The Royal Marsden that same month, Kate told staff, “You think treatment’s finished, crack on with that … daily tasks, but that’s still like a real challenge.”.

It has been revealed that she also acknowledged the ripple effect on loved ones, saying, “I feel like it’s sometimes for the loved ones around us. They need support just as much as I did as the patient.”.

During a visit to Colchester Hospital in Essex in July 2025, Kate offered one of her most honest assessments of post-treatment life.

“You put on a sort of brave face, stoicism through treatment. Treatment’s done, then it’s like, ‘I can crack on, get back to normal,’ but actually, the phase afterwards is really, really difficult,” she said, while speaking with local patients. “You’re not necessarily under the clinical team any longer, but you’re not able to function normally at home as you perhaps once used to. Someone to help talk you through that, show you and guide you through that sort of phase that comes after treatment, I think is really valuable.”.

Recent findings suggest that she continued, “It’s a roller-coaster, it’s not smooth, like you expect it to be. But the reality is you go through hard times.”.

After completing the National Three Peaks Challenge in June 2026, Kate explained via Instagram why cancer care has to go beyond medicine.

“Cancer doesn’t just affect the body. It changes how you think and feel and profoundly affects every aspect of life. I know this personally, and that the journey through and beyond treatment requires more than medicine alone,” Kate wrote via Instagram. “Healing, whether personal or collective, is not just about fixing what is wrong. It is about finding balance in how we live. Between effort and acceptance, between control and trust, between thinking and simply being. Because in the end, bravery isn’t just about pushing forward. It is about knowing how to stay grounded, connected and present, no matter the terrain or landscape you are walking.”.

Speaking to Country Life for a profile published in November 2026, Kate revealed what she was told in the hospital about the road ahead.

Industry observers note that “I was told in hospital that my recovery would not be linear, there will be good days and bad days, that it will take time,” she told the outlet. “This is the same in nature. It shows us that periods of rest, reflection and renewal are equally as important as moments of growth.”.

She also credited the outdoors with helping her heal on a deeper level.

It has been revealed that “Yes, serious illness creates a lot of physical challenges, but there is also a deeper part to all of us. Nature has allowed me to find a deeper connection to my mind, body and spirit,” Kate explained. “I think that’s because nature offers something unique. It doesn’t ask anything of us. It doesn’t judge us or expect us to perform. It simply allows us to be. It really has been my sanctuary and a place I’ve instinctively wanted to go.”.

Kate got frank about how illness reshapes a person in a trailer for her 2026 documentary, Heal.

It has been revealed that “Cancer does change you, it changes your body, it changes you physically,” she noted. “There’s a much, much deeper part to what a cancer diagnosis shifts in you.”.

The princess secretly filmed the project while taking on the Three Peaks Challenge, with all proceeds from Heal going to the Royal Marsden Cancer Charity.

In a voiceover, Kate added, “You know healing is a journey, how to reconnect with the things you once knew and how to find a sense of hope and joy alongside uncertainty. It’s clear we’re not meant to carry life’s challenges alone. Things can renew and grow. Often it is through pain that we realize there’s a greater beauty that lies beyond that.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, queen Elizabeth II and Prince Philip married in 1947, going on to make history by achieving the longest marriage of any British sovereign couple.
  • November 2, 1947: Queen Elizabeth—then Princess Elizabeth—with Prince Philip, Duke of Edinburgh, King George VI and Queen Elizabeth (right) and members of the immediate and extended Royal Family at Buckingham Palace after their wedding.
  • Industry observers note that the Queen and Prince Philip’s love story began back in 1939.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, queen Elizabeth II and Prince Philip married in 1947, going on to make history by achieving the longest marriage of any British sovereign couple. Back then they were, of course, Princess Elizabeth and Prince Philip of Greece and Denmark, tying the knot in the rather austere years of post-war Britain. So, what really happened on their wedding day?

November 2, 1947: Queen Elizabeth—then Princess Elizabeth—with Prince Philip, Duke of Edinburgh, King George VI and Queen Elizabeth (right) and members of the immediate and extended Royal Family at Buckingham Palace after their wedding.

Industry observers note that the Queen and Prince Philip’s love story began back in 1939. Princess Elizabeth was just 13 years old; her dashing distant cousin, Prince Philip of Greece and Denmark, was five years her senior and about to join the Royal Navy. They met as she toured the Royal Naval College at Dartmouth; he was the young officer assigned to escort her around that day.

Determined to marry for love, Elizabeth was stated to be rather taken with Philip, who was described at the time as ‘handsome as any film star.’ The pair were soon writing letters to each other, and later, occasional chaperoned meetings took place.

The couple on their engagement, 1947.

According to recent reports, in 1946 Philip proposed in Scotland, and she immediately said yes. However, her father, King George, reportedly insisted the couple resist announcing their engagement until the Princess, who was just 20, was a little older. In the end, her parents gave in to her wishes, and Philip officially proposed to Princess Elizabeth in 1947, with a three-carat diamond ring he designed using stones taken from a family tiara that belonged to his mother, Princess Alice of Battenberg. It was created by London jeweller Philip Antrobus Ltd.

Princess Elizabeth with Philip Mountbatten on their wedding day.

The Royal Family were adamant that the wedding of Princess Elizabeth and Prince Philip would reflect the country’s post-war situation while also offering a chance for the nation to celebrate.

Like many brides at the time, Princess Elizabeth had to save her rationing coupons to buy the materials for her dress but was given an extra 200 from the government to help. While well-wishers generously sent their own to the royal, they had to be sent back as rules dictated that coupons could not be shared outside of households.

Sources indicate that designed by Norman Hartnell, Princess Elizabeth’s wedding dress was made from ivory silk, duchesse satin and silver thread; the dress featured crystals, 10,000 seed pearls, a fitted bodice, heart-shaped neckline, long sleeves and a 15-foot train. It was made in just seven weeks by 350 skilled women since the wedding took place only four months after the couple’s engagement announcement. Norman Hartnell also designed Elizabeth’s going-away outfit.

It has been revealed that princess Elizabeth’s wedding day tiara was called the Queen Mary Fringe Tiara. It had belonged to her grandmother, Queen Mary, and had been given to her as a wedding present in 1893. It was remade from a tiara/necklace that Queen Victoria had bought from Collingwood and Co.

Recent findings suggest that as Elizabeth was getting ready on the morning of the wedding, it snapped. Luckily, royal jeweler Garrard was apparently on hand to fix it, and the Queen later revealed, “I think he taped up the spring.”.

Princess Elizabeth’s other wedding day jewelry included two pearl necklaces. The shorter of the two necklaces was the “Queen Anne” necklace, mentioned to have belonged to Anne, the last Stuart Queen. The other was known as the “Queen Caroline,” and is said to have belonged to the wife of King George II. Both necklaces were left to the Crown by Queen Victoria and were given to Elizabeth as a wedding present by her father.

Sources indicate that all royal bridal bouquets contain myrtle from a myrtle bush planted by Queen Victoria at Osborne House. Princess Elizabeth’s also had white orchids and was laid on the grave of the Unknown Warrior at Westminster Abbey the day after the wedding.

There were eight bridesmaids at Princess Elizabeth and Prince Philip’s wedding: Princess Margaret, Princess Alexandra, Lady Pamela Mountbatten, Diana Bowes-Lyon, Lady Elizabeth Lambart, Margaret Elphinstone, Lady Caroline Montagu-Douglas-Scott, and Lady Mary Cambridge.

Her two pages were Prince William of Gloucester and Prince Michael of Kent, both aged five at the time.

The bridesmaids were given silver Art Deco-style compacts with the couple's initials and a crown engraved on the lid, set with five cabochon sapphires.

The Duke of Edinburgh's best man was David Mountbatten, the Marquess of Milford Haven.

Knowing that Elizabeth hated cigarettes, Prince Philip reportedly gave up smoking on the morning of his wedding “suddenly and apparently without difficulty,” according to his valet, John Dean.

The wedding took place at Westminster Abbey on November, 20th, 1947 at 11:30 a.m. Princess Elizabeth was the 10th member of the Royal Family to be married at Westminster Abbey.

Princess Elizabeth and Prince Philip walking down the aisle of Westminster Abbey, followed by their bridesmaids and pages.

There were 2,000 guests in attendance, including the likes of the King of Iraq, Princess Juliana and Prince Bernhard of the Netherlands and the Hereditary Grand Duke of Luxembourg and Princess Elisabeth of Luxembourg. The ceremony was broadcast on the radio to millions of listeners.

Together with her father, Princess Elizabeth left Buckingham Palace in the Irish State Coach. (In her later years, it had been Queen Victoria’s state carriage of choice, as she declined to use the Gold State Coach following the death of Prince Albert.).

The wedding ceremony was officiated by the Archbishop of Canterbury, Geoffrey Fisher, and the Archbishop of York, Cyril Garbett.

The organist and Master of the Choristers at the Abbey, Australian William Neil McKie, was the director of music for the wedding and there were 91 singers; the abbey choir was joined by the choirs of the Chapel Royal and St George's Chapel in Windsor.

The service started with a specially composed fanfare by Arnold Bax and finished with Felix Mendelssohn's “Wedding March,” with ceremony hymns including “Praise, my Soul, the King of Heaven” and “The Lord's my Shepherd.”.

The bride and groom knelt on orange boxes covered in pink silk at the altar as a nod to post-war austerity.

On the day of the wedding, Philip was given the title of Duke of Edinburgh by his father-in-law, King George VI. After the Queen ascended the throne in 1953, she made the decision in 1957 to make Philip a prince of the UK, in addition to his dukedom.

The wedding rings were made from a nugget of Welsh gold which came from the Clogau St David's mine, near Dolgellau.

According to Royal biographer Ingrid Seward, who wrote Prince Philip: Revealed, Philip had a secret message inscribed inside his wife's wedding band, a message that only the engraver, Queen Elizabeth, and her husband knew the contents of.

After the service, a wedding breakfast was held in the Ball-Supper Room at Buckingham Palace for 150 guests only, with Filet de Sole Mountbatten, Perdreau en Casserole and Bombe Glacée Princess Elizabeth on the menu.

During the breakfast, the string band of the Grenadier Guards played music while guests were greeted with individual posies of myrtle and white Balmoral on their place settings as the wedding favors.

The couple waving from the balcony of Buckingham Palace.

Famously, the newlyweds went onto the balcony at Buckingham Palace to wave to the huge crowds on the Mall.

Although the royal couple received 11 wedding cakes, the official traditional fruit cake was baked by McVitie and Price and was four tiers and nine feet high. The wedding cake was decorated with both coats of arms, including the monograms of the bride and groom, sugar-iced figures of their favorite activities, and regimental and naval badges.

Mr Schur, chief confectioner at McVitie and Price, putting the final touches to the wedding cake.

The newlyweds cut the cake using the Duke's Mountbatten sword, which was a wedding present from the King.

According to recent reports, over 10,000 people sent telegrams congratulating Elizabeth and Philip, and around 2,500 wedding presents were sent from around the world. These included a cloth from Mahatma Gandhi that he’d woven himself, which Queen Mary mistook for an “indelicate” loincloth.

After their wedding breakfast, Princess Elizabeth and Prince Philip headed to Waterloo station, joined by Elizabeth’s corgi, Susan, catching a train to Hampshire to spend their wedding night in Broadlands, the home of Philip's uncle, Earl Mountbatten.

The rest of their royal honeymoon was spent at Birkhall on the Balmoral Estate in Scotland.

Princess Elizabeth and Prince Philip being showered with rose petals as they leave Buckingham Palace, London, for their honeymoon.

Tech Report: 25 Years Later, Dragon Quest’s Island-Hopping Epic Gets Better in Every Port

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the Dragon Quest franchise has been around for longer than some of us have been alive, and its first entry in 1986 was one of the JRPG genre’s pioneers.
  • Industry observers note that in North America, Dragon Warrior 7 (the last entry in the series to bear that localized title), arrived after two previous installments weren’t released outside Japan.
  • Dragon Quest 7 spent a long time in development and arrived late enough in the original PlayStation’s life cycle that it felt decidedly old-fashioned by the time any of us got the chance to play it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the Dragon Quest franchise has been around for longer than some of us have been alive, and its first entry in 1986 was one of the JRPG genre’s pioneers. Over the years, the launch of a new title in the series has been a substantial deal, especially in Japan. Before players missed work to play Grand Theft Auto 6, they were using sick days to topple wicked dragonlords.

Industry observers note that in North America, Dragon Warrior 7 (the last entry in the series to bear that localized title), arrived after two previous installments weren’t released outside Japan. Interest had waned. When the game hit stores on Nov. 1, 2001, it was as difficult to find as its NES predecessors had been. And when loyal fans finally tracked it down, we wound up being disappointed. But over the years, Square Enix has made some adjustments and tried again on multiple occasions. Happily, each newly introduced release of Dragon Quest 7 gets better than the one before it.

Dragon Quest 7 spent a long time in development and arrived late enough in the original PlayStation’s life cycle that it felt decidedly old-fashioned by the time any of us got the chance to play it. The visuals were a step above anything the Super Nintendo offered, finally rendered in 3D with a camera that players could rotate. But the experience still felt a bit like a step back compared to the flatter but more detailed environments of late PS1-era games like Final Fantasy 9. In some respects, it was a relic from a time many players had moved on from.

Sources indicate that the quest’s opening hours didn’t correct that first impression. I remember playing for three hours without encountering a single enemy mob, which just felt odd. In the typical Dragon Quest game from years prior, you could head outside the castle walls within a few short minutes. An hour into the adventure, you would have already battled dozens or even hundreds of monsters and leveled up your characters several times. Instead, I had to spend that time solving tedious puzzles.

Slow opening hours eventually gave way to a lengthy quest with plenty of appeal, but I didn’t actually stick around to experience those later events until Dragon Quest 7: Fragments of the Forgotten Past launched on the 3DS on Sep. 16, 2016 in the West. Despite making its debut on portable hardware, the newly introduced release offered a superior way to experience the adventure.

The single change I appreciated most was an update to the formerly tedious first few hours of play. The introductory dungeon, with all of its levers and backtracking, was gone. Introductory areas still ate up more time than I was accustomed to, but they fit within a single gaming session and left me with time — and enthusiasm — to progress to more interesting activities.

The 3DS version offered other enhancements, as well. The bottom screen provided a helpful glow when the player approached stone tablet shards, a major component of progression. Players had a lot less guesswork to find essential items, a smart adjustment that eliminated a lot of pointless frustration.

According to recent reports, another upcoming feature recapped the story, in case players stepped away for a few days, weeks, or longer. Accessible from the pause menu, a chronological log listed every major event that had occurred, along with hints about where to go next. (Later games in the series, all the way up to Dragon Quest 11, would keep this addition.) While exploring, party members might also offer suggestions if consulted, sparing players from some of the ambiguity that had been a franchise staple since its first installment.

In a recent development, quality-of-life enhancements didn’t stop there, either. The game also introduced enemy mobs players could see in the field as they explored. Leveling up required less grinding, and menus were modified and streamlined. A map on the bottom screen made it easy to spot nearby points of interest. Most importantly, players could make a quick save outside of churches if they needed to stop playing suddenly. For a portable game, that option was a must.

Sources indicate that dragon Quest 7 on the 3DS remained the best way to play the game for a decade, until Dragon Quest 7 Reimagined introduced in February 2026. Available on Switch, Switch 2, PlayStation 5, Windows PC, and Xbox Series X, the updated take on the classic adventure introduced a breathtaking new art style. Presented like a diorama, the gorgeous visuals paired nicely with quality voice acting to bring the world’s story to life like never before.

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

The newest release also introduced latest changes to the character vocation system, allowing party members to adopt two vocations at once and gain mastery in both of them. Changing a class no longer required a time-consuming visit to Alltrades Abbey, either. And on the world map, striking weaker monsters defeated them automatically with lesser rewards, a welcome compromise that eliminated the need to endure tedious skirmishes. There were other changes, as well, including multiple difficulty presets, a shared inventory, and auto-revive after battle for party members who perished in the fight.

Sources indicate that for RPG fans in 2026, these were smart adjustments. Few players appreciate busy work and random encounters that slow the pace more than necessary. It’s good to see developers revisiting past triumphs and modernizing them for contemporary audiences to enjoy. If at first you don’t succeed, try, try again. It certainly worked for Dragon Quest 7.

  • I’ve had the iPhone Duo for nearly two weeks now, and have officially decided to return it.
  • Recent findings suggest that I use my iPhone one-handed all the time, and based on my experience, iPhone Duo is clearly intended to be used with two hands.
  • In a recent development, perhaps over time I’d get used to needing two hands for most iPhone interactions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’ve had the iPhone Duo for nearly two weeks now, and have officially decided to return it. Here are the three main reasons why the Duo didn’t work out for me, but might for you.

Recent findings suggest that I use my iPhone one-handed all the time, and based on my experience, iPhone Duo is clearly intended to be used with two hands. You can use it one-handed, but for me it’s not nearly as comfortable as the iPhone 18 Pro. It’s too wide and too heavy to be used for long.

In a recent development, perhaps over time I’d get used to needing two hands for most iPhone interactions. But that would be a pretty significant shift for me, as there are so many situations when I don’t have both hands free.

Industry observers note that if you already use two hands with your iPhone regularly—perhaps because you have a Pro Max model—then the Duo’s one-handed experience likely won’t bother you. But the more I used the Duo, the more I found myself missing my iPhone 18 Pro.

The biggest value proposition of a foldable is that it’s a 2-in-1 product, letting you have a standard phone but also a tablet-sized display that fits in your pocket.

I totally get the appeal, and fully expected to love that hybrid design. But after two weeks of trying, I still struggled to find times when I actually wanted to unfold the Duo. And to be clear, that’s a me problem, not an matter with the Duo itself.

Recent findings suggest that I tried a bunch of apps on the inner display, and struggled to find use cases that—for me—made it worthwhile to open the Duo. But based on the feedback I’ve seen from most Duo owners, I’m very much in the minority.

It has been revealed that I know lots of people love the Duo for video, but I don’t watch much video on my iPhone. I almost never watch YouTube, TikTok, or Instagram Reels. And for shows and movies, I stick with my TV screen and an Apple TV 4K.

Multitasking support on iPhone Duo works really well. But when I found myself needing to multitask, I still reached for my iPad Pro with Magic Keyboard attached. A keyboard-free product can’t replace my main computer (nor would I expect it to), and the Duo screen was too small to comfortably work on it.

In a recent development, last year I bought an iPhone Air and absolutely loved it. Initially, the Air’s less capable camera system didn’t bother me, it was “good enough.”.

Industry observers note that after a few months though, I started missing the Pro camera system more. Then I learned that my wife was pregnant with twins, and I knew I wanted the best possible iPhone cameras to capture their early weeks and months. So I bought an iPhone 18 Pro in September.

I’ve been very impressed by iPhone 18 Pro’s Main camera upgrades, and it’s great having a Telephoto lens again too. Since having the best camera system is so crucial for me right now, I knew iPhone Duo couldn’t be my only iPhone.

Sources indicate that I initially planned to dual-carry the two models, using iPhone 18 Pro solely as a camera. But over and over I found myself wishing it was my only iPhone.

Recent findings suggest that I returned mine as well. Beautiful device, but functionally not very good.

Is the iPhone Duo camera good enough for most people? Probably so. But for this year at least, with my twins aging rapidly, it’s not quite right for me. If I loved the Duo for other reasons, I would just use both models. But since I didn’t, I’m happy to stick with the iPhone 18 Pro.

In closing, I want to explicitly state that I don’t think the iPhone Duo is a bad product, and this isn’t a “bad review.”.

The iPhone Duo just isn’t for me. I get the sense, though, that it’s lots of people’s favorite iPhone in years. Apple created its most unique latest iPhone model since the original, and there’s plenty to love about it. I’m very curious to see how popular foldables become over time compared to slab models, because each clearly offers pros and cons. But for me, at least right now, the iPhone 18 Pro is my model of choice.

It has been revealed that what has your iPhone Duo experience been like so far? Love it? Undecided? Let us know in the comments.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Welcome to Trekspertise, a series where we break down the technology, history, details, and decisions that make the Star Trek universe so complex — and so fun.

"Star Trek" is set in a world of professional officers who work on extraordinary faster-than-light starships and who devote their lives to society-bolstering missions of scientific study and diplomatic negotiation. Starfleet is hellbent on wreaking peace throughout the galaxy, trying to ensure that all sentient beings are locked into a well-oiled machine of mutual aid. Starfleet officers work strenuous shifts on their respective missions, devoted to the cause, 24 Earth hours a day, seven Earth days a week.

In a recent development, but a vital part of the "Star Trek" utopia is that officers get to rest at reasonable intervals. Officers may live by Starfleet's code, but they still get to clock out at the end of the day, and they still get to take shore leave when needed. /Film has previously written about the franchise's tradition of kooky shore leave episodes, wherein "Star Trek" characters run into wacky adventures, even when on vacation on seemingly placid resort worlds.

Recent findings suggest that the most commonly mentioned resort world in "Star Trek" is Risa, first mentioned in the "Star Trek: The Next Generation" episode "Captain's Holiday." In that episode, Captain Picard (Patrick Stewart) was forced to take a vacation somewhat against his will, and only aimed to read a few long books, James Joyce's "Ulysses" among them. Naturally, once on Risa, he not only learned about the planet's hedonistic, sex-positive culture, but also became embroiled in an Indiana Jones-like artifact-stealing plot with a sassy, roguish artifact dealer named Vash (Jennifer Hetrick), an awesome character that came to be in a sort-of love triangle with Picard and Q (John de Lancie).

But let's take a closer look at Risa and see what it's all about and how it functions.

Sex is quite free and open on Risa, and they even have their own code for attracting sex partners there. In "Captain's Holiday," Riker asks that Picard pick up a souvenir for him, a Horga'hn, which is a small wooden statue. Picard doesn't know what it is, so when he places it next to him by the pool, it attracts the attention of a comely Risa resort employee named Joval (Deirdre Imershein). When she flirts with him, Picard rebuffs her, which confuses her.

The Horga'hn, she has to explain, is a symbol of Risan sexuality, and putting it on display essentially means you're hot to trot. It's like putting an upside-down pineapple on your door during a cruise (and you can look that one up yourself). It turns out Riker was playing a little prank on Picard.

It has been revealed that risa isn't only about free sexuality, though. There are massage facilities, beaches, sun beds, and special climate-control technology keeps the entire world appropriately pleasant for most visiting humanoid species. The planet is designed to be endlessly pleasant and relaxing.

A lot of the planet's mechanics were described in the "Star Trek: Deep Space Nine" episode "Let He Who is Without Sin...," wherein Worf (Michael Dorn) takes a vacation to Risa with his then-girlfriend Dax (Terry Farrell). A bout of jealousy, and some personal complications, cause Worf to sabotage the planet's weather grid, causing it to rain heavily, interrupting all the world's outdoor activities.

Recent findings suggest that earlier, Worf had connected with some Puritanical anti-pleasure zealots who feel Risa is a symbol of how the Federation has become soft. Apparently not everyone likes Risa, nor Starfleet's insistence that everyone relax from time to time.

Of course, those Puritanical zealots are outliers, and Risa is not a hotly contested world, nor the center of any kind of serious "Star Trek"-wide politic. In both "Captain's Holiday" and "Let He Who is Without Sin..." it is mentioned that no weapons are allowed on the planet, so we know, at the very least, that Risa is just as devoted to peace as the rest of the Starfleet universe.

In a recent development, risa is mentioned a lot in the franchise, spoken of like Hawai'i or St. Barts, in that it's a desirable place to spend one's prolonged vacation. On "Star Trek: Enterprise," set a century prior to the original "Star Trek," the crew of the Enterprise become the first humans to visit Risa, showing that it was a resort world since before the Federation came into being. We know from snippets of dialogue throughout the franchise that Risa has a water park, some underground gardens for exploring, many professional masseuses, and a lagoon where it never rains.

In a recent development, but it seems that business is conducted there sometimes. In the "Next Generation" episode "The Mind's Eye," Geordi (LeVar Burton) plans to go there for an artificial intelligence conference. We never see them, but I can imagine that Risa has souped-up versions of Marriott ballrooms.

In a recent development, sharp-eyed Trekkies might have noticed that, in the pilot episode of "Star Trek: Starfleet Academy" (read our review here), a series set almost nine centuries after the events of "Next Generation," Risa was listed as a Federation world on a background screen. It seems that resort worlds will persist indefinitely.

Sources indicate that looking over the amenities, I think I'd like to go to Risa. Anyone got a line on tickets?

In case anyone has been wondering, Imagineers have been hard at work on the ride, and they’re finally giving fans a first look at the magic they’re crafting.

It has been revealed that the upcoming Indiana Jones attraction was confirmed back in September 2025 at Disney’s Destination D23 event in Orlando, Florida. The news was originally met with concern from Disney World enthusiasts. It’s always exciting to see a park get a new ride, especially Animal Kingdom, which presently has the fewest amount of rides out of the four parks. However, the introduction of Indiana Jones meant the loss of the beloved Animal Kingdom attraction Dinosaur.

Time heals most wounds, though, and now that the sting of losing Dinosaur has started to wane, most fans are finally getting excited for the new attraction. To further build excitement, Walt Disney Imagineering shared the following clip on its Instagram:.

A post shared by Walt Disney Imagineering & Disney Live Entertainment (@waltdisneyimagineering).

It has been revealed that I was definitely not thrilled about the Animal Kingdom changes at first, but I think I’m going to love this new version of Indiana Jones! Dare I say it puts the Indiana Jones temple at Disneyland to shame (and hopefully won't have to deal with brawls over line cutting).

I Honestly Never Thought I’d Live To See The Day Disney World Fixed One Broken Attraction.

It has been revealed that when the ride eventually opens sometime next year, guests will embark on an adventure alongside Indy that will take them to a temple that legend says has a water passageway that leads to an underworld protected by a mythic serpent. Imagineers are still keeping much of the actual ride experience under wraps for now. However, with two other cart-style Indiana Jones attractions at other Disney parks and reports that the Dinosaur ride is being rethemed instead of totally demolished, it’s safe to say that this version of Indiana Jones will take guests on a bumpy ride full of twists, turns, snakes (or serpents in this case), and adventure.

Sources indicate that indiana Jones and the Myth of the Jade Serpent will be found in the upcoming Tropical Americas expansion at Disney’s Animal Kingdom. Specifically, the thrill ride will be part of the Bonanche Bioreseve area of the expansion, which is being modeled after the Maya region. This will mark the second Indy attraction to explore Mayan culture, but the first in the United States.

Sources indicate that perhaps the most exciting thing about the upcoming ride is that real-life Indiana Jones actor Harrison Ford was used as the model for the attraction’s animatronic. While it’s not confirmed whether or not he’ll record lines too, I’m definitely hoping he will. And if he does, then this will definitely be the best Indy ride.

Your Daily Blend of Entertainment News.

Custom EQ is a feature that some AirPods users thought Apple would never ship, but iOS 27 adds it.

Industry observers note that with Custom EQ, Apple now lets you set your own sound profile for AirPods. Per Apple:.

AirPods are designed and engineered by Apple to faithfully represent music, TV highlights and movies, and calls. If you prefer a different sound profile, you can customize how AirPods represent any audio played.

Recent findings suggest that you can change the EQ by going to your AirPods’ settings ⇾ Audio & Routing ⇾ Equalizer ⇾ Custom. From here, you can adjust the sound profile for low, mid, and high frequencies.

Recent findings suggest that apple GymKit has been available for years, but only for Apple Watch. It lets you pair and sync workout data with compatible cardio equipment, like treadmills, ellipticals, indoor bikes, and more.

In iOS 27, GymKit expands to support iPhone using AirPods Pro 3’s heart rate sensor. My colleague Zac gave it a try:.

The setup is simple. I tapped my iPhone to the treadmill, picked Indoor Walk (Indoor Run is also offered), and started the workout from the treadmill. With GymKit, workout data is stored privately on iPhone and removed from the equipment.

It has been revealed that once the workout started, the treadmill received heart-rate data from AirPods Pro 3. Meanwhile, the Fitness app on iPhone received the treadmill’s distance, pace, incline, and calorie data. Treadmills know details that an iPhone and AirPods can’t know on their own, especially incline and precise belt distance.

AirPods Pro 3’s case includes the latest second-generation Ultra Wideband (UWB) chip, letting you find it with greater precision and step-by-step guidance right from your wrist.

According to recent reports, every year, Hallmark unveils a fresh collection of Keepsake Ornaments for the holidays, ensuring that everyone's Christmas tree is filled to the brim. But while some prefer traditional Christmas ornaments featuring Santa Claus, reindeer, snowmen, and all the usual holiday imagery, at /Film, we want our tree packed with pop culture.

That's why we're glad that Hallmark's 2026 Keepsake Ornaments collection has a batch of new ornaments for movie and TV enthusiasts. More specifically, we're always jazzed about the new line-up of ornaments inspired by both the "Star Wars" and "Star Trek" franchises. Each existing for decades and constantly adding new movies and TV demonstrates to their ongoing canon, "Star Wars and "Star Trek" have plenty of history to draw from when creating Christmas ornaments, and as technology has improved, the craftsmanship behind them has only gotten better.

Whether you're starting your Hallmark Keepsake Ornament collection for the first time or adding to the ever-growing ensemble of decorations, these are the best newly introduced Hallmark 2026 "Star Wars" and "Star Trek" Christmas ornaments.

Recent findings suggest that "Star Wars" has some of the coolest spaceships around, and Hallmark has been celebrating them for years. There are various versions of the Millennium Falcon, X-Wing, and all the various TIE Fighters out there from the collections for previous years, and 2026 is adding a couple more ships to the mix.

Sources indicate that first up, "The Mandalorian and Grogu" gets a upcoming ornament in honor of the Razor Crest that Din Djarin comes into possession of in the not-so-successful "Star Wars" movie. Personally, I don't think it's as cool as Mando's previous Razor Crest, and the yellow color makes it feel more like a space taxi than the cool ride of a bounty hunter, but if you're a "Star Wars" completionist, you probably need to have this one.

In a recent development, thankfully, Hallmark has also reached into the past for another "Star Wars" ship ornament by giving the B-Wing a proper decoration. The ship, which is featured in the Battle of Endor in "Return of the Jedi," is a personal favorite of mine, and it's nice to see it join the ranks of the other Rebel Alliance vessels.

Industry observers note that all right, technically, these aren't ships, but since they feature Luke Skywalker and Han Solo in the gunner seats of the Millennium Falcon for these ornaments inspired by "A Latest Hope," they belong here. These even have light and sound inspired by the exciting sequence where the characters take out a small swarm of TIE Fighters.

By the way, don't forget about the A-Wing from "Return of the Jedi" and the TIE Avenger from "Andor." Both ships were released in the 2025 collection, but they're still available this year.

"Star Trek: Picard" gave fans of "The Next Generation" much to be happy about, as it reunited many of the show's cast members for one final round of exploring the final frontier. Now, you can bring two of the show's ships home as Christmas ornaments.

First, there's the U.S.S. Titan-A from the third season of "Picard." Captain Liam Shaw (Todd Stashwick) assumed command of the ship until its crew met their fate. Hopefully, it will fare better just hanging around your Christmas tree.

Speaking of the Titan-A, the ship was reclassified as the Enterprise-G and placed under the command of Captain Seven of Nine, and here, it's turned into a metal ornament honoring its appearance from the final moments of "Picard" Season 3.

For those who like their "Star Trek" animated and with a little more laughs, "Lower Decks" offered both. Hallmark has given the show's ship, the U.S.S. Cerritos, its own ornament. It might be tasked with the less notable, second-contact missions, but it's still part of the "Star Trek" legacy. In fact, it's one of the most important ships in Federation history.

According to recent reports, no, you're not seeing double. Well, I guess you are. But these are actually two different "Star Trek" ornaments inspired by "Original Series" episodes. You have to pay close attention to detail on these Shuttlecraft ornaments, as one is the Einstein from "The Doomsday Machine" and the other is the Galileo from "The Galileo Seven." Each makes unique sounds, with the latter including a holiday message from Leonard Nimoy, recorded for an ornament all the way back in 1992.

There are endless "Star Wars" characters ready to be posed for placement on a Christmas tree, and these are the latest additions for 2026.

According to recent reports, first up, on the Imperial side, there's always a upcoming Darth Vader ornament, and this year, a signature moment from "Rogue One" is turned into one. This is where Vader indicates how deadly he is, taking out a small batch of Rebel Alliance troopers as he tries to chase down the stolen Death Star plans at the end of the movie. The ornament features lights and sounds that recreate this terrifying show of strength, and it's just plain cool.

Industry observers note that speaking of "Rogue One," the movie's hero, Jyn Erso (Felicity Jones), gets her own Hallmark Keepsake ornament. She's armed and ready to take on whatever Imperial troops come her way. However, she likely never had to deal with Snowtroopers, the Stormtrooper variant from "Empire Strikes Back," joining the Hallmark line-up this year. But you know who did have to deal with Snowtroopers? Luke Skywalker. Still, he never encountered them in "Return of the Jedi," which inspired this 2026 ornament of Luke in his signature Jedi outfit.

With far more time on television under its belt, the "Star Trek" franchise has plenty of characters ready to join the Christmas tree. This year's focus is mostly on ships, but there are a few familiar faces getting turned into ornaments for 2026.

First up, though this newly introduced Spock ornament is inspired by "Star Trek: The Original Series," it's actually depicting a moment never seen on the show. Instead, it takes a cue from a 1972 model kit, one of many that imagined adventures that happened off-screen, filling in gaps or taking artistic liberties during the show's popularity.

Sources indicate that elsewhere, we have Nurse Christine Chapel (Jess Bush) from "Star Trek: Strange Newly introduced Worlds," donning her medical white uniform. In addition, though not a new ornament this year, this one featuring Data from "Star Trek: The Next Generation" hails from back in 2023, and it's a fan favorite that's still worth picking up while it's available. The ornament even plays dialogue featuring Data's loving poem in honor of the cat named Spot.

All of these ornaments, and many more from movies and television, are available at Hallmark's website and its brick and mortar stores while supplies last.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that since the beginning of the week, the James Bond frenzy has shown no signs of stopping. On November 16, fresh Bond owners Amazon MGM Studios finally revealed the name of the actor who will succeed Daniel Craig as 007: Robert Pattinson. After years of speculation and months of intense rumors, the next James Bond now has a new face. Now, the next question on everyone’s mind: Who will be the next Bond girl?

The exception in thie great debate is Léa Seydoux. The actor, who seems to be everywhere this year, played Madeleine Swann in Craig's final Bond films, Spectre (2015) and No Time to Die (2021). Her magnetic performance made Madeleine an unforgettable Bond girl, especially since her character plays a decisive role in the arc of Craig’s character: at the end of No Time to Die, the famous spy sacrifices himself to save her and their daughter, Mathilde. For the first time since its creation in 1953 by British author Ian Fleming, the secret agent in Her Majesty’s service was gone.

Léa Seydoux and Daniel Craig pose as they arrive on the set of No Time To Die on September 09, 2019 in Matera, Italy.

In a recent interview on Vogue's The Run-Through podcast, Seydoux was candid about how little interest she had in her successor. “I don’t really care,” she noted with a laugh. “I don’t really care, guys. How can you?”.

Industry observers note that when pressed on who Pattinson's female lead might be, Seydoux expressed mixed feelings about the British spy's latest iteration. With the purchase of the Bond IP by Amazon, “It became American," Seydoux stated. “But I’m sure the movie will be great because it’s directed by Denis Villeneuve, who’s a very talented director. I’m sure he will do something great.”.

Industry observers note that the online megamart took control of the storied franchise in 2023, after which Amazon founder Jeff Bezos controversially sought feedback on the title character's casting via X. The announcement of Villeneuve as the next film's director brought things back from the brink.

It has been revealed that bezos, who confirmed that he was “very involved” in the film's casting process, also seems to give Seydoux pause. In an interview with Variety, she admitted “was a bit sad when I heard that it was sold (…) but now that it’s Denis, I was like, Oh, at least it’s him, so it will be cinema.”.

Denis Villeneuve, who directed Seydoux in Dune: Part Two, will release the final installment of this epic science-fiction trilogy will be on December 16. After that, he'll be free to focus on his next major project: reviving the world’s most famous secret agent. It remains to be seen who he will choose to star opposite Robert Pattinson as his female companion—but we know that despite her fondness for the director, Seydoux will not return: Just last month, the French actress told People “I really loved being on this franchise, but now it’s ... done.”.

Sources indicate that crime dramas often attract big stars, and MobLand is no exception. The Paramount+ series stars Tom Hardy as mob fixer Harry Da Souza, with Pierce Brosnan and Paddy Considine in supporting roles and Helen Mirren having a ball as the thoroughly evil matriarch of the Harrigan crime family.

Industry observers note that while families are complicated in even the best of circumstances, that's especially true of the Family. After you've watched the recently released second season of MobLand, try one of these other shows mixing crime and family (or Family) drama.

It has been revealed that theo James plays army officer Eddie Horniman (a name mentioned as often as possible), heir to the Horniman estate (there it is again) who, upon the death of his father, is named the Duke of Halstead. He learns that his dad was tied to various criminal enterprises, and that his scouse brother is millions of pounds in debt to a drug dealer. What else is the dapper, military-trained Duke to do but learn to navigate the violent underworld while looking cool? You won't be surprised to learn that this British crime drama comes from creator/writer/producer Guy Ritchie, who also has a hand in MobLand. Stream The Gentlemen on Netflix.

According to recent reports, another series from Taylor Sheridan (the Yellowstone guy), this pandemic-era hit stars Jeremy Renner as Mike McLusky, head of a family that’s been keeping the peace, through means fair and foul, in the title's organization town for decades. The "business" of the corrupt burg happens to be incarceration, and the McLuskys thrive when business is up, even if Mike has slightly different ideas about how to run things. The show deals broadly with systemic racism and inequality in the prison system, but mostly it's a modern-day western about bringing justice to a corrupt town. It will conclude with a fifth season, streaming in 2027. Stream Mayor of Kingstown on Paramount+.

Sources indicate that A consistently compelling combination of smart plotting and lurid sex and violence, Banshee stars Antony Starr as Sheriff Lucas Hood...kinda: He's actually a man recently released from prison who takes over that identity when the latest sheriff in the small town of Banshee is killed before anyone really has a chance to get to know him. It's all part of a complicated initiative to reunite with his lover Ana (Ivana Miličević), and to get back the $15 million in diamonds he lost when he went to jail—but the town is ruled over by various criminal factions, and being sheriff doesn't guarantee any kind of safety; rather, the opposite. Stream Banshee on HBO Max.

Industry observers note that mobLand creator Ronan Bennett previously made this acclaimed series that succeeds by maintaining a narrow scope—in this case, a single London council estate. Dushane (Ashley Walters) and Sully (Kane Robinson) are residents and drug dealers at Summerhouse, maintaining an increasingly precarious grip on the criminal element in the community. Most compellingly, the series maintains an extensive supporting cast of locals both in the drug trade and impacted by it, building a disturbingly compelling world. A little confusingly, the first couple of seasons were renamed Top Boy: Summerhouse when the show moved to Netflix, so you'll want to start there before moving on to plain ol' Top Boy. Stream Top Boy: Summerhouse on Netflix.

Based loosely on a nonfiction work investigating the Mafia-like Camorra in Campania, this show focuses on the head of the Savastano clan, Pietro Savastano (Fortunato Cerlino), and his ambitious lieutenant Ciro Di Marzio (Marco D'Amore). When Pietro is arrested at the series' outset, a civil war erupts between family members and among the factions vying for control. Gone are the suits and poker games of many a mob drama—this is a brutal, street-level take on organized crime that forsakes the typical trappings of the genre. Stream Gomorrah on HBO Max.

Recent findings suggest that I'm here for the Pierce Brosnan of it all, but there's also a very strong vibe match in this series that casts the one-time James Bond actor as the head of a literal crime family, even if this one's set in the American West. Adapting Philipp Meyer's 2013 Pulitzer Prize-nominated novel of the same name, the series follows Eli McCullough, a ruthless cattle baron making moves to get in on the burgeoning oil industry in the Rio Grande Valley of 1915. A parallel narrative sees Eli as a young man, kidnapped and raised among a Nʉmʉnʉʉ family. While his backstory lends the character welcome complexity, in the present, he's as determined to build his empire as he is to prepare his son and grandson to take over when he's gone. Stream The Son on Prime Video.

Tom Hardy playing a tough guy isn't terribly unexpected, but here the setting is London, just after the end of the War of 1812. Hardy plays James Delaney, who returns from Africa after ten years away (he says he'd been taken prisoner, but his story doesn't entirely add up) for the funeral of his father. Dad left nothing but a little hunk of land off of Vancouver, not worth much until the war's conclusion creates newly introduced maritime trade opportunities. Suddenly, the United States, Great Britain, and the East India Company all have eyes on the real estate, and all are willing to do whatever it takes to acquire it—and the stakes become clear once James realizes that his father's cause of death wasn't natural. Stream Taboo on Peacock and Tubi.

Best not ponder too much on the fact that this one's based on a video game, as its pedigree is only hinted at via the levels of action and violence (certainly compared to some of the other highlights on this list). Colm Meaney plays Finn Wallace, the absolutely indispensable leader of London's criminal underworld, a man who's been holding everything together for decades, until his shocking murder at the outset of the series (that's not a spoiler, and we spend more time with him via flashbacks). The completely random killing by someone who had no idea what he was doing begets chaos and open violence. Finn's son Sean (Joe Cole) has been raised to take his father's place, but local, Pakistani, and Albanian gangs all move in to take control from the Finn family in the power vacuum. Stream Gangs of London on AMC+.

The great Forest Whitaker stars as the real-life Bumpy Johnson, who returned from a prison sentence to find his neighborhood falling apart and in the grip of Italian mobsters. A more than capable crime boss in his own right, Johnson resolves to take on the Genovese crime family, eventually forming a tentative alliance with Malcolm X (Nigél Thatch and, later, Jason Alan Carvell). Johnson is the lesser evil as far as Malcolm and others are concerned, and a complicated figure as both crime lord and family man with aspirations of saving his neighborhood. The show will conclude with a two-hour finale, likely airing in 2027. Stream Godfather of Harlem on Hulu.

Sources indicate that adopted into an Italian organized crime family as a baby, Park Joo-hyung took on the name Vincenzo Cassano, eventually becoming a mafia consigliere. After his adoptive father Don Fabio dies, Fabio’s biological son comes gunning for his brother, whom he now sees as competition. Cassano flees to Seoul, on the hunt for a secret stash of money, and in the process discovers a love interest and a new adversary in a giant business conglomerate that definitely deserves to be taken down. An incredibly popular K-drama, this one definitely puts a unique spin on the tropes of the mob genre. Stream Vincenzo on Netflix.

#74214. Tech Report: Epic accuses Apple of withholding 122,000 documents, seeks daily fines

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (935 w)
📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 9to5mac ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Epic accuses Apple of withholding 122,000 documents, seeks daily fines

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (935 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, in a new filing, Epic Games accuses Apple of withholding more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions and asks the court to impose daily fines until the tech giant complies.
  • As a result of the lawsuit Epic Games brought against Apple in 2020, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers ruled in 2021 that Apple would have to, among other things, allow developers to direct users to alternative payment methods outside the App Store.
  • Apple responded by allowing external payment links, but imposed a commission of up to 27% on purchases made through them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, in a new filing, Epic Games accuses Apple of withholding more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions and asks the court to impose daily fines until the tech giant complies. Here are the details.

As a result of the lawsuit Epic Games brought against Apple in 2020, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers ruled in 2021 that Apple would have to, among other things, allow developers to direct users to alternative payment methods outside the App Store.

Apple responded by allowing external payment links, but imposed a commission of up to 27% on purchases made through them. This, in turn, led the court to find Apple in civil contempt for violating its injunction. Since then, Apple has been trying to overturn that ruling, a dispute that has now reached the Supreme Court.

According to recent reports, at the same time, district court proceedings will determine what, if any, commission Apple may charge on purchases made through external payment links. Apple submitted its proposal on August 13, calling for commissions ranging from 5% to 15%, and Epic is expected to respond after Apple completes its document production.

In a new filing, however, Epic is accusing Apple of withholding more than 122,000 documents related to how it arrived at its proposed commission rates.

One of the many aspects of the ever-sprawling battle between Epic Games and Apple centers on document production.

In its new filing, Epic claims Apple has repeatedly failed to produce documents detailing how it arrived at its proposed commission rates, accusing the company of withholding materials it deems irrelevant to the proceedings.

Epic argues that Apple previously used questionable claims of attorney-client privilege to withhold documents during the contempt proceedings, but has now changed tactics.

Apple does introduce one tactical change from its prior campaign of delay. Whereas during the contempt proceeding Apple used bogus claims of privilege to evade its discovery obligations, this time Apple withholds thousands of documents on bogus claims of irrelevance. For example, Apple is withholding well over 99% of the documents returned by running the agreed-to search terms on the files of the four custodians Apple states decided on the proposed fee (Tim Cook, Eddy Cue, Carson Oliver, and Kevan Parekh (Apple’s newly introduced CFO)) and three other key individuals (Nate Barton, Alex Roman, and Phil Schiller). Apple claims these withheld documents are not relevant to this proceeding-even though they hit on case-specific terms such as “proffer,” “contempt,” “injunction,” and “link-out.” To put this into context, while Apple produced 632 custodial documents returned by these search terms (including families), Apple is withholding over 122,000 based on a claim of non-responsiveness. Moreover, Apple claims that it completed its production from the files of these custodians, yet its production does not include a single substantive email discussing the rates Apple ultimately proposed; any notes or communications reflecting what occurred at any meeting where these rates were discussed or decided; any internal analysis of the financial or business impact of the proposed commissions; any App Store profit and loss statements; or any support for Apple’s assertion that its incremental link-out costs are “essentially zero.”.

Epic goes on to state that “Apple cannot be trusted to fix this problem on its own,” proposing instead that the court order Apple to produce all non-privileged documents matching the search terms agreed upon by both parties, regardless of whether Apple considers them relevant.

It has been revealed that under this proposal, Apple would still be allowed to review documents for attorney-client privilege, but it would be up to Epic to determine which of the remaining documents are relevant to the case. Epic argues that existing confidentiality protections would prevent it from using any of the information for purposes unrelated to the litigation.

Given Apple’s position, Epic respectfully submits that the Court should order Apple to produce to Epic all non-privileged documents that hit on the Parties’ agreed-upon search terms, so that Epic itself can sift the wheat from the chaff. Doing so will avoid further delays and place no burden on Apple. Moreover, doing so would not raise any of the concerns that required Special Master involvement in the prior proceeding, namely concerns around the production of privileged Apple information to Epic. Under Epic’s proposed remedy, Apple would be allowed to continue its review for privilege. For these reasons, Epic asks this Court to order Apple to produce all non-privileged documents that hit on any of the Parties’ agreed-upon search terms by December 2, 2026 (one week after Apple’s deadline to substantially complete production), irrespective of any relevance or responsiveness assessment.

Finally, though Epic does not propose a specific dollar amount, it “asks that the Court impose on Apple a daily monetary sanction for each day Apple fails to comply after December 2, 2026.”.

According to the court docket, a hearing on Epic’s motion was initially scheduled for November 24 before Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers. However, a new order filed today, which has yet to be made public, refers the discovery dispute to a magistrate judge and includes a notice terminating deadlines and hearings.

Netflix’s (Very) R-Rated 45-Episode Sci-Fi Anthology Doesn’t Get the Attention It Deserves

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In 1981, the animated cult classic Heavy Metal fused hard rock and metal music with sci-fi and fantasy storytelling into an anthology film full of rich hand-drawn animation and rotoscoping from a dedicated team of animators.
  • Almost four decades after the film’s release, filmmakers David Fincher and Tim Miller attempted to reboot Heavy Metal, which eventually morphed into the Netflix sci-fi anthology, Love, Death & Robots.
  • Black Mirror may be Netflix's most famous sci-fi anthology, but if you're looking for something a little more hardcore, Love, Death & Robots is the perfect show for you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 1981, the animated cult classic Heavy Metal fused hard rock and metal music with sci-fi and fantasy storytelling into an anthology film full of rich hand-drawn animation and rotoscoping from a dedicated team of animators. Some of these stories were adapted from Heavy Metal magazine, which has been publishing boundary-pushing genre tales with explicit content since 1977.

Almost four decades after the film’s release, filmmakers David Fincher and Tim Miller attempted to reboot Heavy Metal, which eventually morphed into the Netflix sci-fi anthology, Love, Death & Robots. Although the series inevitably carries the DNA of Heavy Metal and its contemporaries, Love, Death & Robots carves out its distinct identity over 45 exceptional episodes. While sci-fi is at the heart of these anthology tales, the show blends everything from horror to comedy to complement the bountiful art styles that are a celebration of animation as a medium.

Black Mirror may be Netflix's most famous sci-fi anthology, but if you're looking for something a little more hardcore, Love, Death & Robots is the perfect show for you.

Anthologies inevitably contain some middling episodes that miss the mark, and this is also the case with Love, Death & Robots. But the highs are so impressive that it's easy to overlook any episodes that are narratively shallow (despite still being gorgeously animated).

An example of an exceptional episode is “Zima Blue,” based on Alastair Reynolds’ acclaimed short story about an enigmatic artist named Zima who uses a specific shade of cyan blue in his artwork. While “Zima Blue” works with a surprising twist, the episode is about the existential search for purpose in life. It is also beautiful to look at, thanks to a clever mix of 2D and 3D animation that makes everything feel surreal.

Another standout is “Jibaro,” where a group of armored conquerors stumbles upon a bejeweled siren in a lake. Except for a deaf knight named Jibaro, all the men are driven into a violent frenzy after hearing the woman’s piercing scream. Jibaro approaches the woman, and the two are drawn together in a moment of intense attraction. Unfortunately, Jibaro’s greed overtakes any semblance of empathy, turning the episode into a metaphor for the violation that comes with colonialism. This 15-minute short uses hyperrealistic CGI with keyframe animation and motion-capture to evoke a jarring, dream-like quality that is worth revisiting.

The most interesting aspect of Love, Death & Robots lies in its explicit, no-holds-barred tone and subject matter. Explosive violence and casual nudity aside, the show doesn’t shy away from exploring humanity’s troubling tendency to play god, which informs our relationship with machines. Episodes like “Three Robots” and “Bad Traveling” focus on our moral failings, while “Sonnie’s Edge” and “Snow in the Desert” dissect a post-humanist landscape and the blurred lines between flesh and machinery. Love and obsession are also major themes, along with mortality, revenge, grief, and cosmic terror.

This wide scope of storytelling makes Love, Death & Robots feel fresh and inventive, even when the odd episode starts feeling like an exercise in style over substance. The show’s fourth volume proves how far it has come in terms of prioritizing quality over quantity, overcoming animation and storytelling challenges with smart, impressive short episodes. Some episodes, like “Spider Rose,” are follow-ups of previous stories, piling on unexpected themes and character conflicts that are refreshing to watch. The deaths are still gory and ultra-violent, but this artistic excess pays off in the end.

According to recent reports, love, Death & Robots has something for everyone. You can expect hard science fiction, war horror, nihilistic drama, and comedy to weave a perfectly bingeworthy series that takes pride in its stylistic animation. Live-action segments are also thrown in for good measure for those who seek variety. Not every episode is a hit, but when the show does make an impression, it leaves an indelible mark by setting higher standards for animated anthologies of a similar mold.

Love, Death & Robots can be streamed on Netflix.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, if you thought keeping up with King's literature was tough, take a look at how many times his work has been adapted for the screen.
  • Sources indicate that the 2004 film adapts the author's novella "Secret Window, Secret Garden" and stars Depp as an author accused of plagiarism by a shifty individual who makes his life hell.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Johnny Depp is presently trying to revive his Hollywood career with "Ebenezer." But back in the early 2000s, he was riding high in the wake of his debut "Pirates of the Caribbean" performance as Captain Jack Sparrow. Oddly enough, he then followed up 2003's "Pirates of the Caribbean: The Curse of the Black Pearl" with a little-known Stephen King adaptation that's worth a watch ... if you can tolerate extended Depp exposure.

According to recent reports, if you thought keeping up with King's literature was tough, take a look at how many times his work has been adapted for the screen. To date, the prolific author has written more than 70 books and 200 short stories, and while the screen adaptations don't outnumber the literary originals, there's still a heck of a lot of them — with "Secret Window" belonging to the long list of forgotten Stephen King adaptations list.

Sources indicate that the 2004 film adapts the author's novella "Secret Window, Secret Garden" and stars Depp as an author accused of plagiarism by a shifty individual who makes his life hell. Unfortunately — and I can't stress this enough — this movie features Johnny Depp, who has managed to disgrace himself in an impressive amount of ways in recent years. But long before the lawsuits, troubling accusations of abuse, and "epic bromance" (to quote Vanity Fair) with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (yes, the man widely thought to be responsible for the violent death of journalist Jamal Khashoggi), Depp was kinda cool. It's sort of hard to imagine if you didn't grow up in the actor's heyday, but it's true, I promise. Unfortunately, "Secret Window" didn't do much to help him maintain his goth boy appeal or Captain Jack Sparrow-induced megastar charm. But it was a good enough King adaptation that's worthy of a revisit.

Stephen King's "Secret Window, Secret Garden" originally appeared in the 1990 novella collection "Four Past Midnight." It followed Morton Rainey, a Maine-based writer who's accused by John Shooter, a man from Mississippi, of having stolen his story for his own recent novella. After Mort denies having plagiarized anything, Shooter takes things up a notch, terrorizing the writer until he eventually comes to a stunning realization.

Sources indicate that the film adaptation is written and directed by David Koepp, who has also penned movies as varied as "Jurassic Park" and "Panic Room" and would thereafter reunite with Johnny Depp on the 2015 box office flub "Mortdecai." Their first collaboration wasn't a triumph, either, but it did have a fun performance by John Turturro and was interesting because it adapted one of King's stories in which the lead character is essentially a version of the author. (Perhaps that's why he didn't make a cameo in "Secret Window.").

Sources indicate that koepp's movie shifts the action from Maine to upstate New York. There, Mort (Depp) finds his wife, Amy Rainey (Maria Bello), in bed with another man before retreating to his cabin and sinking into depression. While there, he's visited by Shooter (Turturro), who accuses the writer of having plagiarized his short story "Sowing Season." When Mort reads Shooter's manuscript, he's shocked to find it's basically the same narrative as his own story "Secret Window." Still, he maintains his innocence, prompting a campaign of terror from Shooter. Turturro's mystery man promises to "burn [Mort's] life and every person in it like a cane field in a high wind," which essentially means harassment and even murder.

Aside from shifting the setting, "Secret Window" makes significant changes to Stephen King's original novella, especially in terms of the ending, which I won't spoil here. Suffice it to say, it's not all that hard to spot the twist coming in "Secret Window." Perhaps that had something to do with the film earning a less than stellar 46% critic score on Rotten Tomatoes.

Recent findings suggest that "Secret WIndow" is worth watching for John Turturro, a sort-of-interesting premise, and according to the critics, at least, for Johnny Depp himself. Antonia Quirke of the London Evening Standard praised David Koepp for choosing to "indulge in a riveted idolatry of his star," who, according to the critic, was the best thing about the movie. Quirke wasn't the only one, either. The Latest York Observer's Andrew Sarris thought Depp had "demonstrate[d] once again that he never disappoints as an actor, even in something as fraudulent as 'Secret Window.'" Richard Roeper, on the other hand, was quite taken with what he described as a "thriller that doesn't compromise itself with a pat Hollywood ending" while Mick LaSalle of the San Francisco Chronicle found "Secret Window" to be an "eerie, playful thriller and an all-around entertaining time at the movies.".

The film ranked 34 out of 59 on /Film's ranking of every Stephen King movie, which isn't bad. Unfortunately, there's no way around the Depp factor. If you can look past his aforementioned indiscretions (to put it mildly), then by all means give "Secret Window" a go. If, however, you're nauseated by the prospect of Depp attempting a "Pirates of the Caribbean" comeback, maybe give it a miss. On the other hand, if you like the idea of Depp being menaced by a murderous crackpot, have a look.
