Apple today announced that App Store prices for apps and In-App Purchases will be adjusted in five countries starting December 3, following changes in taxes and foreign exchange rates. Here are the details.

In a new post published on its developer portal, Apple today unveiled a series of changes to App Store pricing, as well as updates to tax rules affecting developers and customers in several countries, including the US.

According to the manufacturer, developers’ proceeds from eligible app and In-App Purchase sales have been adjusted in four countries, reflecting the following tax updates:.

Specific to Botswana and Rwanda, Apple said that “Exhibit B of the Paid Applications Agreement will be updated to indicate that Apple collects and remits applicable taxes.”.

Apple added that a upcoming “Software as a Service (SaaS)” attribute is now available for several App Store tax categories, including App Store Software, Software Training Material, Dating, and Boosting. Developers can review and enhancement their tax category selections in App Store Connect.

Additionally, starting December 3, developers who rely on Apple’s automatic pricing adjustments will see changes to app and In-App Purchase prices in:.

Apple usually makes these adjustments to account for changes in taxes and foreign exchange rates, and notes that prices won’t change in countries selected as the base storefront, for auto-renewable subscriptions, or in storefronts where developers manually manage their prices.

The announcement does not go into detail about how much prices will change in each country, or whether they will increase or decrease.

Finally, starting January 1, 2027, apps and In-App Purchases in the SaaS, App Store Software, Software Training Material, Dating, and Boosting categories will become subject to sales and use taxes in California.

Apple noted that “prices on the United States storefront are displayed to customers exclusive of taxes, so the tax change will not affect them,” but added that while developers’ proceeds will remain unchanged, “the total amount customers are charged, inclusive of tax, may increase.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This article contains spoilers for "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.".

The original "Hunger Games" raised the stakes for Katniss Everdeen (Jennifer Lawrence) and Peeta Mellark (Josh Hutcherson) by establishing that tributes from their home, District 12, have only ever won the Hunger Games twice in 74 years. That means they only have one mentor, the alcoholic Haymitch Abernathy (Woody Harrelson), unlike other Districts' tributes that have two mentors each.

Recent findings suggest that "Hunger Games" author Suzanne Collins told the story of the first District 12 victor in "The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes" — Lucy Gray Baird (Rachel Zegler), who won the 10th Hunger Games decades before Katniss was born and then vanished. Now, "Sunrise on the Reaping" tells how Haymitch won his own Hunger Games.

Haymitch was at a disadvantage before he even entered the arena, since there were no District 12 victors available to mentor him. To address this concern, the Capitol "borrowed" victors from other districts and assigned them to mention Haymitch and his fellow District 12 tributes. Those mentors are Mags Flanagan (Lili Taylor) and Wiress (Maya Hawke), younger versions of characters who first appeared in the second "Hunger Games" film/book, "Catching Fire.".

It has been revealed that wiress (played by Amanda Plummer back in "Catching Fire") isn't in the movie much, but "Hunger Games" fans will likely recognize the actress playing her. The daughter of Ethan Hawke and Uma Thurman, Maya Hawke is one of the more charming "nepo babies" to come out of recent Hollywood.

Hawke has been acting in film and television since 2017, when she played Jo March in a BBC production of "Little Women." In 2019, she not only appeared in Quentin Tarantino's "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" as "Flower Child," a member of the Manson family; she also got her big break. 'Ghost Accounts' Are Putting Your Security at Risk, but You Can Protect Yourself

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (473 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • These so-called "ghost accounts"—all the old, forgotten logins that are still active but not in use—could expose your data in the event of a breach, increasing the risk of your information being used in malicious ways.
  • As McAfee describes, ghost accounts may retain lots of sensitive data, such as your contact details (phone numbers, emails, and addresses), purchase histories, payment details, and passwords.
  • You're less likely to be keeping tabs on activity in older accounts, which may also have weak or reused passwords that haven't been updated in years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

These so-called "ghost accounts"—all the old, forgotten logins that are still active but not in use—could expose your data in the event of a breach, increasing the risk of your information being used in malicious ways. That's why it's important to go through the effort to find and delete dormant accounts. Here's how to get started.

As McAfee describes, ghost accounts may retain lots of sensitive data, such as your contact details (phone numbers, emails, and addresses), purchase histories, payment details, and passwords. While this doesn't mean your information is sure to be compromised, the more places it lives, the more opportunities there are for bad actors to get ahold of it.

You're less likely to be keeping tabs on activity in older accounts, which may also have weak or reused passwords that haven't been updated in years. If that company or service experiences a data breach, not only is your stored data there exposed, but that information (including your password) can be used to access other accounts using tactics like credential stuffing and phishing. This also increases the risk of identity theft, as threat actors can use your name, birth date, and other information to open fraudulent accounts.

Recent findings suggest that unfortunately, finding and removing forgotten accounts can be tedious. If you have a password manager, the easiest way to start is to audit older items as well as look at security reports that identify weak or reused passwords, as well as data breaches that have impacted your accounts. If you've saved credentials in your browser keychain, go through the same process to find dormant accounts.

Next, audit accounts you've created using single sign-on, such as Google, Apple, or Facebook. For Google, this is under Account Settings > Linked apps. For Apple, go to System Settings > [Your Name] > Sign in with Apple on your Mac (or the same path in the Settings app on iOS). On Facebook, this is under Settings & privacy > Apps and websites. Disconnecting these accounts won't automatically delete them, but you can add them to the list to take action. Finally, you can search your email(s) on HaveIBeenPwned and username(s) on IDCrawl or WhatsMyName to find dormant accounts.

Once you've found accounts you no longer use, the next step is to deactivate or delete them, which you may be able to do through the settings or by reaching out to customer support. At the very least, remove all identifying information and change the password, and if possible, update the address to a burner using your browser's or password manager's hide-my-email feature. If you no longer have access to an old account, that doesn't mean it's been deactivated and your information removed, so you may need to reach out to customer support to find out how to access and delete it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

HBO rolled out on November 8, 1972, and has since produced some of the finest demonstrates in television history. It has also produced plenty of swiftly forgotten and overlooked curios, many of which are actually quite good. The Dustin Hoffman-led "Luck" was, according to critics at least, one example. This horse racing drama looked set to be another ongoing hit for the network until it was canceled following the deaths of three horses involved in production, bringing a tragic end to the show despite the fact it had already been renewed.

It has been revealed that david Milch began his career on "Hill Street Blues" before co-creating one of the best shows of the 1990s in "NYPD Blue." That alone would be enough to make him a TV legend, but Milch wasn't done. He managed to steer clear of the ill-advised "NYPD Blue" spin-off "Public Morals," which was canceled after one episode, but he did oversee his share of short-lived crime series in "Brooklyn South," "Total Security," and "Big Apple." It wasn't until 2004 that he struck gold again with the HBO series "Deadwood," arguably the best Western TV show ever made. After that, however, Milch's career involved creating little-known series that came and went without making much of an impact.

It has been revealed that his 2006 series, "John from Cincinnati," was a strange affair that lasted just one season. "Luck," on the other hand, looked as though it could break the trend and go the distance. Set in the world of horse racing, the Hoffman-fronted series also benefited from the directorial talents of none other than Michael Mann, and became a critical hit, earning a second season renewal. But that second season never materialized after some unfortunate on-set events which forced HBO to cancel "Luck" despite the fact filming had already started on Season 2.

"Luck" was somewhat of a passion project for David Milch, who told the Los Angeles Times, "I've been thinking about doing a show like this for 25 years." The creator explained how his father had taken him to horse racing events since he was age five or six, and how he saw the horses as "heart-stopping beautiful." All of which just makes the story of "Luck" even more tragic.

Dustin Hoffman plays Chester "Ace" Bernstein, a gambler who after coming home after a three-year stay in federal prison immediately concocts a plan for revenge against those who helped put him away. His bodyguard, driver, and right hand man, Gus (Dennis Farina) acts as front for Ace's investment in race horse Pint of Plain. Meanwhile, Hoffman's gambler sets out to restore the failing Santa Anita racetrack as part of his plan for retribution. Nick Nolte also appears as a veteran trainer who now owns his own colt.

It has been revealed that "Luck" premiered in January 2012 to positive reviews and looked as though it might have the potential to become one of the best HBO reveals of all time. By the end of that month, the show had already earned a second season renewal. On January 31, 2012, the Los Angeles Times reported that HBO had ordered a further 10 episodes that were set to debut in January 2013, with production on the newly introduced season set to get underway in February. According to the outlet, the debut episode brought in 1.1 million viewers and the renewal was "hardly shocking" given Hoffman and Nolte's involvement. What was shocking, however, was that on March 14, 2012, the Los Angeles Times once again reported on the show, this time to announce it had been canceled altogether.

According to recent reports, "Luck" Season 1 earned an 82% certified fresh rating on Rotten Tomatoes, with critics praising the cast and writing in particular. But behind all this success, there was trouble brewing. People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (PETA) had been on top of HBO and "Luck" since January 2012, the month in which the show debuted. According to The Hollywood Reporter, the organization had written to the channel to enquire as to the treatment of horses used in the show, and had followed up on numerous occasions thereafter.

As a report from PETA explains, two horses were euthanized during production of the first season. According to the group, "older, arthritic horses had been used in dangerous (and deadly) racing sequences" leading to the two euthanizations. What's more, the report cites "insiders at Santa Anita Race Track" as having provided information about a third horse that died on-set. Rather than push on, HBO pulled the plug and "Luck" was added to the expansive list of the best reveals canceled after only one season.

According to recent reports, A statement from HBO (via the LA Times), read, "It is with heartbreak that executive producers David Milch and Michael Mann together with HBO have decided to cease all future production on the series 'Luck.'" The network claimed to have maintained "the highest safety standards throughout production," but acknowledged that "accidents unfortunately happen and it is impossible to guarantee they won't in the future." "Luck" Season 1 continued to air, but production on Season 2 was brought to an end despite plenty of footage having already been shot. Today, Season 1 remains available on HBO Max.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that most Stephen King novels dabble with incredibly grim subject matter. Owing to this, it is an impressive feat when an adaptation manages to push the boundaries of darkness even further. Quite a few movie and TV adaptations of the author's work have managed to defy expectations and deliver even bleaker stories. Case in point, 2007's The Mist leaves viewers with a completely hopeless ending.

While MGM+'s The Institute does not match the extremes of Frank Darabont's The Mist, it does push the darker elements of the original story to a newly introduced level. In season 1, The Institute felt more like a watered-down version of the original. It stayed true to the original themes and character beats of the book but featured less graphic violence and psychological horror.

From a visual standpoint, even The Institute season 2 is not too different. Despite its TV-MA rating, the show rarely pushes its disturbing imagery to match Stephen King's writing. In terms of storytelling, however, the show has officially exceeded the darker aspects of the book, which makes it even more compelling than it initially seemed.

In a recent development, in Stephen King's The Institute, the main young characters overcome the overarching evil forces towards the end. They take down the very facility that tortured them and emerge victorious in their battle for freedom. The Institute season 1's ending portrays something similar, where Luke and his friends destroy the titular facility, albeit with a few major losses.

However, in season 2, their victory is completely stripped. They soon realize that they are dealing with far bigger forces. The facility they destroyed was a mere pawn in a far bigger conspiracy. After jumping out of the proverbial frying pan in season 1, they realize they are now on the fire with powerful people deadset upon finding them.

Industry observers note that the main character, Luke, also came off as a steadfast hero. He always took a stand against the people running the Institute and did not hold himself back from going all-out against them. In season 2, he is cursed with the power of foresight. His precognition abilities improve, allowing him to see how his decisions could even get his friends killed.

Recent findings suggest that as a result, instead of throwing all caution to the wind, he makes some moral compromises and plays safe. He even betrays his friends, believing that it would help him save them from their imminent doom. Speaking of doom, The Institute season 2 also does not shy away from killing off one of season 1's main heroes, Wendy, in the very beginning.

These developments instantly establish the high and incredibly bleak stakes The Institute's main characters are now dealin with.

Expanding the original story of a complete book can always be a tricky endeavor. Even some of the greatest adaptations, like Game of Thrones, have suffered after extending beyond their source material. Fortunately, for The Institute, it followed a fairly generic and derivative storyline in season 1 while introducing some intriguing ideas.

Recent findings suggest that this paved the way for the series to become all the more compelling in season 2. So far, The Institute has been doing an incredible job of expanding ideas surrounding precognition, free will, and determinism in season 2. This allows the series to be even more thought-provoking than the original Stephen King book. It almost feels like a Philip K. Dick adaptation in its ongoing story beats.

Industry observers note that hopefully, moving forward, The Institute season 2 will only get better. Instead of treading the same path as its predecessor and relying on familiar ideas from the sci-fi genre, the Stephen King adaptation should take more creative risks and not shy away from being as dark (if not more) as the original book.

The Institute, released in 2025, follows 14-year-old genius Luke Ellis, who is kidnapped and wakes up at a mysterious facility filled with children possessing unusual abilities. Meanwhile, Tim Jamieson, a former police officer, seeks a fresh start in a nearby town, inevitably intertwining his fate with Luke's.

(Clearly Amazon, which took over the franchise in 2025, has other ideas.) As for the more cosmetic complaints, I guess those all come down to personal taste.

As for the Twilight-related concerns, I understand them because, when Pattinson was revealed as Batman back in 2019, I thought​​​​​​​ “Oh no, the Twilight guy? How could this guy, who seemed so…soft, be the Dark Knight?” I hated the idea. Then, a few months after the announcement, I saw the Robert Eggers film The Lighthouse and completely changed my mind.

The Lighthouse, which is at the moment streaming on HBO Max, is generally described as a horror film or as psychological horror with some fantasy elements, but I found it to be more of a comedy than anything else. I honestly think that, up until The Lighthouse, I’d literally never seen Pattinson in a movie before. Literally nothing I’d heard of with him had appealed to me, so it wasn’t Pattinson that lured me to The Lighthouse. Part of the reason I went to see The Lighthouse was Willem Dafoe, who I love. Another factor was a review I’d read by film critic Tim Grierson, who described​​​​​​​ the movie as “a terrific comedy about having a terrible roommate.” As a fan of The Odd Couple who regularly laments a lack of comedies in theaters, that was enough to convince me to check it out.

The Lighthouse really is just about two guys in a lighthouse dealing with the loneliness of the job, which requires them to be stuck at sea for weeks at a time. Dafoe plays a grouchy old sea-dog, while Pattinson is his young apprentice. The movie is a laugh riot, with lots of drinking, some wild singing, and both men becoming increasingly unhinged. One dreams he has sex with a mermaid, the other masturbates all the time, and both are brought to their breaking point by the end.

To be clear, nothing about Pattinson’s character in The Lighthouse made me think that he would be the perfect Batman. His character is a young man who’s green to this profession, but he’s a bit jaded from past failures and secretive about his personal life. He's fairly serious at the beginning, but he jumps into a rage more and more as the film progresses. I guess there’s some overlap with Bruce Wayne/Batman there, but not very much.

Industry observers note that the reason why The Lighthouse convinced me of Pattinson's ability to be Batman was that he completely disappears into the role. Mere minutes into the movie, I entirely forgot who I was watching and any skepticism I ever had about the guy. Of course, the mustache and 19th-century New England accent helped with that, but it was more than that. Robert Pattinson is just one of those actors who can completely disappear into a role without any trace of the guy you thought you knew. As much as that’s the desire for any acting role, it doesn’t really happen quite that often, but Pattinson does it in The Lighthouse and I’ve seen him do it in several films since.

In a recent development, of course, with Pattinson in the news right now, a lot of his movies are being recommended, and while I love him in The Batman, The Odyssey, Tenet, and others, all of those movies have a lot of plot and action going on. In contrast, The Lighthouse​​​​​​​ is pretty bare-bones. You get to see two guys just acting without much else to distract from it.

The chemistry between Pattinson and Dafoe is also just fantastic. Those two are so funny and interesting together, especially when they are at each other’s throats. It kind of makes me hope for a Lighthouse reunion in one of Pattinson's​​​​​​​ Bond films, with Dafoe cast as a Bond villain. I mean, Dafoe feels like a guy who would make a perfect Bond villain anyway, and, given his chemistry with Pattinson, I think that would be really exciting to see.​​​​​​​.

Perhaps I’m getting ahead of myself a little bit there, but if you, like I did, think of Pattinson as nothing more than that Twilight guy, I’m telling you, you’re wrong, and you only need to see him have sex with a mermaid to wipe that impression clean from your mind​​​​​​​.

The Lighthouse is available to stream on HBO Max.

A Classic Twilight Zone Episode Is Like A Sci-Fi Version Of An Agatha Christie Mystery

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (874 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashfilm

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the second season of "The Twilight Zone" has some of the series' greatest twist endings, as the show proved unafraid to push into even more out-there science fiction and fantasy.
  • Somewhere in the rural United States, on a dark winter night, a UFO crashes out of the sky.
  • In a recent development, "You've heard of trying to find a needle in a haystack?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the second season of "The Twilight Zone" has some of the series' greatest twist endings, as the show proved unafraid to push into even more out-there science fiction and fantasy. One absolutely outrageous ending I haven't forgotten since childhood comes at the end of "The Twilight Zone" Season 2 Episode 28, "Will The Real Martian Please Stand Up?", written by series creator Rod Serling.

Somewhere in the rural United States, on a dark winter night, a UFO crashes out of the sky. Two state troopers investigate and track the missing pilot to a roadside diner, where a bus trip to Boston has stopped over for food and rest. The bus driver (William Kendis) remembers picking up six passengers, but there are seven in the diner — and he can't remember which of the six faces are the ones who boarded the bus with him.

In a recent development, "You've heard of trying to find a needle in a haystack? Well, stay with us now, and you'll be part of an investigating team whose mission is not to find that proverbial needle, no, their task is even harder. They've got to find a Martian in a diner," says Rod Serling in the episode's opening narration.

Writing about "The Twilight Zone" for /Film, Valerie Ettenhofer compared "Will The Real Martian Please Stand Up?" to an Agatha Christie novel. That comparison stands up quite sturdily. The episode is a closed circle mystery in the vein of "And Then There Were None" or "Murder on the Orient Express," complete with a twist ending that denies the simple answer of one suspect being the guilty person. But instead of looking for a murderer like Hercule Poirot would, the detectives are searching for an alien invader disguised as a human.

Industry observers note that like the best Agatha Christie mysteries, "Will The Real Martian Please Stand Up?" winds up the tension by trapping the characters together, because the bridge the bus was meant to cross is out of order. The winter setting complements this; cold weather amps up stress while forcing people to huddle together. Watching the episode decades later, it reads like an ancestor of John Carpenter's "The Thing" — both are about groups of people trapped in the cold and trying to find an alien hidden among them.

But unlike the many Agatha Christie books and movies out there, "Will The Real Martian Please Stand Up?" has to do the setup, mystery, and payoff in only 24 minutes. There's no "characters get picked off one by one" plot structure here, because with the episode's tight timeframe and seven suspects, there's just no way to do that. The episode still manages to capture escalating paranoia, like when even the two married couples among the bus passengers begin to suspect each other. The bug-eyed Mr. Avery (Jack Elam), who keeps laughing at the situation and prodding the others, is the obvious red herring in the ensemble.

There's also never any doubt the Martian is real and rejecting the pretense of ambiguity keeps the episode focused. There's physical proof in the footprints leading out of the pond where the UFO crashed to the diner, and as the episode goes on, inexplicable phenomena like lights flashing and sugar canisters exploding open plague the diner. Rod Serling's intro narration promises a real Martian, too. If this was all a misunderstanding, then it wouldn't be "The Twilight Zone.".

The real Martian is the curt businessman Ross (John Hoyt), and you can spot an impressive amount of foreshadowing. Ross is one of three passengers traveling alone, leaving him without an alibi for his identity. (The POV panning shot when the troopers enter the diner shows him pointedly sitting alone. He also turns his head away as if trying to escape notice.) Avery jokes Ross is "the most suspicious of the bunch" and probably doesn't realize how right he was.

Recent findings suggest that at the episode's denouement, the bridge is cleared and everyone departs without getting an answer. But then Ross saunters back into the diner, alone, telling the clerk Haley (Barney Phillips) that the bridge collapsed and everyone else died. That's when he reveals a third arm hidden underneath his coat, mixing his coffee as he explains his fellow Martians are coming to colonize Earth.

It has been revealed that rod Serling doesn't end on that semi-predictable note. Ross' reveal sequence includes close-up reaction shots of Haley, suggesting mounting terror as he finds himself alone with an alien invader. But then Haley agrees. "This is an extraordinary place to colonize. We folks on Venus had the same idea," taking off his cap to reveal a third eye. Haley was beneath both the audience and the troopers' suspicion — he wasn't on the bus, and he technically wasn't the Martian they were looking for, either. The ending avoids feeling like a cheat, too, because the whole mystery rests on there being an alien invader; if one of the diners is a Martian, is it that big a stretch that another is a Venusian?

The "Will The Real Martian Please Stand Up?" twist may not be more than a clever parlor trick, but what a trick it is.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that after launching Moonlock for Mac last year, MacPaw is bringing its scam-detection app to iPhone today.
  • When MacPaw launched Moonlock on the Mac, the manufacturer described its new app as something that “complements Apple’s built-in security tools, protects from Mac-specific malware, and helps you understand cybersecurity better.”.
  • In practice, the Mac app includes real-time protection against potential threats.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that after launching Moonlock for Mac last year, MacPaw is bringing its scam-detection app to iPhone today. Here are the details.

When MacPaw launched Moonlock on the Mac, the manufacturer described its new app as something that “complements Apple’s built-in security tools, protects from Mac-specific malware, and helps you understand cybersecurity better.”.

In practice, the Mac app includes real-time protection against potential threats. Users can also manually scan their Mac for malware, including suspicious files hidden in system folders and email attachments.

Recent findings suggest that beyond that, Moonlock includes a VPN to encrypt internet traffic, a network inspector that shows where apps are sending data and lets people block connections to specific countries, and an AI-powered scam detector that analyzes messages pasted into the app for signs of phishing. It also helps users review and adjust macOS security settings.

Today, MacPaw is launching Moonlock for iPhone, a move the company indicates “helps people recognize potential scams, understand their iPhone’s security and take practical steps to improve it.”.

Recent findings suggest that unlike the Mac version, Moonlock for iPhone doesn’t scan for malware, as iOS prevents third-party apps from accessing other apps and their files. Instead, it focuses on identifying potential scams, checking for exposed personal information, and helping people improve their iPhone’s security.

On the iPhone, Moonlock lets users quickly check suspicious texts, screenshots, and QR codes for phishing, in addition to checking whether their email addresses have appeared in known data breaches.

Recent findings suggest that as MacPaw explains it, Moonlock’s Scam Detect “helps people check suspicious messages they encounter throughout the day. Whether it’s a text message, a screenshot shared by a friend, or a QR code, customers can paste, scan or share content directly with Moonlock and receive an assessment explaining why something may be suspicious.”.

Here’s Oleg Stukalenko, Head of Product Management at Moonlock by MacPaw, on today’s launch:.

It has been revealed that “When we released Moonlock, our goal was to make cybersecurity something anyone could understand and use. But so much of what people do today, from banking to everyday conversations, happens on their phones. Bringing Moonlock to iPhone felt like the natural next step. We want to help people spot a scam before they tap, see where their security stands, and know exactly what to do next.”.

MacPaw adds that Moonlock for iPhone also includes the following features:.

MacPaw’s Moonlock for iPhone is free to download, with subscriptions available for $9.99 per month or $49.99 per year.

Check out Moonlock for iPhone on the App Store.

#74176. Every Version of 'A Christmas Carol,' Ranked (and Where to Stream Them)

Every Version of 'A Christmas Carol,' Ranked (and Where to Stream Them)

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2059 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that charles Dickens’ A Christmas Carol is the greatest story about Christmas ever written—even better than the one with Mary and Joseph and the manger.
  • I've carefully considered every major theatrical and TV adaptation of A Christmas Carol and rated each in terms of holiday spirit, Dickensian whimsy, and Scrooge-osity to arrive at the definite, no-argument-possible best-to-worst list of Christmas Carols.
  • According to recent reports, to rank Christmas Carols, you have to decide what A Christmas Carol is to you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that charles Dickens’ A Christmas Carol is the greatest story about Christmas ever written—even better than the one with Mary and Joseph and the manger. The 1843 tale of a miser browbeaten by self-righteous ghosts is (probably) the most filmed story of all time. Dozens of cinematic adaptations of A Christmas Carol have been released in theaters and on TV since Scrooge; or Marley's Ghost came out in 1901. Hundreds or thousands if you count re-imaginings and very special episodes of sitcoms. But which version is the very best?

I've carefully considered every major theatrical and TV adaptation of A Christmas Carol and rated each in terms of holiday spirit, Dickensian whimsy, and Scrooge-osity to arrive at the definite, no-argument-possible best-to-worst list of Christmas Carols.

According to recent reports, to rank Christmas Carols, you have to decide what A Christmas Carol is to you. My criteria for inclusion: It has to be full-length (at least around an hour long); it has to have been released widely, either in theaters, on network television, or through a larger streaming service, and it has to be fairly close to a direct adaptation—modernizations, re-imaginings, sequels, and that episode of The Six Million Dollar Man don’t count (sorry, Scrooged fans). Using those criteria, I’ve winnowed the Carols down to the 17 you see below, ranked from best to worst, along with where you can stream each one.

Sources indicate that it's tough to pick a single adaptation of A Christmas Carol as the absolute best of all time, but the 1984 TV movie version starring George C. Scott is unassailable. Other versions do some things better, but this one does everything right—no mistakes. It stays close to the original text; it's perfectly produced; and it has a consistency of tone and vision that makes it the most balanced of all versions of the story. A Christmas Carol might not have the best Scrooge of all time, but George C. Scott's performance is a solid nine out of ten, and this version features the most adorable and pitiable Tiny Tim of all and the best Ghost of Christmas Present, played by Edward Woodward, who played the policeman in The Wicker Man.

Where to stream it: Roku, Tubi, Pluto TV.

In a recent development, shot in the midst of the Great Depression, the first sound version of A Christmas Carol digs deeper into the despair and horror of the story than any other adaptation. It’s a bleak, German expressionist Christmas flick, and Seymour Hicks’ sickly, haunted portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge fits the tone perfectly. Instead of delighting in his own crapulence, Hicks plays Scrooge like Satan in The Divine Comedy—he's not the ruler of Hell; he's its most tormented prisoner. Scrooge's miserliness is played as pathology. He wears dirty, torn clothing and shivers miserably while eating gruel because he can’t bring himself to burn a single scrap of coal. Even when he converts, it seems like a manic episode instead of Christmas spirit, suggesting this could be a story about an old man going mad.

Where to stream: Sadly, the version on free streaming services like Tubi and Plex is colorized, but you can watch it on YouTube in glorious black and white.

Industry observers note that this big-budget musical take on the Yuletide classic turns Dickens up to 11. Scrooge is huge, a raucous, crowd-pleasing musical with hundreds of extras, elaborate sets, and a scenery-chewing central performance from Albert Finney to hold it all together. But Finney and company also manage to keep the emotional core of the story intact. The music is great, with memorable tunes like “I Hate People,” a song that Finney snarls instead of sings. Scrooge has the best ghosts of any version of A Christmas Carol, too—you can't beat the cheesy awesomeness of big-money 1970s special effects.

Where to stream it: Tubi, Pluto TV, Plex.

Recent findings suggest that before Hallmark devoted its corporate life to forgettable holiday-themed romantic comedies, it co-produced one of the best versions of A Christmas Carol ever made. This entire movie belongs to Patrick Stewart, whose nuanced, layered portrayal of Scrooge is the best that has ever been done. His "conversion" scene is so visceral and honest, it brought a tear to my eyes, even though I've seen the exact scene performed in at least 40 other movies, stage plays, and episodes of 1980s sitcoms. Sadly, the paucity of basic cable budgets in the 1990s results in some chintzy-looking sets and laughable special effects that mar an otherwise top-notch production.

Where to stream it: Digital rental only.

Sources indicate that horror director Ti West's Carol adaptation muddies the moral clarity of Dickens' tale and suggests there's something deeply troubling beneath all the Victorian holiday catharsis. With a few exceptions, Ebenezer hits the familiar beats of A Christmas Carol: It delivers the crowd-pleasing rich-jerk-turns-good story moviegoers expect, but West layers in subtle hints along the way that suggest the floorboards are rotten, and if you dance with Christmas joy too hard, you'll fall into the dark basement below. Ebenezer seems to whisper to audiences, "How much does the conversion of one miserly wretch matter in the face of systemic injustice? And isn't he going to snap out of it when the fright wears off anyway?" Bonus: As you'd probably expect from a Ti West movie, the ghosts are genuinely scary.

Where to watch it: In theaters now.

I'm sticking A Muppet Christmas Carol randomly here on the list because you can't reasonably compare it to other versions of the story. The Muppet version is a thing unto itself. Like the Ol' Dirty Bastard, its style has no father. A Muppet Christmas Carol is absolutely delightful from start to finish, for children, grown-ups, cats, dogs, space aliens, and anything else you got. It shouldn't even work to set Michael Caine's serious portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge against a supporting cast of puppets, but somehow it all seems natural.

Alastair Sim takes Ebenezer Scrooge on a real journey in this movie. In the first act, he plays Scrooge like Capitalism personified, an uncaring, amoral monument to pure acquisition. He seems like a Scrooge who'd scare away ghosts, but when Marley indicates up dragging his trademark chains, Sim is instantly reduced to pop-eyed fear, like the single chink in his armor is the supernatural. Scrooge then regresses to a childlike, bashful figure as ghosts lead him to different visions, finally emerging from his symbolic death to his rebirth as a Christmas-obsessed guy who lives to serve others. This movie might be among the best of the genre, but an unnecessary subplot about Scrooge's business sandbags the movie through part of the second act.

In a recent development, mr. Magoo's Christmas Carol was the first animated version of A Christmas Carol and the first animated holiday special ever shown on American TV. The main character, Mr. Magoo, was the star of a one-joke, limited-animation cartoon popular in the early 1960s about an old man who couldn’t see very well, so it’s surprising how carefully crafted and effective this version of A Christmas Carol is. It's weirdly meta too: Jim Backus voices Mr. Magoo, who is a (blind) actor performing as Scrooge in A Christmas Carol on Broadway, so the play is bookended with "this guy can't see!" bits. The songs are strange, memorable and funny (listen to "Razzleberry Dressing" above once and you'll never forget it), but the emotional core of the story remains surprisingly powerful. Jim Backus is amazing.

Where to stream it: Peacock, Roku, Tubi.

It has been revealed that I'm breaking my own rule about not including shortened versions of the story because this animated Carol is that great. Its evocative, graceful, hand-drawn look belongs to animation legend Richard Williams and was inspired by the illustrations from the original version of A Christmas Carol. It's a cartoon, but it's not a kiddie cartoon, so the darkness of the ghosts isn't glossed over. Plus, Scrooge is voiced by Alastair Sim, reprising his role from 1951's Scrooge.

It has been revealed that there's nothing wrong with this brightly lit, by-the-numbers take on A Christmas Carol, but it seems designed to appeal to as broad an audience as possible, so the rough edges of the story have been sanded off. The ghosts aren’t that scary. Scrooge isn’t that miserly, etc. It’s fine for a Christmas movie to be lighthearted fun, but the lowered stakes ultimately blunt the emotional resonance of the climax, leading to a mediocre Christmas Carol.

Industry observers note that I'm including this version of A Christmas Carol because it's Lifehacker editor Meghan Walbert's favorite. Sorry, Meghan, but this flimsy 1970s TV movie adaptation hasn't aged well. Henry Winkler does a good job as Scrooge, and it's cool to see Burgess Meredith and other old-timey stars, but overall, this is a schmaltzy, plodding film that unwisely replaces a lot of Dickens' best writing with the work of 1970s TV hacks.

Where to stream it: Pluto, Tubi, Amazon Prime.

In a recent development, I really wanted to like Disney’s A Christmas Carol. Robert Zemeckis is a great director and Jim Carrey is a force of nature, but I couldn't get through it. There might be a lot to recommend this version of the story, but using 2009’s technology to create realistic-looking characters was such a puzzling choice. The whole movie looks like a video game cutscene from a PS3 game, and I kept wanting to hit “A” to skip ahead to the gameplay.

Recent findings suggest that it doesn't seem like the producers of this obscure 2012 straight-to-streaming feature had much money to work with, which is too bad. If they had, they might have been able to better realize some of the intriguing ideas behind this movie. It's a straight-up horror take on the tale, but it just isn't scary. Sadly, you can't carry a feature film on good intentions. Overall, a swing and a miss.

Where to stream it: Tubi, Amazon Prime.

Recent findings suggest that the animation in this 1997 musical cartoon version of A Christmas Carol is dated, pedestrian, and ugly. The songs are forgettable, and Scrooge has a pet bulldog for some reason. (The one good joke is that he named his dog "Debit.") It’s just not good, which is a shame, because the cast is overflowing with talent, including Tim Curry as Scrooge, Ed Asner, and Whoopi Goldberg.

Where to stream it: Roku, Pluto TV, Xumo.

Recent findings suggest that this BBC drama goes for a philosophical, moody version of Scrooge, but it doesn’t come together. It’s dark, grim, and so ponderously self-serious that it collapses under its own weight. In an effort to present aspects of A Christmas Carol that haven't been seen before (like "How Marley got his chains"), A Christmas Carol rewrites the original text from the ground up, but it comes across like Dickens' first draft with a bad case of Surf Dracula.

Where to stream it: Hulu, Disney+.

In a recent development, the current state of Dickens adaptation is not good. Netflix's uninspired, sappy, CGI version of A Christmas Carol tries to tart the story up with slapstick, songs, and jokes, but it’s all cynical, lowest-common-denominator horseshit. The dialogue has been dumbed down and joked up. Scrooge has a silly dog for comic relief. They added scatological humor. Think about this: The minds behind Scrooge: A Christmas Carol read Dickens and concluded, “This story would be better with a wacky dog and fart jokes.”.

A Christmas Carol is such a solid story, even a grade-school production of it can be fun to watch. But a cynical production of it is extra terrible, given the message of the story. This terrible ego project is a bottom-of-the-barrel Christmas Carol because it feels like a money grab. Kelsey Grammer sucks as Scrooge, mugging his way through a lightweight performance. Jason Alexander sucks as Marley. Jennifer Love Hewitt is, well, actually pretty good as Scrooge’s Christmas-past romantic interest. She is a rare bright spot in this dreary movie, however. Everything else is mid to terrible. It’s shot and lit like a TV show; the sets are bland and the songs forgettable. Overall, it has the cynical feeling of assembly-line, “let’s get this shit over with” TV production.

Where to stream it: Tubi, Pluto TV, Plex.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Aqara has declared the global launch of six newly introduced smart lighting products with full Apple Home support and what the tech giant describes as “spatial intelligence.”.

The upcoming lineup includes a vertical floor lamp with 18 individually addressable lighting zones, and a new LED strip offering seamless color gradients, dynamic flowing effects, and music synchronization ….

All of the new products are Matter compatible, allowing them to fully integrate with Apple Home, in addition to supporting the full range of competing ecosystems: Amazon Alexa, Google Home, Samsung SmartThings, Home Assistant, and Homey.

With a compatible sensor like the FP400, all of the new products support spatial intelligence.

This enables automation to respond not only to whether someone is present, but also to exactly where people are within a space and how they move through it. For example, the ambient lights can turn on and off based on your movement from the couch to the dining room table.

Industry observers note that its intelligent AI sensing algorithm drastically improves reliability by reducing false triggers caused by environmental factors like pets, airflow, and robotic vacuums. A built-in ambient light sensor also helps trigger smart home scenes based on both human activity and lighting conditions.

You might initially struggle to spot the new products in the company’s new releases section on its Amazon store. That’s because instead of each having its own section, you need to click or tap on the product in the top image.

In a recent development, pricing ranges from $24 for new light bulbs through to $320 for the 100-foot-long permanent outdoor rope lights. You can find all the new products here.

5 Best Performances In The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping, Ranked

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1757 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashfilm

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Major spoilers ahead for "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.".
  • Industry observers note that the newest movie in the "Hunger Games" franchise, subtitled "Sunrise on the Reaping," is here, and as I wrote in my review for /Film, it's a worthy addition to this genuinely excellent film series.
  • As Haymitch competes in the already-dangerous Hunger Games — made much more dangerous thanks to the fact that it's the second Quarter Quell, meaning it's an extra "special" (demented) version with double the child tributes — he encounters dozens of characters, some of whom we've met before in different timelines and some of whom are brand new.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Major spoilers ahead for "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.".

Industry observers note that the newest movie in the "Hunger Games" franchise, subtitled "Sunrise on the Reaping," is here, and as I wrote in my review for /Film, it's a worthy addition to this genuinely excellent film series. Directed by Francis Lawrence, who has helmed every single Hunger Games movie except for the inaugural outing "The Hunger Games" in 2012 (which was directed by Gary Ross), "Sunrise on the Reaping" starss Joseph Zada as a younger version of Woody Harrelson's character, Haymitch Abernathy. Haymitch is one of the only known victors of the titular Games who hails from the downtrodden District 12 in the dystopian nation of as Panem. (Some housekeeping: District 12 is the mining district and impoverished enough that its child tributes for the Hunger Games almost never win; Panem is the redesigned totalitarian North America led by the oppressive Capitol, which is located in what we know as the Rocky Mountains.).

As Haymitch competes in the already-dangerous Hunger Games — made much more dangerous thanks to the fact that it's the second Quarter Quell, meaning it's an extra "special" (demented) version with double the child tributes — he encounters dozens of characters, some of whom we've met before in different timelines and some of whom are brand new. So which actors deliver the very best performances in "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping?".

It's a stacked cast and it's legitimately tough to choose, but ultimately, I've picked five performers who build upon the previous movies and performances from storied actors who defined these roles originally ... and do so beautifully.

It has been revealed that the only real beef I have with Elle Fanning's performance as Effie Trinket in "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping," such as it is, is that she doesn't get nearly enough screen time for my liking. Effie Trinket, who appears in this film as a sort of assistant stylist and District 12 prep team member who saves the sartorial day after her boss Magno Stift (Billy Porter) falls down on the job, is a character we know from the original "Hunger Games" movies; in those, she's played by Elizabeth Banks.

Sources indicate that effie is a larger-than-life character whose journey is, I'll be honest, sort of disjointed. When she's the chaperone for Katniss Everdeen and Peeta Mellark (Jennifer Lawrence and Josh Hutcherson) during the original stories alongside Woody Harrelson's grown, downtrodden Haymitch Abernathy, she seems slavishly devoted to the Capitol, but also becomes part of the rebellion in the two-part finale "Mockingjay." In "Sunrise on the Reaping," Effie seems to be a willing ally to Haymitch, but her loyalty still lies with the Capitol. (We also get to meet her younger sister Proserpina, played by Iris Apatow, for the first time in the series, expanding Effie's world just a little.).

It has been revealed that fanning, a recently minted Oscar and Emmy nominee for her sensational projects "Sentimental Value" and "Margo's Got Money Troubles," is unsurprisingly great during her unfortunately limited screen time, particularly her delivery of Effie's most memorable line from the novel ("I confess to having a moment!"). Honestly, there are so many prequels possible in the wider Hunger Games world, and if Suzanne Collins ever wanted to a deep dive on Effie's whole "deal" and give her her own story, I wouldn't hate that. But she'd need to convince Fanning to return to really make the movie sing.

I love Kieran Culkin, and I bristle when people accuse him of delivering the same performance over and over again. From where I'm sitting, that couldn't be further from the truth! Two of his most well-known and well-regarded performances — Roman Roy on "Succession" and Benji in "A Real Pain," the former of which earned him an Emmy and the latter of which earned him an Oscar — are very different. Roman is a broken man-child desperate for love that escapes him and that he does nothing to earn. Benji is a walking raw nerve, who is loved by complete strangers but is still desperately striving to make his own family accept him. Culkin's role in "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" skews more towards Roman, but it's still a fun departure for the actor, and he's great.

According to recent reports, culkin plays TV host Caesar Flickerman. He's the second actor to play this specific character (Stanley Tucci originated the role in the original "Hunger Games" films) and the third actor to play a Flickerman TV presenter (Jason Schwartzman played Caesar's ancestor Lucky in the prequel "The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes"). We know next to nothing about Caesar's psyche or inner life, and that's fine — he's just the guy who helps make a spectacle out of child murder. In any case, Culkin's bombast matches Tucci's wearier but still explosive host. When he's not snarling at assistants, he's Cheshire Cat-grinning at the doomed tributes. Across the board, he fits into this role perfectly. Culkin is not only a great casting choice, but a worthy addition to the franchise, and he delivers one of this prequel's best performances.

Ralph Fiennes is on what the kids might call a "generational run." In 2022, he played the sadistic and vengeful chef Julian Slowik in "The Menu," followed that up with a stunning performance as a troubled, grieving cardinal in "Conclave," and a two-film turn as the kindly and offbeat Dr. Ian Kelson in "28 Years Later" and "28 Years Later: The Bone Temple." Now, Fiennes has become the third actor in Hunger Games (and cinematic) history to play Panem President Coriolanus Snow. He follows Tom Blyth, who played a young and mostly unspoiled version of the future tyrant in "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes," and the late, great Donald Sutherland, who portrays the oldest version of Snow that we see in the original films.

According to recent reports, it shouldn't be news to anybody that Fiennes delivers an exceptional performance in "Sunrise on the Reaping." He is one of the finest actors of his generation and has consistently proven that across multiple decades. What was news to me, though, was how perfectly Fiennes bridged the gap between Blyth and Sutherland. Blyth's Snow begins his journey as a teenage boy desperate to prove his worth, and "Songbirds and Snakes" ends with him newly embittered by heartbreak and driven by ambition. Meanwhile, Sutherland's Snow is comfortable with being a source of pure evil and confident in his actions.

Fiennes' Snow sits beautifully in the middle as a man who seems like he still has an ounce or two of sympathy and regret left — he even asks Haymitch about the fate of Lucy Gray Baird (Rachel Zegler), the woman who loved and left him in "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes" — but is still ruthless enough to replace a tribute tragically killed in a pre-Games accident with a brainwashed lookalike. He's excellent.

In a recent development, without a perfectly cast Haymitch, the entirety of "Sunrise on the Reaping" fails. Woody Harrelson's Haymitch is deep in the throes of an alcohol addiction when we meet him in "The Hunger Games," and he's a disaffected, purposefully withdrawn man who clearly avoids getting close to District 12 tributes he views as doomed. Joseph Zada's Haymitch, in contrast, begins his journey as a young man with a lot to live for and a lot to love about his life. He loves his mother and younger brother and is besotted with his girlfriend Lenore Dove Baird (Whitney Peak), a member of the Covey. Everything changes when Haymitch is randomly chosen to participate in the Games — he's not reaped, but chosen as a hasty replacement when the kid who was reaped makes a run for it and gets sniped in the head. Even then, Haymitch puts on a brave face, reassures his family, and even comforts the youngest District 12 tribute, Louella McCoy (Molly McCann), on their journey to the Capitol.

Industry observers note that as Haymitch makes allies, forms a potential strategy to blow up the arena alongside his mentor Beetee Latier (Kelvin Harrison Jr.) and Beetee's tribute son Ampert (Percy Daggs IV), and eventually allies with the other District 12 girl, Maysilee Donner (Mckenna Grace), he suffers setback after setback. Zada manages to chart every single reaction and emotion we see from Haymitch in a way that feels real and earned. As he takes hit after hit in his quest to win the Games and return home — even though he'll only find more tragedy there — we feel every hit along with him. Zada is magnetic as Haymitch, and he's got a long career ahead of him thanks to this performance.

Every time I see a casting announcement involving Jesse Plemons, I'm excited. The dorky guy from "Friday Night Lights" — Mr. Kirsten Dunst himself — has become one of the entertainment industry's most reliably excellent actors. I'm struggling, as I write this, to think of a time where Plemons was actively bad in anything, and I'm coming up short. He can do absolutely anything, based on the fact that he's hysterically funny in "Game Night" and the most terrifying guy I've ever seen in "Civil War." I'm sure it was a daunting ask for Plemons to step into the role of Plutarch Heavensbee in "Sunrise on the Reaping" for one massive and tragic reason: Philip Seymour Hoffman, who originated the role, passed away in 2014. I commend Plemons for taking the role, and I feel like I need to say that he bears a somewhat uncanny resemblance to the late Oscar winner (and even played Hoffman's son in 2012's "The Master"). He's also incredible.

Industry observers note that hindsight isn't always a gift for an actor, but in the case of Plutarch, Plemons clearly utilized everything we know about the character's future in "Sunrise on the Reaping." Plemons' Plutarch is a mere Capitol cameraman (Hoffman's Plutarch had been elevated all the way to Gamemaker), but he's shrewd, a favorite of Snow, and already a rebel ready to pursue a full takedown of the Capitol. Knowing that this comes to fruition across both parts of "Mockingjay" makes this look at Plutarch's early days of rebellion all the more satisfying, and Plemons is pitch-perfect as a man who's absolutely fascinating on the inside. It's the best performance in the movie.

"The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" is in theaters now.

  • Tracker works because the case changes every week and the four people solving it never do.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, tracker may have outdone itself this week by pairing Colter Shaw (Justin Hartley) with an unlikely ally who couldn't be more different from our hero on paper. "That's The Job" brings newcomer Josh Holloway into the picture as bounty hunter/gun-for-hire Luke Kelso, who finds himself on the wrong side of Colter's latest job. Just after our favorite rewardist united with his entire cast last week, the CBS program introduces a one-off character who we hope to see again.

This week's episode picks up in Gray Haven, South Carolina, where bed and breakfast owner John Iddo (Tinpo Lee) closes everything down for the night. However, upon seeing someone outside, he goes out to investigate, only to be suddenly attacked. The next day, Colter is on the road when he gets a call from his latest flame, Jenna Nova (Gillian Bolt), who is on a job collecting a vintage car with her father, Mario (Daniel Edward Mora). The pair rapid-fire some banter about drinks and darts, reminding us why this pair work so well together. It's a sweet little moment as Colter pulls into his next job, and quite the juxtaposition with how the episode ends. Arriving at the B&B, Colter speaks with Eliza (Ruby Jay), John's employee and daughter figure who is concerned about his disappearance. Colter presses her to tell him everything, and Eliza reveals that he takes sleeping pills for insomnia. Walking outside, he finds some blood and evidence of a struggle, as well as what looks like a kill switch for a water sports vehicle. It's then that Eliza reveals that John had gotten into a recent confrontation with some jet ski guys who may have stolen credit card information from B&B guests.

Tracker works because the case changes every week and the four people solving it never do. Here is which of them you are, what it notes about you, and the case for yours being the best of the four.

Sources indicate that you would rather handle it yourself and you are usually capable of doing so. Colter is a survivalist who lives in an Airstream and takes reward money for finding missing people, which is a premise that only works because he is clearly running from something of his own.

In a recent development, you know somebody, and that somebody owes you a favour. Reenie is the lawyer Colter calls when a case needs a door opened legally, and she is the only person on the show who can get further with a phone call than he can on foot.

It has been revealed that you are two steps ahead and you rarely mention it. Bobby is the one who finds the thing that unlocks the case, usually from a desk, usually about ninety seconds before anybody realises they needed it.

You turn up, change the temperature of the room, and leave people arguing about you. Russell is Colter's brother, ex-military, and the show has never once let the audience settle on whether he is a help or a problem, which is exactly why he keeps coming back.

It has been revealed that when Colter goes to confront the parties responsible, he finds himself surrounded by two guys — which really just means that they're outnumbered. Colter pushes back, pinning one of the jet ski bums and pressing him for more information about John. He’s told that another employee, Lenny Remy (Dylan Kenin), is the man to talk to. Apparently, Lenny went by John's place to send a message, but they hadn’t heard from him since. So, Colter calls Randy (Chris Lee), and it seems like Lenny is bad news. The tech whiz sends our hero to the last pinged location: a trailer park on the other side of town. Entering a condemned manufactured home, Colter finds Lenny beaten and tied up in the closet. According to Lenny, “some psycho” beat him up after he attacked John, knocking him out before he woke up there. When Lenny finally came to, he heard an argument between John and the mystery man — this was a few hours ago. That mystery man? None other than Josh Holloway's Luke, who drops John off at some location after telling him none of it is personal.

According to recent reports, colter continues to look around and finds a few security cameras nearby. Typically, this is when he dials Randy and gets all the footage he needs, but according to Tracker's resident tech guru, it appears that the camera went blank for an hour or so. Colter theorizes that the hired man ran a jammer, which Randy discovers came from a laptop, which is then tracked to the local Dogwood Motel. When Colter arrives, he breaks into a nearby room next to Luke, who readies a firearm of his own. After blasting through the door, Colter narrowly avoids being shot. The man runs, and Colter follows. The result is probably the best fight sequence we've seen this season, maybe on the show period, before Colter gets Luke to talk. From what the bounty hunter knows, he simply dropped John off at a lawyer's office. With the police on the way, Luke decides to go with Colter, albeit as more of a prisoner than a partner.

Recent findings suggest that as Luke soon reveals, he was paid $100K to grab John and not ask questions. This leads to a quick debate over the ethics of their respective professions, where Luke eventually reveals that John’s real name isn't John at all. Rather, he was told that he was really David Watanabe, a man who previously harmed the lawyer in question by supposedly ripping off a Japanese hotel, killing a man, and escaping to the United States. This rattles Colter a little, but a phone call from Reenie (Fiona Rene) puts all the facts back in order. As it turns out, John didn’t kill anyone at all, but rather saved a woman from her abusive husband, Hiro Tanaka (Sonny Saito). After the ex-wife, Mika (Chika Kanamoto), escaped, she turned over evidence of Hiro’s crimes, sending him to prison for decades. Now that Hiro is back, he's itching for revenge.

Although unsure about it at first, Luke eventually agrees to help Colter, who tells him that he needs to make things right. Upon arriving at Hiro's offices, they head inside to find the place empty. It seems as if, after Luke delivered John to the former gangster, he took him and ran. They even find John’s fingernails ripped off and littered on the floor. At this point, it seems as if the pair have hit a dead end, only for Tracker to lay down the tragedy quite thickly this week. After Colter notices a broken lock to a nearby dumpster, they find John dead inside. Although Luke at first wants to take a step back from it all, Colter gives him a choice: either let John die for nothing or use this to help him find and save Mika. Of course, Colter's heroic charm is quite convincing, and Luke agrees to help, tracing Hiro’s number to a local library.

According to recent reports, at the library, Mika closes up for the night only to be surrounded by Hiro and his men. The criminal reveals that he killed John, only for Mika to fight back, killing one of the two goons and escaping into the nearby bookshelves. It isn't long before Colter and Luke arrive, splitting up to cover more ground. This was the right call, as Hiro corners Mika, ready to deliver the final blow when Luke stops him. Unfortunately, Hiro gets a shot off and wounds Luke pretty bad — but before he can finish the job, Colter shoots the gangster dead and stabilizes his newfound partner. With all this fast-paced gunplay, we need to get Colter, Luke, and Jensen Ackles' Russell Shaw in a room.

According to recent reports, the next day, Colter runs into Mika at the hospital, who stuck around to thank Luke when he woke up — it turns out that the bounty hunter is out of surgery and is in recovery. Colter dips in to check on Luke, who wonders if our favorite rewardist has a "walk-away number" when it comes to the job. Of course, Colter doesn't. “I like what I do,” he explains. “I like fixing things. I like bringing people back together.” For Colter, the job gives him purpose and others hope, and so, despite all the profit he makes, it’s never been about the money. But "That's The Job" doesn't end here. True to the title, Colter now has to go and do the hard thing by informing Eliza about John's death, and it's a heartfelt, intimate moment that reminds us that, sometimes, not even Colter Shaw can bring about a happy ending.

Tracker goes beyond Colter Shaw's abilities as he partners with an unlikely ally to see things through.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • VWFNDR + MBL, an Android camera app that doesn’t overprocess and delivers high-quality DNG (RAW) files, is getting a 2.0 release with improved color grading and an expansion to the iPhone.
  • Industry observers note that VWFNDR + MBL introduced on Android in May 2026 with a few points that stood out.
  • The app has been downloaded over 300,000 times since then, and is now getting a pretty substantial update.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

VWFNDR + MBL, an Android camera app that doesn’t overprocess and delivers high-quality DNG (RAW) files, is getting a 2.0 release with improved color grading and an expansion to the iPhone.

Industry observers note that VWFNDR + MBL introduced on Android in May 2026 with a few points that stood out. A unique UI that adapts to the shot, minimal processing for a natural look, and support for DNG files at a level that only Google’s Pixel Camera app can truly compete with.

The app has been downloaded over 300,000 times since then, and is now getting a pretty substantial update.

On Android, this comes in the form of new color grading profiles built into the app. “NATURAL,” “NIHON,” or “B+W.” The app still saves an unprocessed DNG alongside the JPG and the grading adapts across the frame rather than having a fixed result, keeping highlights and shadows in place.

Industry observers note that colour grades: MBL still records unprocessed Bayer RAW DNG, and the JPG it renders alongside now uses one of three grades: NATURAL, NIHON, or B+W. Grading happens on VWFNDR’s own spatial engine. Instead of applying a fixed LUT, it adapts across the frame, much like a raw editor, so highlights and shadows keep their detail. The DNG stays untouched.

Here’s what the output looks like:.

The rest of VWFNDR + MBL 2.0 takes place off of Android.

In a rare case of the tables turning, MBL was released first on Android, and only on Android for the first several months. But VWFNDR is now bringing the app to iPhone with support for variable aperture on iPhone 18 Pro and Content Credentials, Apple’s version of the C2PA standard that’s meant to prove a photo is real and not AI-generated.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, all 62 episodes of Prime Video's acclaimed sci-fi masterpiece deliver gripping interplanetary warfare, extraordinary characters, and epic storytelling. Released back in 2015, this dystopian sci-fi series spanned six seasons on Prime Video until it concluded in 2022, based on a series of celebrated novels that began with 2011's Leviathan Wakes. Praised for its elite world-building, science-backed mechanisms, and great visuals, this is one sci-fi series that all fans of the genre must check out, as all 62 episodes are truly perfect from start to finish.

Recent findings suggest that the Expanse is a true sci-fi masterpiece on Prime Video, given its 95% Rotten Tomatoes score across 62 episodes and 6 seasons. The series delivers peak dystopian sci-fi on streaming and still sets the gold standard for the genre 11 years after its premiere on Prime Video. Critics and audiences agree that it is, somewhat quietly, one of the greatest sci-fi series of the 21st century, with The Ringer saying of its final season, "For all the worthy comparisons to Game of Thrones, there's one thing The Expanse achieved that its HBO counterpart couldn't: This show stuck the landing." For a complete sci-fi binge that's worth the investment, The Expanse can't be beat.

The Expanse has one of the most intriguing premises with a massive scope in all modern sci-fi set between conflicting communities on Earth and in outer space. With each competing for political power and cosmic influence, The Expanse is set several centuries in the future, when humans have colonized several areas of the solar system, including Mars and the Asteroid Belt between Mars and Jupiter.

Recent findings suggest that when the series begins, Earth remains the most dominant force within the solar system, but a newly advanced society and military presence on Mars threatens to disrupt that order. Earth's key vulnerability, however, is its dependence on off-planet resources from far-off colonies.

Sources indicate that much like the distribution of power between nations on Earth, colonies each import, export, and trade resources, which become the driving forces behind power and control in this new dynamic. This is one of the ways that The Expanse feels reality-based and plausible given the circumstances, while also maintaining modern science elements that never lean too heavily into the fantasy genre.

Recent findings suggest that even the battles that take place in outer space are based on realistic physics, separating it from other epic space franchises such as Dune and Star Wars. This emphasis on political considerations and resource allocation resembles the most crucial and basic foundation of human civilization and conflicts between world superpowers.

While The Expanse carries a vast scale across planets and colonies, the heart of the series throughout all six seasons is the crew of the Rocinante spaceship. Featuring members from Earth, Mars, and the Belt, the crew forms an unlikely bond and allegiance despite their cultural differences, which forms the emotional core of the series. Several key figures include James Holden (Steven Strait), an ex-military officer and captain of the ship, Naomi Nagata (Dominique Tipper), an engineer from the Belt, Amos Burton (Wes Chatham), a mechanic from Earth, and Alex Kamal (Cas Anvar), a pilot from Mars.

Sources indicate that these four begin on the Canterbury, a freighter ship transporting water from Saturn's rings to the Belt, which is destroyed in season 1. James, Naomi, Amos, and Alex must work together to survive and discover who destroyed the Canterbury and why. As their journey continues, they eventually come into possession of a Martian gunship they rename the Rocinante, a reference to the famous 1605 novel Don Quixote. All this only scratches the surface of the characters and story in The Expanse, which has a new prequel series set to be released in 2027. It's truly a modern sci-fi masterpiece that is perfect from start to finish across all 62 episodes on Prime Video.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that in 2014, Jason Momoa co-wrote, directed, produced, and starred in "Road to Paloma," a drama thriller designed to highlight the lack of justice for sexual abuse victims on Native American reservations.
  • This "legend" is actually based on the true story of a member of the indigenous Chemehuevi people who fell in love with a woman named Carlotta in the early 20th Century.
  • The story has since taken on a mythical status, and was adapted for the substantial screen with 1969's "​​Tell Them Willie Boy Is Here," which depicted events mostly from the perspective of Robert Redford's lawman.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that in 2014, Jason Momoa co-wrote, directed, produced, and starred in "Road to Paloma," a drama thriller designed to highlight the lack of justice for sexual abuse victims on Native American reservations. Momoa, who is of Native American descent on his mother's side, made his directorial debut with "Road to Paloma," which managed a sort of okay 54% on Rotten Tomatoes. Eight years later, he helped oversee another film centered on Native American heritage, this time in the form of a retelling of the legend of Willie Boy.

This "legend" is actually based on the true story of a member of the indigenous Chemehuevi people who fell in love with a woman named Carlotta in the early 20th Century. The pair absconded but were found and separated by their families. After Willie Boy moved to Banning, California, Carlota soon followed. But her father, William Mike, disapproved of the couple reuniting. He ended up dead, possibly due to having been intentionally shot by Willie Boy or as the result of an accident. After this began what's been called "the last Western Manhunt" in which Willie Boy was pursued by a Sheriff and his small posse over roughly 600 miles.

The story has since taken on a mythical status, and was adapted for the substantial screen with 1969's "​​Tell Them Willie Boy Is Here," which depicted events mostly from the perspective of Robert Redford's lawman. It was ultimately overshadowed by the actor's other Western from 1969: "Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid." In 2022, however, Momoa, writer Thomas Pa'a Sibbett, and director Christian Camargo took another shot at adapting the same story in a very different way with "The Last Manhunt." If you'd like to see how it turned out, the film is currently streaming for free on Tubi.

In a recent development, jason Momoa has a few underrated projects, but "The Last Manhunt" seemed more personal. According to Variety, the "Aquaman" star heard the story of Willie Boy while in the Joshua Tree area, where he owns a home. He and writer Thomas Pa'a Sibbett then developed the story, even meeting with direct descendants of Carlotta's family. The result was a version of the legend based on the Chemehuevi's oral tradition. As Sibbet told Variety, "This is a living story for the Chemehuevi people. It has a special place for them. So we can honor their oral traditions by just listening to them.".

Recent findings suggest that momoa brought in Christian Camargo to direct, with whom he starred in the Apple TV series "See." Camargo previously wrote and directed 2013's "Days and Nights," which was based on Anton Chekhov's play "The Seagull" and boasted an impressive cast including Mark Rylance, William Hurt, and Ben Whishaw. Unfortunately, Camargo failed to do the Russian playwright's source material proud. "Days and Nights" at the moment sits at 0% on Rotten Tomatoes with critics ripping into the drama for having nothing to say.

All of which makes "The Last Manhunt" seem like an absolute triumph in comparison. The film stars Martin Sensmeier as Willie and Mainei Kinimaka as Carlotta, who trek across the desert after the death of Carlotta's father. They're pursued by Sheriff Wilson (Camargo) and a small group of indigenous people who want Willie to face justice for the killing. As the manhunt goes on, the ever more tragic consequences pile up. Momoa also appears in the film as Substantial Jim, a Native member of the posse. But he's only in a handful of scenes and isn't given much to do.

"The Last Manhunt" didn't make much of an impact upon its 2022 release. After debuting at the first ever Pioneertown International Film Festival, it received distribution by Saban Films. But its limited theatrical release in November 2022 came and went and the film has just sort of languished on digital platforms ever since.

Thankfully, it's now on Tubi and is worth a watch if you're a Western fan. A 20% Rotten Tomatoes score probably isn't the best selling point, however. Luke Y. Thompson of the AV Club gave "The Last Manhunt" credit for "great visuals and the best of intentions" but ultimately found it to be little more than "a basic posse movie" that's "not exciting enough to just do that well." Catey Sullivan of the Chicago Reader, on the other hand, praised the film for "reclaiming the narrative of a Native hero" and delivering a story that "is at once an epic romance and gripping thriller." There's also plenty of acting talent on display. Alongside Martin Sensmeier and Mainei Kinimaka as the leads and Jason Momoa's brief appearances, there's Lily Gladstone as Carlotta's mother Marie, Zahn McClarnon as her father, William Johnson, as well as Wade Williams and Raoul Max Trujillo as trackers in pursuit of the couple.

Sources indicate that so, while "The Last Manhunt" is far from one of the best Westerns of the 21st Century, there's enough here for fans of the genre. Those interested to see whether Momoa and his cohorts managed to finally do justice to the Willie Boy legend should also find "The Last Manhunt" worthwhile. The film is available to stream on Tubi right now.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, apple TV's offbeat spy thriller "Slow Horses" just completed its sixth season this past October, and it won't be calling its quits anytime soon, having since been renewed for several more seasons. The vast majority of critics and fans believe the show hasn't lost a step (even with the departure of original head writer Will Smith at the end of Season 5), and its Mick Herron-penned source material still has meat on the bone. Thus, "Slow Horses" will likely run as long as Gary Oldman wants to keep chopping and literally stinking it up as Slough House chief Jackson Lamb.

Industry observers note that the narrative arc of "Slow Horses" Season 6 was particularly gripping, as its team of misfit spies found themselves being unceremoniously liquidated. Lamb can't protect his operatives, so they're all forced to go into hiding. It's a perilous state of play for River Cartwright (Jack Lowden), the series' underdog protagonist who shows flashes of Lamb's spycraft expertise but can't quite put it all together. He needs help, and he receives it from seemingly beyond the grave when Olivia Cooke's agent Sidonie "Sid" Baker turns up in River's grandfather's house.

Sid was presumed dead in Season 1, but she's back in action in Season 6, and she throws a charge into the proceedings as the romantic spark between her and River threatens to burst into a white-hot flame. We should expect nothing less from Cooke because she's been superb throughout his career, and that extends to her crucial role in Darius Marder's 2020 critical darling "Sound of Metal.".

Recent findings suggest that in what might be her best work to date, Cooke stars in Darius Marder's Oscar-winning drama as a singer whose drummer boyfriend (Riz Ahmed) is dealing with rapidly encroaching deafness. Cooke could've easily been relegated to a stand-by-your-wounded-man role in "Sound of Metal," but she branches out and, via Marder and Abraham Marder's screenplay (and a story co-credited to Derek Cianfrance), locates the sadness in a woman trying to save the person she cares about more than virtually anyone else in the world. Unfortunately, as the film progresses, it becomes clear that her character no longer serves a function in her lover's life. It's a painful thing to watch, but they're on different journeys now, and while healing is entirely possible, they just can't heal together.

In a recent development, cooke has never been better, but she's still one plum role away from transcendence. I can't wait to see how that plays out.
