#74163. Why Do AI Posters All Look Like That?

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1292 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Lifehacker ↗ Open Full Page

Why Do AI Posters All Look Like That?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1292 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every poster for a business or event has pictures of uncanny-looking people, buildings that don’t look right, and always that one font.
  • At this point, gone are the days of chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini simply generating text immediately in response to a prompt.
  • According to recent reports, to borrow a classic and implausible example, if you were to give an AI chatbot the instruction “Make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich,” it would start by generating step-by-step instructions on how to make the sandwich before trying to make one (if it could).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You know “the look” by now. Every poster for a business or event has pictures of uncanny-looking people, buildings that don’t look right, and always that one font. But why? If generative AI is supposedly able to “think” and be “creative,” why do so many of its results come out looking exactly the same? The answer is complicated, and it has to do with what chatbots define as “thinking.”.

At this point, gone are the days of chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini simply generating text immediately in response to a prompt. Some very fast models do, but most employ what’s known as “thinking models”, which are a bit of a misnomer. The “thinking” really just consists of generating a set of sub-prompts before executing the main one. And it’s in that hidden, generated text that most of the “choices” (to the extent that we can call the statistical output of an AI model a “choice”) occur that determine how a design looks.

According to recent reports, to borrow a classic and implausible example, if you were to give an AI chatbot the instruction “Make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich,” it would start by generating step-by-step instructions on how to make the sandwich before trying to make one (if it could). Most of this happens invisibly in the background, and many proprietary chatbots won’t show you their in-process “thinking” prompts even if you ask.

In the case of an AI poster, it might break down “make a poster” into smaller steps such as “create a design brief for a poster.” To demonstrate this while doing some testing for this piece, I added additional prompts for ChatGPT to explain the “design briefs” it generated, which included details like layout, colors, and typography.

The problem is those instructions are still subject to the same flaws as any other AI-generated text. They can’t properly fact-check; they can’t walk into the real world and see the thing they’re describing; and they can hallucinate or fall back on stale formats that become easy to notice after a while.

According to recent reports, for example, while testing, I had ChatGPT generate a poster for a Lifehacker-themed nightclub. In every case, the underlying brief it generated outlined some basic details, but occasionally it added things I hadn’t asked for. This included additional text, iconography, and in one case it even added the “design brief” explanation I had requested as the bottom half of the poster.

Sources indicate that those mistakes filter into the final product, when the brief is then fed into the image generator that ultimately makes the poster. In my case, ChatGPT showed me the underlying explanations for its reasoning (though even that could be different from what was actually sent to the image generator), but most people who use a chatbot for this task won’t see these factors before getting the final result.

According to recent reports, while most chatbots won’t show you exactly what underlying “thinking” they use, most can be coaxed into describing the vague outlines of how they reached certain outcomes. And those descriptions provide some insight into why certain chatbots keep outputting similar results over and over. It doesn’t take long for some patterns to emerge. For example, any prompt to generate a poster for a nightclub almost invariably generated a brief that had specifications for a color palette including “electric purple,” “electric yellow,” and “electric pink.”.

According to recent reports, the reason for this should be pretty obvious: When the statistical model underlying LLMs needs to come up with an example for “colors for a nightclub poster,” the most obvious answers are neon, high-energy colors. Unless you know something about the specific club’s vibe (and write that out and feed it to the chatbot), the AI will have to fill in the gaps with something. And that something will be based on the same statistics it uses to predict any word.

In a recent development, this pattern of repetition was everywhere in all the design rationale ChatGPT gave me. Across multiple attempts to generate a Club Lifehacker poster, the generated design brief added an overarching “concept” that described the fictional club’s atmosphere as “high-energy” and “futuristic.” Every bot mentioned using images with the “silhouette” of either the DJ or a dancing crowd (often both). All the text had to be “bold” and “futuristic.".

In a recent development, if there's one dead giveaway that a poster was made with AI, it's that one brush-stroke font that they all seem to use. Now, this is a bit more speculative, but I have a theory on where that specific design comes from. And it’s worth noting upfront that this seems to only apply to posters generated by ChatGPT specifically.

Sources indicate that one of the most common factors I found in my design brief testing was the use of phrases like “brush lettering” or “brush script.” Brush lettering is a design term that refers to using any number of methods like markers, paint brushes, or brush pens to write text. In digital design, that can take the form of fonts that are designed to emulate the look of fancy, handwritten text.

In every test poster I created, however, ChatGPT seemed to take the phrase “brush lettering” rather literally. Every instance I encountered of a design brief that mentioned any kind of “brush” text generated an image with letters that looked as though they were created with a broad paint brush. A human designer would understand “brush lettering” to mean “something that looks handwritten," but ChatGPT didn’t seem capable of understanding the phrase as anything other than using an actual paint brush.

The generated posters aren’t even using a “font,” strictly speaking. (Often, letters that should be identical had slight variations.) The image generator part of the chatbot is still a diffusion model, so it can’t employ a vector-based font, per se. But the brush-style font is so common that its look surfaces in any statistical model.

Recent findings suggest that this is an odd quirk of ChatGPT specifically, and it’s possible that it could change in the future. Especially if OpenAI intentionally tries to train this behavior out of its chatbot. However, it’s helpful to illustrate the underlying mechanism. The only way a chatbot can conceptualize design elements in a visual medium is to generate more specific text to feed to the image generator. And that text is just as prone to mistakes and blandness as any other AI model.

I’ve been examining this with a focus on the kinds of posters ChatGPT generates because they’re very common, but posters (or any AI-generated content) from other models might look different. Every model has its own tendencies. For example, a lot of vibecoded websites are made with Anthropic’s Claude, and you can often tell by the tiny text, buttons with rounded corners, and tile-based layouts.

To a certain extent, this is inevitable. While AI models are very different from humans and do not make “choices” in the same way people do, design elements still have to come from somewhere, and whether human or AI, it’s impossible to make these decisions in a vacuum. Humans will have preferences based on the things they like or emotionally resonate with, and AI models will have tendencies based on what their statistical model determines is the most appropriate output.

Industry observers note that that means that an AI model’s “style” is naturally going to change over time. Even if a model improves or makes fewer mistakes, it’s impossible to ever change the fact that all ChatGPT images are made by ChatGPT. Whatever you generate with any particular model will have a lot in common with what everyone else who uses the same tool generates.

Prime Video’s 5-Season Fantasy Series Doesn’t Have a Single Bad Season

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1109 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Collider

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It's been a tough decade for fans of fantasy television.
  • Based on the book trilogy of the same name written by Lev Grossman and created for television by Sera Gamble and John McNamara, The Magicians is often described as Harry Potter, but in college.
  • We'd be here all day if we were to list everything there is to love about The Magicians.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It's been a tough decade for fans of fantasy television. Despite the early, world-shattering success of Game of Thrones and the prestige fantasy boom that followed, the last few years have seen a severe drop-off in quality for many promising projects. After the abrupt cancellation of The Wheel of Time, the disappointment of Season 2 of both The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power and Game of Thrones spin-off House of the Dragon, fantasy television hasn't hit another peak yet. Thankfully, fantasy fans don't need to look too far for a more reliable television experience, as there's one series that has never released a single bad season: The Magicians.

Based on the book trilogy of the same name written by Lev Grossman and created for television by Sera Gamble and John McNamara, The Magicians is often described as Harry Potter, but in college. It's a subversive take on high fantasy that infuses the awe of learning magic on Earth with all the hilarious misadventures of maturity. The Syfy series follows Quentin Coldwater (Jason Ralph), an awkward fantasy fan himself, whose dreams come true when he learns that magic is real and is invited to attend Brakebills, a college for the magically gifted, as a graduate student. Over the course of five seasons now available to stream on Prime Video, Quentin subsequently realizes his favorite fantasy series is real, becomes schooled in the true meaning of magic, and goes on all sorts of hilarious adventures alongside an equally unhinged supporting cast.

We'd be here all day if we were to list everything there is to love about The Magicians. Not only does the series feature a talented cast of performers who consistently nail their roles, impressive special effects, and a unique message about the origins of magic, but by and large, The Magicians is an excellent example of how to adapt rich source material for the screen. Grossman's novels are already engrossing and filled with relatable characters, lore, and tragic backstories, but Gamble and McNamara take advantage of their long-form format to flesh out the trilogy's supporting players and make the world their own in a way that still honors the wayward spirit of the original. The result is a strong foundation for a series that only finds latest ways to entertain, devastate, and enthrall you over time.

According to recent reports, some of The Magicians' best changes involve its main cast. Not only does the series greatly expand on characters like Margo (Summer Bishil) and Kady (Jade Tailor) — both of whom are based on characters who go by different names in the novels — but it also upgrades Fen (Brittany Curran) from a sidenote in the books to one of the show's most hilariously chaotic mainstays. Furthermore, the series honors the queerness of characters like Eliot (Hale Appleman) and Quentin with heartbreaking storylines that go beyond the teases and more ambiguous circumstances of the original trilogy. This earnest focus is what allowed The Magicians to release its most beloved and iconic episode, Season 3's "A Day in the Life," and also consistently deliver some of the show's most beautiful moments between the two in later seasons.

Aside from expanding Grossman's world and honoring his characters, these additions are also what allow The Magicians to sustain its level of high quality across all five seasons. Although the series stretches its source material to more or less encompass its full run, the reality is that the show could have wrapped things up in at least three seasons if its creators had opted for a more straightforward adaptation. The reason The Magicians never experiences a sudden shift in quality or narrative drop-off is that the show's storytelling never becomes dependent on the books.

Unlike Game of Thrones, which found itself in serious trouble once the show caught up to George R.R. Martin's series, The Magicians developed so many fresh takes on Quentin and his friends that it had plenty of additional material to explore, allowing The Magicians to come into its own over time rather than stray from the conventions of someone else's world.

Between the show's exploration of the underworld, multidimensional antics, and depiction of morally disturbed gods, The Magicians partially maintains its narrative momentum through largely original storylines, but it also keeps things refreshing for fans of the show and books alike. With constant pop culture references dropped by one of television's most underrated duos, it's no exaggeration to say Margo and Eliot's mere presence makes every one of their scenes better, and The Magicians' spontaneous musical numbers are another great example of how the series takes full advantage of its talented cast while also honoring the irreverent tone of the novels.

Featuring creative episode formats involving split perspectives, alternate universes, and time loops, The Magicians also takes a page out of the narrative playbook of less fantastical indicates like Community, allowing innovative approaches to the show's unique medium to complement the self-sustaining power of its adaptation.

It has been revealed that as with any fantasy series, there are some changes The Magicians makes that don't quite land. Despite the power of Julia's (Stella Maeve) journey and some welcome tweaks the showrunners introduce to her character, her short-lived ending in the series is conflicting, to say the least. Nevertheless, the heights The Magicians hit are far more memorable than its misses, and it is through the show's strengths that it manages to remain compelling throughout all five of its seasons.

A decision to kill one of the main characters, for instance, exemplifies how Gamble and McNamara were willing to deviate dramatically from their source material to move their story forward in a refreshing way. This absence allowed The Magicians to double down on its changes without relying on the novels' original protagonist, opening the door for new heroes and villains to literally steal the show.

Recent findings suggest that it's not for nothing that The Magicians still feels like it has even more story to tell after its Season 6 cancellation, and it's this level of success that makes the series the perfect roadmap for the future of fantasy television. At a time when series are either buckling under the weight of their source material or making changes that undermine the underlying narrative, The Magicians' ability to both respect and surpass its inspiration should be studied by streamers and other creatives in the industry.

By keeping what works, expanding ideas that deserve more screen time, and being willing to kill someone else's darlings to do what's best for the story, The Magicians delivers five seasons of phenomenal television that never misses a beat.

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1527 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Slashfilm ↗ Open Full Page

5 Actors Who Should Play Felix Leiter In Robert Pattinson's James Bond Movies

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1527 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashfilm

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Amazon MGM is shaking things up with their upcoming James Bond movie, and why the heck not?
  • Sources indicate that for now, however, we're yet to learn who will surround this A-list Bond.
  • Sources indicate that the character, first introduced in the inaugural Bond novel, "Casino Royale" in 1953, has traditionally been a CIA agent and Bond ally.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Amazon MGM is shaking things up with their upcoming James Bond movie, and why the heck not? The end of Daniel Craig's Bond tenure in "No Time To Die" left the franchise in a sorry state of affairs and it's time to rejuvenate the saga with some fresh blood and latest ideas. Robert Pattinson's casting as Bond suggests things are on the right track. The British actor is the first major star to debut in the tux, breaking more than 60 years of tradition and suggesting Amazon and director Denis Villeneuve are ready to try new things.

Sources indicate that for now, however, we're yet to learn who will surround this A-list Bond. The supporting cast provides yet more opportunity to refresh the series, and while he might not be as crucial to the 007 formula as, say, the Bond girls or M, Felix Leiter presents a particularly exciting opportunity in that regard.

Sources indicate that the character, first introduced in the inaugural Bond novel, "Casino Royale" in 1953, has traditionally been a CIA agent and Bond ally. Since the first 007 movie, 1962's "Dr. No," we've seen various iterations of Felix and multiple actors in the role. Some have been older and avuncular, some have been younger American 007 counterparts, and some have been boring bureaucrats. But for the most part, the character of Felix Leiter is yet to be fully explored. As such, the upcoming "Bond 26" presents a chance to do something completely new with Felix, and we think we have the actors for the job.

Recent findings suggest that in 2017, James Bond's greatest ally got his first solo mission in comic books. The "Felix Leiter" comic book mini-series, from writer James Robinson and illustrator Aaron Campbell, gave the titular CIA agent his own story and missions separate from his British counterpart. The story saw him leave the foreign intelligence service and become a private detective, but that's beside the point in this instance. What could be really interesting is if Amazon MGM uses "Bond 26" to introduce a version of the character who could similarly carry his own on-screen spin-off. Aaron Pierre would be perfect for the job.

Sources indicate that pierre is fresh off a great performance in HBO's "Lanterns" and previously delivered a memorable turn in Jeremy Saulnier's gripping 2024 actioner "Rebel Ridge." As such, he's proved he has leading man chops. "Lanterns" also saw him convincingly play an ex-Marine, which just so happens to be part of Felix's background — at least in the books. With DC Studios now reportedly being dismantled by real-life Bond villain David Ellison, Pierre might be looking for a job and Amazon MGM should give him one.

According to recent reports, why not turn Felix into an action hero of his own? Everyone is surely expecting Bond spin-offs now that Amazon owns the IP, and as the comic book series proved, Felix is an ideal candidate. Of course, the character can't overshadow Bond in the upcoming film, but that doesn't mean you can't build him up over time to be a worthy competitor to Robert Pattinson's MI6 sleuth. Whether he remains a staunch Bond ally or there's some competition between the two it would make for a fresh dynamic in keeping with Amazon and Denis Villeneuve's new direction for the franchise.

Recent findings suggest that everybody knows that Jack Lowden almost became the new face of the James Bond movies, before missing out on the lead role to Robert Pattinson. The "Slow Horses" star would have made an excellent 007 and regardless of how exciting it is to have Pattinson in the tux, it's also a shame we won't see what Lowden would have done with the part. But that doesn't mean he can't play another role in Amazon MGM's new Bond-verse, and Felix Leiter seems like an interesting option.

It could, I suppose, be seen as a bit of an insult to hand a Bond hopeful a supporting role. But it shouldn't, given the aforementioned potential for spin-offs and exploring Felix Leiter's character more extensively. Things could get really interesting if Denis Villeneuve and "Bond 26" writer Steven Knight made Felix into more of a rival to Bond. With Lowden and Pattinson's Bond audition history, there's a built-in tension there already. If Lowden were to play an American Bond counterpart who clashes with Pattinson's agent, that would be a hugely compelling on-screen rivalry to watch play out.

Yes, Felix has historically been a Bond ally. But with the franchise entering a newly introduced era why not switch things up? Have Lowden play a version of Felix who gives Bond a run for his money. Capitalize on the Pattinson/Lowden audition history and watch the dollars roll in. With "Slow Horses" being as good as it is, it only feels right to bring Lowden into the fold in some capacity and this could be a really interesting way to do so.

If you haven't seen "Lioness" you might be wondering who this dashing stud of a man is. Well let me tell you. Thad Luckinbill is one of the most charismatic, endlessly watchable actors in Taylor Sheridan's spy thriller series. As CIA senior case officer and all round hardman Kyle McManus, Luckinbill brings a mix of smarmy charm and ruthlessness, deadly efficiency that would make for an exciting compliment to Robert Pattinson's Bond.

Recent findings suggest that kyle is, in many ways, the opposite of 007. He's loud, brash, and outspoken. But he shares much in common with Bond in that they're both supremely confident and solipsistic. If Luckinbill could bring some of that Kyle energy to Felix Leiter, the character could become either a wonderful foil to Pattinson's more urbane spy, or perhaps even pose a bit of a threat.

Sources indicate that when he first appeared in "Casino Royale" back in 1953, Felix Leiter was a former Marine working for NATO's Joint Intelligence Staff who allied with Bond. He and 007's connection was a way to represent the United Kingdom and United States' "special relationship." With Pattinson so easily exuding the public school boy aura of Bond (it's one of the reasons he could be the best Bond yet) and Luckinbill effortlessly encapsulating the more traditionally brash American approach, these two side-by-side could make for a brilliant Trump-era representation of the somewhat strained yet still resilient "special relationship.".

Industry observers note that "Tenet" was full of confusing moments, to the extent that the entire thing was arguably one major confusing moment. What wasn't in doubt, however, was the fact that Robert Pattinson and John David Washington had chemistry.

In a recent development, fittingly, Washington played a CIA agent known only as The Protagonist in Christopher Nolan's confounding thriller, alongside Pattinson as his handler, Neil. Together, they were an American and British spy team who brought very different energies to their roles. Neil was quite prepared to blow a freeport sky high, while Washington's Protagonist remained wary, making for a fun dynamic between the pair. Neil always seemed to be one step ahead and ready to do whatever was needed to get the job done, while The Protagonist remained constantly surprised by his cohort's knowledge and boldness.

If Washington is cast as Felix Leiter in "Bond 26," we could see a similar dynamic between the pair, which wouldn't be the worst thing in the world — especially if it were given more space to develop outside of Nolan's narrative machinations. Or, we could see a reversal of the dynamic, whereby Felix is even more of a daredevil rogue than Bond. Either way, the duo have proved their on-screen chemistry and would make a great Bond/Felix pairing.

You can chart Robert Pattinson's transformation from teen heartthrob to versatile character actor mostly via his portrayal of freaky little weirdos. The man just has a knack for playing off-kilter and slightly creepy types. But he's far from the only actor in Hollywood who seems to have that dark, subversive energy simmering below a relatively calm exterior.

Sources indicate that jesse Plemons is arguably just as exciting an actor as Pattinson. He's been consistently delivering compelling performances over the last decade or so and while his particular energy might work well as a villain, it could also be really interesting to see him working with, or at least alongside, Pattinson's James Bond. Both actors are capable of fully inhabiting their characters and simply seeing them bounce off of one another would surely make for some of the most interesting scenes in "Bond 26." Or, Plemons could bring the same "Civil War" energy that previously made his co-star cry to the role and give Bond a real run for his money.

Casting an actor of Plemons' talents in the role also allows the producers to really lean into a Felix spin-off in the future. Plemons has the chops to make a character study of Bond's favorite ally work, and I for one would watch the heck out of a Plemons-led Felix Leiter miniseries. Otherwise, the actor is yet to play a character like Felix, and it would be an interesting change of pace for him.

Recent findings suggest that this week's column is bleak. First, there's the looksmaxxing trend where teenagers are taking dangerous chemicals to correct perceived physical shortcomings. Then there are the AI job interviewers. Depressing, but at least some young people are having a little fun with their dystopian hellscape.

You can judge a generation by the illegal drugs it pioneers. In the 1960s, hippies smoked weed and dropped acid to expand their consciousness; the yuppies of the go-go '80s fueled their drive to acquire with Colombian cocaine; but kids today don’t want to go deeper or work harder. They have a smaller, sadder goal: They take drugs to look better. The substance of choice for a growing number of teenage boys are steroids, peptides, and other exotic chemicals designed to enhance appearance.

Would-be muscle-men have been injecting themselves with black market ‘rhoids since the Eisenhower administration, but that was a small cult of adult weirdos with a specific goal. In 2026, kids are into it, and they aren’t using steroids to win a $500 prize in the Mr. Topeka contest; they’re using unapproved research chemicals to looksmaxx. Looksmaxxing is an online movement of young men trying to maximize their physical appearance. Teenagers are taking the normal desire to look their best to dangerous, pathological levels. Driven by a combination of undiagnosed body dysmorphia and relentless social media algorithms that turn amoral “red pill” kooks into gurus, teenage boys are ingesting a panoply of exotic and dangerous compounds in a quest to fix the angle of their jawlines, change their skin tone, lose weight, grow taller, and otherwise “correct” perceived physical problems.

Industry observers note that in the "good old days" of steroid abuse, people generally stuck to abusing anabolic-androgenic steroids that had at least been tested for decades. Teens today are buying SARMs (Selective Androgen Receptor Modulators) and synthetic peptides marked "not for human consumption" from shady laboratories online. Steroids primarily affect the muscles, but many of these newer substances target different biological systems. A recent Rolling Stone article reports that kids are “heightmaxxing” by swallowing erdafitinib, a drug that treats advanced urothelial cancer, because the drug is known to trigger growth spurts (that can result in a curvature of the spine and other nasty side effects). They’re also trying MK-677 to get taller, an experimental growth hormone secretagogue that carries the risk of insulin resistance, water retention, and high blood pressure. Others are injecting Melanotan II, a synthetic peptide that forces a long-lasting deep tan, with side effects of extreme nausea and the sudden, aggressive darkening of moles. (And they're doing steroids too.).

In the looksmaxxing community, softmaxxing is doing generally-considered-acceptable things to look better, like getting enough sleep, exercising regularly, and eating a balanced diet. Hardmaxxing is taking more extreme measures like plastic surgery, smashing your face with a hammer, or taking experimental drugs.

In the bodybuilding and looksmaxxing community, “natty” refers to a natural, non-steroid-enhanced physique.

It has been revealed that here's something more lighthearted than the growing popularity of illicit self-esteem chemicals: the bicep heart and waist heart trends. The Bicep heart came first. Thirst trap videos started appearing on Instagram and TikTok in October in which dudes make a heart with their hand and bicep. Then people started posting variations where they frame the shot with someone they love inside the heart. The bicep heart swiftly led to women posting the waist heart.

Okay. So maybe it's not that lighthearted of a trend. While there are some videos of dudes with skinny arms doing the bicep heart, it's mostly jacked dudes. And the waist heart doesn't seem like it would work at all unless you are a specific shape, as this video illustrates. So maybe this isn't a silly meme but an illustration of how young people are inundated with content that can trigger feelings of physical unworthiness, even if they're just looking for silly memes.

Recent findings suggest that as if searching for a job wasn't alienating and horrible enough, some companies have begun using AI agents to conduct interviews. Begging a robot to let you work in a cubicle farm is as dystopian as anything Phillip K. Dick ever imagined, but don't count humanity out yet. Young people are sticking a finger in the eye of the machine by creating comedy videos that focus on trolling these AI job interviewers. They're hilarious because AI is the ultimate straight person in a comedy team, and the raw compute costs to run these interviews means corporate money is burning with each second of wasted time. Here are some of the top creators in the genre.

Bo Bongo: This YouTuber demonstrates up to AI interviews shirtless but insists he's wearing a "corporate tube top," then focuses on daring the interviewer to notice he's doing things like smoking a cigarette or eating a rotisserie chicken.

Cam Whitt likes to wind up AI by arguing, interrupting, telling outrageous lies, and asking the dumbest questions imaginable, like, "When does the interview actually start?" and "How do I figure out what my name is?".

Crunchyroll Has A Newly introduced #1 Anime, And It Blows One Piece Out Of The Water

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (789 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Screenrant

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that one Piece has grown accustomed to being at the top of charts, but Crunchyroll has unveiled a major competitor.
  • It has been revealed that while it's nothing unusual for anime to temporarily displace one of the greats of the Massive Three, Frieren's dominance has been well above par.
  • This also isn't the first time that Frieren has dethroned One Piece, with Frieren and Jujutsu Kaisen outpacing One Piece's manga sales in 2026 per ORICON's midterm 2026 report.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that one Piece has grown accustomed to being at the top of charts, but Crunchyroll has unveiled a major competitor. Frieren: Beyond Journey's End is the most popular series on the streaming service, according to Crunchyroll's list of most popular anime. One Piece is trailing behind at number six, as of the time of writing.

It has been revealed that while it's nothing unusual for anime to temporarily displace one of the greats of the Massive Three, Frieren's dominance has been well above par. Since the premiere of Frieren: Beyond Journey's End's anime back in 2023, the series has been constantly at the forefront of best-of lists and has regularly been the most popular anime on services like Netflix—in fact, the anime has retained a steady 100% on Rotten Tomatoes since its launch.

This also isn't the first time that Frieren has dethroned One Piece, with Frieren and Jujutsu Kaisen outpacing One Piece's manga sales in 2026 per ORICON's midterm 2026 report. All of these data points indicate something much larger than Frieren's individual quality; it represents Frieren's unique role within a broader cultural zeitgeist, and dethroning One Piece on Crunchyroll might just be the latest development that can prove that point.

On the surface, Frieren: Beyond Journey's End and One Piece might not seem to share much in common. One Piece's story hardly needs rehashing; the long-running shōnen juggernaut is an action-adventure series based on the scruffy pirate Luffy and the Straw Hat Crew as they travel the world in search of a mythical ultimate treasure called the One Piece so that Luffy can become King of the Pirates.

It has been revealed that frieren, on the other hand, chronicles the adventures of the elven mage Frieren, who sets off on a journey to collect spells after her party had once defeated the Demon King. The catch is that elves age particularly slowly in Frieren, living over 1000 years; her initial 50-year journey felt like a blip for her until she reunites with her party and sees them in old age. After the death of the party's hero Himmel, Frieren sets out on another journey and slowly assembles a new gang of friends, this time aiming to understand human emotions, experience, and mortality.

There isn't obvious connective tissue between the two series; to find it, one has to dig a bit deeper. One Piece's world-building is second to none, and it's inarguable that the shōnen massively raised the bar for what stories popular series could tell. One Piece didn't develop in a vacuum—its storytelling and worldbuilding are a continuation of predecessors like Hunter x Hunter and Dragon Ball.

Frieren didn't develop in a vacuum, either; its emotional resonances and character depth reflect conventions that One Piece played a massive role in making viable cornerstones of shōnen storytelling.

Industry observers note that perhaps there's no better example than One Piece's iconic Fan Letter special, in which the lives, environments, and consequences of the events taking place in One Piece's main story are intimately explored. That level of depth, retrospection, and introspection is precisely the motor powering Frieren under the hood, and it's the reason the series has become so successful. It's not so much that Frieren outshines One Piece; it's more that Frieren lovingly builds on the foundation One Piece has spent years laying.

Recent findings suggest that there's also something to be said about how a series like Frieren can ring true with some of One Piece's most satisfying emotional contrasts. Like One Piece, Frieren can be light and digestible, but it can also feel epic, dark, and all too human. Frieren sets those emotional contrasts to work in a vastly different context—one where they're arguably far more focused and intentional.

It has been revealed that in a fun turn of events, series like Frieren can therefore turn into thematic gateways for casual anime fans to try a series like One Piece, whose sheer length might otherwise intimidate them. One Piece, for all intents and purposes, has a long-standing and steadily growing fanbase. Taking into account how the anime industry has boomed since the pandemic largely thanks to streaming libraries, it makes sense why tight, bingeable seasonal releases like Frieren might briefly overtake long-running episodic series like One Piece, which now numbers nearly 1200 episodes.

However, Frieren's continued (and repeated) success can't be chalked up to a simple fluke. It's legitimately an absolute anime masterpiece that takes some of One Piece's most beloved features, dials them in, and flawlessly executes a deeply human journey all its own. Taking over giants like One Piece on Crunchyroll is a massive milestone to be celebrated, and for Frieren: Beyond Journey's End, it's well-deserved.

Reachability is available on other iPhone models to move onscreen content down vertically, closer to your thumb. But on iPhone Duo with iOS 27.3, Apple has a unique twist on the feature.

Instead of helping you reach content vertically, Reachability on iPhone Duo works horizontally.

If you’re using the outer screen and find that buttons or other UI elements are out of reach, you can swipe from the side to have onscreen content shift closer to your thumb.

Sources indicate that you can always disable Reachability if you find yourself accidentally triggering it too often. But if one-handed iPhone Duo use gives you trouble, Reachability is a great newly introduced option to have.

In iOS 27.3, Apple adds a fresh setting so people can enable whichever behavior they prefer.

According to recent reports, by default, iPhone Duo will work as it always has, staying unlocked after being closed. But inside Settings ⇾ Display & Brightness, iOS 27.3 provides the option of automatically locking upon being closed instead. You could achieve something similar before with Shortcuts, but now there’s a built-in setting too.

It’s not exactly a “new feature,” but iPhone Duo owners will also find that the system keyboard has changed in iOS 27.3. Apple tweaked the outer display keyboard to push keys closer together and make one-handed use easier.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Westerns have continuously trickled down in numbers as a genre for film and TV through the decades. While neo-Westerns seem to get a lot of traction, with a filmmaker like Taylor Sheridan having a filmography filled almost completely with entries in the genre—including his epic American Frontier Trilogy—there are few traditional Westerns that still get released to a wide audience. An argument could be made that there isn't much of a market anymore, or maybe that a lot of people just don't like Westerns, but that's about as much a blanket statement as saying you don't like action movies or chick flicks. That's fine if you don't like Nicholas Sparks knockoffs, but if you besmirch The Princess Bride or When Harry Met Sally by lumping them in with that sort, you best prepare to have a donnybrook on your hands. Rather, when it comes to traditional Westerns, short of homages or parodies, very few directors seem to have a deep desire to make them. That is, of course, except for the man with no first name given, and that's S. Craig Zahler.

According to recent reports, the character actor of directors, S. Craig Zahler continues to work under the radar of general audiences, even though the movies he's made have been widely well-received by critics. He's a writer/director with a succinct style—bordering on niche—that's recognizable for its lockdown visual style, methodical pace, and engrossing, stage play-like dialogue, contrasting against viciously brutal violence and inhuman villains. All of this was established with his debut film, Bone Tomahawk, which is about a group of cowboys in the Old West, led by Sheriff Hunt (Kurt Russell), working to save the town doctor, Mrs. O'Dwyer (Lili Simmons), from savage, cannibalistic troglodytes. To put it into context, if you've ever heard the Mark Twain quote where he compared masterful writing to wine, and his to water...well, Zahler's movies are like the film-making equivalent of a White Monster Energy Drink (i.e. not for everybody, but the ones who like them will REALLY like them).

Industry observers note that aside from Bone Tomahawk, Zahler has also quietly flexed his Western skills by both being the uncredited screenwriter of last year's underrated Frontier Crucible, and by being a prolific novelist, with his two most famous being A Congregation of Jackals and Wraiths of the Broken Land, which, combined with Bone Tomahawk, are thematically linked to make a twisted Western trilogy. Wraiths of the Broken Land will also forever live as a "What could have been" scenario since it was announced back in 2016 to be adapted by Ridley Scott and Drew Goddard, but has since languished in the fires of Development Hell. Presumably because of how dark the novel gets and Zahler's distinct style being hard to sell to general audiences.

In a recent development, if spaghetti Westerns were considered subversions of traditional Westerns, Zahler's stories are subversions of spaghetti Westerns. Zahler's biggest strength as a storyteller is his ability to craft his stories into twists and turns that you're not expecting, and to go hard with wherever the story leads him. His method is to write each day until he shocks himself with what comes out, working from the idea that if he surprises himself while writing, the audience won't see it coming, either. That's probably how he came up with the horrid things that can be done with fishhooks, dead baby turtles, rifle barrels heated over an open fire, and everything about the "Wishbone" scene in Bone Tomahawk.

Industry observers note that there's a blunt harshness to his action and violence, and especially the depiction of life on the frontier. He doesn't play favorites, and isn't afraid to shock and abhor his viewers or readers under the guise of telling the stories the way he wants to tell them. Sometimes, that means the lead characters are just as cruel as the villains, and almost without fail, that means the villains are pitiless and verge on being inhuman entities. It's like Zahler read Blood Meridian before writing A Congregation of Jackals and thought Judge Holden was too affable and normal looking, so he came up with Quinlan and his gang. And then he put Blood Meridian down because Cormac McCarthy's lack of quotations and speech tags around dialogue can be hard to follow sometimes . . .I'm guessing.

What makes Zahler's stories so good is that even though their content might be too disturbing for some, his characters are consistently very fleshed-out and captivating to follow. And for every morally gray character, there are a few, like Sheriff Hunt in Bone Tomahawk and Merrick Beckford (Myles Clohessy) in Frontier Crucible, who feel like they could've come right out of a John Ford Western just for how noble they are. And in some cases, what actually makes the more disturbing things even more upsetting is it's happening to characters you like. Bone Tomahawk in particular is interesting, because—unlike something like From Dusk Till Dawn, which does a complete genre flip from crime film to vampire movie—it gradually devolves from a traditional-looking Western into a cannibal horror film. Almost as if the characters are traveling from one genre and entering into another (which is made clearer through the changing landscapes).

Industry observers note that S. Craig Zahler is a unique writer and filmmaker who's able to tell stories across different mediums, but one never usurps the other when it comes to quality. When it comes to his takes on Westerns, the stories feel uniquely his own, but they don't seem like he's trying to deconstruct the genre or emulate the style with a modern twist (or have them take place in a modern setting). They feel like stories that he wanted to tell that just happened to take place in the Old West and didn't feel the need to go the way of paying homage.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on October 2, 2026 during the 2026 New York Film Festival. Janus Film will release the film in limited theaters on Friday, November 20.].

Recent findings suggest that paul Thomas Anderson‘s eye for vivifying music onscreen dates back to the late 1990s when, after “Boogie Nights,” he made Technicolor mini-masterpiece music videos with his ex-girlfriend Fiona Apple — or made a San Fernando Valley-sized shrine to Aimee Mann with his third feature, “Magnolia.” Since then, he’s kicked around with HAIM while turning one third of its Los Angelino triumvirate, Alana Haim, into a screen actress. He’s shot for Radiohead and made a regular collaboration with band member Jonny Greenwood to create some of the 21st century’s most memorable scores. Many young cinephiles now associate the mischievously lilty notes of “Phantom Thread” with the poison promise of fresh love and obsessive creation. Related Stories Rian Johnson Leaves the Door Open to Star Wars Return: ‘It’s a World I Deeply Love’ Box Office: ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Debuts to Mighty $120 Million, Reviving Lionsgate’s Most Important Franchise.

In a recent development, last December, PTA teamed up with Geese frontman Cameron Winter to film, while operating his own Panavision camera, his solo stage performance at Carnegie Hall, running through sparse piano arrangements of tracks off his solo album, “Heavy Metal.” The result, a 72-minute film now being distributed roadshow-style by Janus Films before inevitably living on the Criterion Collection, is a stunning arrangement of its own: a deeply achey, sincere but never cloyingly earnest concert movie that’s tender to the point of frailty. (Benny Safdie counts as a co-producer, and the film’s scratchy Fresh York quality and setting can’t help but have his imprint.).

The matted-hair, lithe Winter can seem a bit uncomfortable in his own skin in the public eye, as he did onstage ahead of “Cameron Winter at Carnegie” at its New York Film Festival world premiere at Alice Tully Hall. But on the piano, laser-beamed into his songcraft, he’s quietly electrified, at seemingly at peace as his tenorous vocal glissando and nimble fingerwork on the piano produce shiveringly tender folk ballads that echo Harry Nilsson and Van Morrison. (The usual comparisons to Tom Waits and Rufus Wainright are right, too, but Winter is his own strange thing.) If you weren’t previously sold on the wily Winter antic rock chaos of Geese — rapidly becoming one of the most popular contemporary art rock bands of these times — you’re about to. Paul Thomas Anderson has created a rhapsodic shrine to the man that is nonetheless ballad-sized in its emotional scale.

In a recent development, winter, in December, played and sang to a sold-out crowd of more than 2,700 at the stately cultural temple that is Carnegie Hall, and this film can at times feel like a religious experience, an incantation, a lonely vigil. The singer/songwriter was 23 at the time of the performance, one year older than Bob Dylan when he headlined Carnegie Hall, and similarly at the precipice of major fame. Fixed on a mobile rig that will at times careen and whoosh across the stage when not otherwise holding on Winter, Anderson’s camera catches the expressionism and chiaroscuro of stage lights illuminating and fading off the singer’s face.

The result is hynoptic, a concert film up there with “Stop Making Sense” but for introverts. Songs like the popular single “$0” acquire an even more wrenchingly somber quality as a lovelorn protagonist rues being exploited by a relationship (“You’re making me feel like a dollar in your hand / You’re making me feel like I’m a zero dollar man”). Stripped of production, his indie hit “Love Takes Miles” plays even better. While many of the songs sort of hover in the same key and bleed into one another, that makes for an all the more transfixing experience. The lack of an interstitial anything save for a sweet prologue and moving coda make for experience also that’s immersive, deep, and the kind whose truth you can feel somewhere in your body even if you can’t quite articulate it.

In a recent development, “Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall premiered at the Newly introduced York Film Festival. Janus Films will release it in theaters starting November 20.

5 Greatest YA Movie Franchises Of All Time, Ranked

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that young adult stories have always made for compelling movie adaptations, especially when you look at the massive YA movie boom that began in the early 2000s.
  • Recent findings suggest that the very best YA movie franchises turn relatable and familiar coming-of-age experiences into major cinematic experiences, balancing honoring the source material with offering new perspectives at the same time.
  • Recent findings suggest that this ranking will consider a few different key factors, including overall quality, consistency, how well it adapts and expands the source material, world-building, and cultural impact.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that young adult stories have always made for compelling movie adaptations, especially when you look at the massive YA movie boom that began in the early 2000s. Magical worlds, dystopian futures, complicated love triangles, and the supernatural surrounding various coming-of-age stories will always have strong entertainment potential, though some are better than others.

Recent findings suggest that the very best YA movie franchises turn relatable and familiar coming-of-age experiences into major cinematic experiences, balancing honoring the source material with offering new perspectives at the same time. As such, it's notable that our choices for the top five greatest YA movie franchises are all still ongoing with brand-new projects in some form or another, from Harry Potter to The Hunger Games.

Recent findings suggest that this ranking will consider a few different key factors, including overall quality, consistency, how well it adapts and expands the source material, world-building, and cultural impact. Keeping that in mind, here are the five greatest YA movie franchises ranked from great to greatest.

Disney and 20th Century Fox's Chronicles of Narnia movies brought C.S. Lewis' beloved fantasy novels to life, starting with 2005's The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe. Audiences were introduced to the Pevensie children who discover the magical land of Narnia and ultimately join the fight against the White Witch.

Without question, the first movie remains the peak of the franchise, though 2008's Prince Caspian offered a compelling darker journey with the Pevensies' return to a very different Narnia. 2010's Voyage of the Dawn Treader also adapted the source material fairly well. However, the franchise lost momentum and stalled after the third film, so much so that the rest of the books in Lewis' series were never adapted in this iteration of the franchise. That's a large reason why this ranks so low on this list, despite still being one of the GOATs.

Looking ahead, it will be very interesting to see how Netflix and Greta Gerwig's The Magician's Nephew fares next year, a brand-new take on the franchise that looks to be incredibly unique.

Recent findings suggest that dreamWorks' How to Train Your Dragon franchise is one of the most emotionally satisfying animated movie sagas ever made, with its focus on a young outcast Viking named Hiccup and a dragon named Toothless. Managing to change his entire village's hatred of dragons, the franchise gets better with every entry as Hiccup gradually evolves into a great leader and hero for his people.

Industry observers note that there's an incredibly rich coming-of-age story baked into the entire franchise that is also full of some of the greatest dragon designs and animated action sequences of all time (not to mention one of the very best movie scores as well). Having expanded into television, short films, and most recently the start of a whole live-action adaptation, the enduring popularity and audience engagement are a clear testament to its GOAT status, though here's hoping the rest of the live-action franchise lives up to its animated counterparts as the first movie did.

It may not yet have the same cultural footprint as the top three from a live-action standpoint, but it still delivers one of the most satisfying and complete narratives on this list.

In a recent development, speaking of cultural impact, few YA movie franchises have had quite as big an impact as Twilight. Based on Stephenie Meyer's bestselling novels, the supernatural romance series saw Bella Swan falling in love with Edward Cullen, a vampire struggling between his own feelings for her and his more dangerous impulses. The series only expands from there, featuring a love triangle with werewolves (Jacob), rival vampires, and major supernatural political conflicts.

Running from 2008–2012, the five-film Twilight franchise was a huge cultural phenomenon that is still talked about today, particularly as the key franchise that helped launch Robert Pattinson's ongoing stardom as one of the biggest stars today (who else has ever played Batman and James Bond simultaneously?) The Twilight saga also inspired several other YA movie romance adaptations and supernatural stories. Despite the inconsistency between films and major melodrama throughout, its cultural impact and massive fanbase can't be dismissed.

Industry observers note that suzanne Collins' The Hunger Games novels became one of the most compelling YA movie franchises of the 2010s. Set in the dystopian nation of Panem created from the ashes of what was North America, the main four-film series focuses on Katniss Everdeen (Jennifer Lawrence), who volunteers to take her younger sister's place in a televised battle to the death, featuring children randomly selected from each of the nation's 12 districts for the entertainment of the wealthy elite living in the Capitol.

Following her survival in the first book/movie along with Peeta Mellark (Josh Hutcherson), what follows is Katniss' evolution into a major symbol of revolution known as the Mockingjay as the nation falls into civil war, examining the power of propaganda, class inequality, political manipulation and corruption, and the cost of revolution itself (there's also a major love triangle).

It has been revealed that running from 2012-2015, the original four-film Hunger Games series provided an incredibly satisfying adaptation of Collins' primary trilogy, with Catching Fire standing out as a very strong sequel. However, the franchise has since continued with 2023's The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes, exploring the younger years of President Snow, while Sunrise on the Reaping has just been released this year and is now playing in theaters, starring a young Haymitch Abernathy and more legacy characters in a major prequel revealing the events of the second Quarter Quell.

Both spin-off prequels prove the ongoing narrative potential of the world of Panem and The Hunger Games as one of the strongest YA movie franchises ever...aside from one that absolutely holds the top spot.

It truly is difficult to imagine any YA movie franchise surpassing Warner Bros.' Harry Potter films. Beginning with 2001's The Sorcerer's Stone, audiences were introduced to a magical world and school for witchcraft and wizardry that is endlessly captivating and full of wonder, even as the eight-film series evolves into a major magical war against the dark forces of Voldemort.

In a recent development, few cinematic trios are as beloved as Harry, Ron, and Hermione, and even fewer have been given as much time to grow and evolve on-screen across 10 years of storytelling. Likewise, Harry Potter's incredibly consistent cast throughout those 10 years is a huge advantage for the franchise. By all accounts, the main Harry Potter saga is one of the most emotionally satisfying journeys in all of cinema (Forget just YA movie franchises).

Beyond the original saga, the ongoing potential of the Wizarding World was shown with the Fantastic Beasts prequel series. Despite its mixed results, the films still maintained high fan engagement and added to the franchise's overall cultural impact.

In a recent development, looking ahead, Warner Bros is set to release its new Harry Potter streaming series on HBO Max at the end of the year, a full reboot with an all-new cast that intends to adapt one book per season. On the one hand, it's a testament to the original movie franchise and its enduring cultural impact as a huge piece of IP. On the other, the Harry Potter movies are still so beloved that trying to reboot the franchise is a massive risk and is already facing controversies ahead of its premiere this Christmas.

At any rate, Harry Potter's iconic world-building, memorable performances, and extraordinary cultural influence all serve to make it the most complete and greatest YA franchise on this list. More than any other YA series, Harry Potter made audiences feel like they were essentially growing up alongside its heroes. As a result, it's highly doubtful there will ever be a bigger GOAT when it comes to YA movie franchises.

It has been revealed that harry Potter is a multimedia franchise about an orphaned boy who enrolls at Hogwarts School of Wizardry, where he learns the truth about himself, his family, and the terrible evil that haunts the magical world. Adapted from the novels, Harry Potter is an eight-episode film saga that follows the journey of Harry Potter and his friends, Hermoine Granger and Ron Weasley, as they navigate the tricky world of growing up, school life, and magic. Starting from year one and moving to their seventh year, the films chronicle the students' time at Hogwarts while unfurling a sinister plot that centers around the unsuspecting Harry. With the return of the dark wizard, Voldemort, the students and professors at Hogwarts will fight to carry on as the world around them may change forever. Harry Potter has expanded beyond the world of its films and novels with several video games, a spin-off film series titled Fantastic Beasts, and even attractions at Universal Studios.

Industry News: What ‘Digger’ Has in Common with Gary Oldman’s Winston Churchill and Charlize Theron’s Megyn Kelly

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (922 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Indiewire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tom Cruise‘s performance in Alejandro González Iñárritu‘s “Digger” is one of the boldest and most entertaining of the actor’s career, as he suppresses not only his usual movie star charisma but his entire way of walking and talking to play paunchy, aging oil tycoon Digger Rockwell.
  • Industry observers note that to aid in his complete transformation, Cruise called on one of the best prosthetic designers in the business, Kazu Hiro.
  • “Alejandro is an amazing director, and he has lots of ideas,” Hiro told IndieWire.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tom Cruise‘s performance in Alejandro González Iñárritu‘s “Digger” is one of the boldest and most entertaining of the actor’s career, as he suppresses not only his usual movie star charisma but his entire way of walking and talking to play paunchy, aging oil tycoon Digger Rockwell. Cruise is barely recognizable in the role, which is about as far from heroic characters like Pete “Maverick” Mitchell and Ethan Hunt as Cruise’s Ron Kovic in “Born on the Fourth of July” was from race car driver Cole Trickle almost 40 years ago.

Industry observers note that to aid in his complete transformation, Cruise called on one of the best prosthetic designers in the business, Kazu Hiro. Hiro has turned Gary Oldman into Winston Churchill (“The Darkest Hour”), Charlize Theron into Megyn Kelly (“Bombshell”), and Dwayne Johnson into “Smashing Machine” Mark Kerr, but transforming Cruise into Texas oilman Digger Rockwell was a whole upcoming task — one made even more challenging by Iñárritu and Cruise’s persistent striving for perfectionism, and constant eagerness to try new approaches. Related Stories If There’s Generative AI in ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,’ It’s Not the First Time David Fincher’s Used It Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage.

“Alejandro is an amazing director, and he has lots of ideas,” Hiro told IndieWire. “Every day he comes in with a new idea, and we have to come up with an answer for how to achieve it. And Tom is really professional, and expects everybody else to be at that same level, ready for any situation. After the first day of testing, I learned that I had to stay flexible to respond to whatever they wanted.”.

Sources indicate that to that end, Hiro created modular prosthetics whose parts could easily be swapped out and moved around, so that Cruise and Iñárritu could constantly try new looks. “Sometimes with heavy makeup, you can’t change it,” Hiro said. “I created prosthetics that could be mixed, so we could make new designs on the spot — try this forehead with these cheeks and this nose, then change it.” Creating Cruise’s look was a constantly evolving process throughout the long prep period. “We didn’t have a clear answer until the end of rehearsal.”.

Industry observers note that hiro’s mandate at the beginning was a bit open-ended, which gave him room for artistic exploration but also made it difficult to zero in on a precise look. “Alejandro mentioned the character was 76 years old and an oil tycoon,” Hiro said. “He also said he didn’t want the character to look like Tom, but he still wanted to see Tom in the character.” To try to find a concrete image for Digger Rockwell, Hiro immersed himself in research.

“I researched real oil tycoons and how they aged and what kinds of lifestyles they had,” Hiro mentioned. “Those lifestyles affect how they age.” As Hiro did more and more research, however, he realized that there was no one look that defined the entire profession he was trying to represent. “Everybody looked so different, so in the end I relied more on the storyline and how this particular character behaved.” The idea, in keeping with the slightly heightened style of the film as a whole, was to exaggerate Cruise’s features but keep the character realistic.

Hiro began with a 3D scan and life cast of Cruise, which he used to sculpt his designs. His paramount concern was allowing the actor to be as expressive as possible under the makeup. “The key part is to make the prosthetic very soft so he can move,” Hiro remarked, noting that three weeks before shooting, Iñárritu called with a significant change. “He decided that Digger should be 65, not 76, so I quickly made a upcoming design. Tom is around that age, but he looks much younger than a normal 65. Under his eye was exposed and the rest of the face was covered, but I made it thin to give him freedom.”.

Sources indicate that in addition to Digger’s face, Hiro was also tasked with creating an upper body for an early scene in which Cruise would be seen stripped down to his pajama pants. The body prosthetic was intended only for that one scene, with a lighter bodysuit created for the rest of the movie. “We made a light version of the padding for under the costume, because we don’t need to see the skin after that first scene,” Hiro said. “For the first scene we made a silicone prosthetic that was a lot heavier — the body padding was around 10 pounds, but the silicone was 40 or 50.”.

Sources indicate that during one of Cruise’s costume fittings, he told Hiro he wanted to feel the weight of the silicone throughout production. “He tried the body prosthetic on and remarked, ‘I like this, I want to wear it every day,'” Hiro said. “I told him it would be really heavy and hot, but he said he was training and would be fine.” Since gluing the body prosthetic on every day would be extremely time-consuming, Hiro created a strong spandex foundation and glued the prosthetic to it so Cruise could slip it on each day.

“He wore that for the whole film,” Hiro stated. “One time he said, ‘This is so heavy, it’s really hard on my back.’ I thought, ‘Okay, you asked for it,’ but he went through with it and finished the film, so that was amazing.”.

There's Actually a Simple Explanation for All These Widespread Outages

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (892 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It feels like every time you look at your phone lately, another company is having an outage.
  • Industry observers note that that pattern, in turn, has begun to fuel anxiety among the general public.
  • Sources indicate that but to skeptics of the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It feels like every time you look at your phone lately, another company is having an outage. Last week, there was Microsoft, whose outage took down services from Outlook to Teams. Then, the FAA grounded all flights across the U.S. following "communication concerns." This week, a number of banks experienced outages, as did Apple. Even the NSA's internal communications network went dark. Some of the biggest corporations and organizations in the world can't seem to keep their services running, leading to widespread disruptions and confusion. When it's a one-off, it's an annoyance; when it's outage after outage, it starts to feel like a pattern.

Industry observers note that that pattern, in turn, has begun to fuel anxiety among the general public. What could possibly be causing Apple, Microsoft, JP Morgan Chase, and the NSA alike to go dark at roughly the same time? Is it a coordinated cyberattack? An AI revolt? Is the end finally nigh? To an outside observer, it certainly appears like something coordinated and nefarious is happening here. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is insistent that there is "zero evidence" that hackers or bad actors caused any of these outages, and President Trump is particularly unconcerned by the whole ordeal, saying, "It's life," and "Things like that happen.".

Sources indicate that but to skeptics of the U.S. government, these trickles of information aren't necessarily reassuring. While I agree with calls for someone from the government (perhaps the president himself) to make an official announcement explaining the situation, the root cause does appear to be clear at this time: The short answer? AI is at fault here, but not in the way you think.

Recent findings suggest that love it or hate it, AI is a force to be reckoned with. While you might know that AI can generate hyper-realistic videos and manage your emails on your behalf, certain models are adept at discovering new security vulnerabilities in software. These models aren't just helpful tools; they far surpass the abilities of human researchers. You might remember Anthropic initially pulled the brakes on its breakthrough model, Claude Mythos, when it found that the model could root out security vulnerabilities in just about anything.

According to recent reports, mythos, and models like it, are a double-edged sword. On the one hand, they can be major assets for developers and researchers to find latest security vulnerabilities that humans otherwise wouldn't have discovered, and patch them accordingly. Unfortunately, the same can be said for bad actors, who can use these models to learn about new security flaws and attempt to exploit them before researchers have a chance to find them. As such, software developers across the spectrum, from small-time devs to major corporations, have been racing to patch as many security vulnerabilities as they can find—and they're finding a lot.

You might notice your PC's security updates, for example, are shipping with more patches than usual—historic levels, even. Microsoft keeps breaking its own records with its Patch Tuesday updates, including over 1,400 fixes with its October revision. The manufacturer's October 2025 Patch Tuesday update, by comparison, included fewer than 180 fixes.

In a recent development, it's key to understand that just about every tech giant that develops software is furiously working to patch its systems before hackers or AI agents exploit vulnerabilities first. And while there are successes (Microsoft is now protecting its customers from thousands of flaws each month), this speed is also inadvertently breaking things along the way. That's not just speculation: According to The Washington Sun, both Wall Street executives and the NSA explained to members of Congress that patching security flaws discovered by AI models caused this week's widespread outages.

According to recent reports, barring some campaign to cover up a coordinated attack on systems and services, it does seem like these outages are simply the result of companies breaking their own products in an attempt to stop AI-assisted hackers from exploiting undiscovered flaws. But that's not all that reassuring, either. AI models are only going to keep getting better at finding vulnerabilities; likewise, AI agents are only improving at hacking into systems autonomously. Companies will need to ramp up their efforts to patch their software before both hackers and AI agents discover those flaws first, and so the cycle will continue. Unless something changes, we may see routine outages as companies try to fix things as rapidly as possible.

Recent findings suggest that the implications aren't specific to any one company, either. Our world increasingly relies on fewer companies to keep us all connected. We saw that last year, when cloud hosting providers like AWS and Cloudflare each experienced outages. When these services go down, so do all of the networks that rely on them. If AWS or Cloudflare break something while trying to patch their systems, whole parts of the internet go dark.

Sources indicate that of course, it'll only be more difficult for the general public—if not the developers themselves—to recognize when outages are the result of maintenance or a cyberattack. Just because recent outages don't appear to be nefarious in nature, that doesn't mean future outages will be so innocent. 7 Fantasy Books To Read if You Love 'Percy Jackson & the Olympians'

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1493 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Collider

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Percy Jackson & the Olympians is a series of novels by American author Rick Riordan which was a massive success.
  • The series is perhaps most famous for its stellar Disney+ TV adaptation, as well as its disastrous early 2010s movies starring Logan Lerman.
  • Industry observers note that tristan Strong Punches a Hole in the Sky is, admittedly, a bit of a mouthful.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Percy Jackson & the Olympians is a series of novels by American author Rick Riordan which was a massive success. The story is about Percy, a young boy who discovers he is a demigod, i.e. that his father was the Greek god Poseidon. He is then whisked away to a secluded camp in the wilderness, where other demigods train and learn to fight the ravenous monsters from Greek mythology that prowl the world, unseen by ordinary human eyes.

The series is perhaps most famous for its stellar Disney+ TV adaptation, as well as its disastrous early 2010s movies starring Logan Lerman. If you're a big fan of the book series and how they seamlessly blend 21st century life with mythology, there are plenty of other books out there that you might also wish to check out.

Industry observers note that tristan Strong Punches a Hole in the Sky is, admittedly, a bit of a mouthful. Lengthy title aside, this novel by Kwame Mbalia was actually presented and approved by Rick Riordan himself, basically linking the book with the legacy of Percy Jackson. The "Rick Riordan Presents" branding basically focuses on similar stories that feature mythological elements from various cultures that intersect with real life, and this tale is no exception to that rule.

According to recent reports, instead of being about Egyptian, Greco-Roman, or Norse mythology, which are arguably the most popular, this one features West African deities and folklore. This is combined with Black American folktales as well, creating a fascinating blended universe. The main character, the eponymous Tristan Strong, is actually incredibly likable. Plus, the story deserves points for bringing a mythology to life that rarely gets the chance to. Representing a rich, yet overlooked culture, combined with tween-friendly plotlines and lovable characters make this novel a real diamond in the rough. It's no wonder it was approved by the big man himself; you just can't beat that.

According to recent reports, caytlyn Brooke's Among the Hunted is the first novel in the Skyglass series, which is all about Greek mythology. It doesn't serve as a retelling of an existing narrative established in the mythos. Rather, it crafts a fresh story that is seamlessly integrated into the existing mythology, so that nothing feels out of place. As of yet, no other Skyglass books have been published, but it is implied that there are more on the way.

It has been revealed that among the Hunted centers on Kaitani, a nymph warrior who serves Olean. She has fallen in love with Hermes, the messenger of the gods, and is shouldering an unbearable guilt following the death of her closest friend. It's a horrible existence, made even worse by the fact that Zeus begins actively hunting Kaitani's sister. This causes her to embark on a quest for revenge, finally releasing the emotions she's been bottling up for 100 years. Now, she has just one goal: kill an immortal. This book is a bit more mature than typical YA novels, but it's still appropriate for teens and adults alike. If you're in this age group, and you love Percy Jackson and need some more Greek mythology, this is definitely something you should check out.

Sources indicate that it might sound like a broken record to recommend this one, but Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone is still a great book for Percy Jackson fans. This is mainly due to the fact that Harry Potter basically revolutionized the whole YA genre, creating a market boom of similar stories, of which Percy Jackson was part of. However, the similarities go beyond surface-level trends, and go right down to the bones of each story.

It has been revealed that each series features a reluctant hero for a protagonist; a secluded, specialized academy for magical individuals; quippy dialogue; and various monsters from mythology. Both series have their fair share of adventure and comedy in equal measure. While Harry Potter doesn't feature any gods or deities from mythology, it has enough in common with Percy Jackson that it is often the next thing readers move on to when they've finished with Percy's story. In fact, many Potter fans also move straight on to Percy Jackson once they're finished.

Recent findings suggest that the Serpent's Secret is the first in a series called Kiranmala and the Kingdom Beyond, a YA trilogy based on Bengali folklore. The eponymous protagonist, Kiranmala, is an ordinary 12-year-old living in New Jersey, who has been repeatedly told by her parents that she comes from a place outside this Earth, and that she is secretly an Indian princess. Though she never believes the stories, it turns out they were right, as she finds herself confronted by a horrifying rakkhosh demon, which abducts her parents. This is made more convoluted when two princes arrive and whisk her away to an alternate dimension.

It has been revealed that rather than being about Hinduism as a whole, the novel draws inspiration from lesser-talked about Indian traditions, imbuing its narrative with winged horses, talking birds, and a vengeful Serpent King. It's one of the most thematically interesting worlds told in a YA novel, and it fits in perfectly with the massive YA boom that began in the late '90s and peaked in the late 2000s/early 2010s. Fans of Percy Jackson will absolutely love this one, especially since it features ancient traditions and stories blending with aspects of real life in the 21st century.

Recent findings suggest that wolves is Book One of I Bring the Fire by C. Gockel. The book is primarily about Loki, the Norse god of trickery, and opens up with Loki waking up in a prison cell. This time, he has no idea what he's actually done to land himself there, but he does know one thing: his dear father, Odin, and brother, Thor, are up to something. Loki isn't sure what that something is, but he is sure that he doesn't like it one bit. Meanwhile, in a sleepy American Midwest town, a girl is on her way to her grandmother's house when her fate becomes intertwined with Loki's.

Industry observers note that this hidden gem is perfectly suited for fans of Percy Jackson. After all, it has gods from a dead religion interacting with ordinary people and existing in the real world. The series also features the signature sass and chaos that Percy Jackson became famous for, alongside a cast of memorable characters and a grand adventure. It might not be the best book ever written, but it's something that fans of Percy Jackson will absolutely want to check out.

The Song of Achilles is a stand-alone novel that became a major hit with audiences. Written by Madeline Miller, this novel is a retelling of the Trojan War through the eyes of one of its most famed warriors, Achilles. Alongside Achilles is his lifelong friend, Patroclus, both of whom are trained by Chiron the centaur in the arts of warfare. When Helen of Sparta is kidnapped and the Greeks lay siege to Troy, Achilles and Patroclus answer the call. However, their relationship blossoms into something beyond friendship.

According to recent reports, indeed, the two do end up forming a romantic relationship, which was actually fairly commonplace in Ancient Greece. This book has a little bit of everything: there's romance, war, action, and adventure in equal measure, providing a fresh spin on an age-old story. The Song of Achilles won quite a few awards, including the Orange Prize for Fiction, one of the UK's most prestigious literary awards. If you're a teen or an adult, this book is an excellent recommendation for fans of Percy Jackson and the Olympians.

Sources indicate that the Odyssey is the quintessential Greek myth, initially penned by Homer nearly 3,000 years ago. Rather than a novel, the book is formatted as an epic poem, which was a common storytelling medium at the time. While it wasn't technically considered fantasy when it first came out, it certainly fits the bill in hindsight. The story became so popular, even for the time, that it eventually became part of the official Greek canon, meaning it is an official part of Greek mythology.

Since the poem is one of the most famous things ever written, as well as one of the oldest surviving works of fiction, pretty much everybody knows the story by now. It's about a warrior named Odysseus who is returning home to Greece after spending years fighting in the Trojan War. This journey home is no easy feat, though, as Odysseus and his crew encounter numerous beasts and beings as they sail across the Greek islands. This is such an ideal pick for Percy Jackson fans because it's one of the main works that inspired it all in the first place. Fans will definitely recognize some of their favorite featured creatures from Riordan's series in the Odyssey, and will come to understand the origins of Greek epics.
