📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The legacy-quel is alive and well, and it only makes sense that a sequel/reboot/reimagining would eventually come for “Home Alone,” Chris Columbus’ 1990 holiday classic starring Macaulay Culkin.

There was buzz that Culkin over the summer pitched an idea to Disney as to where a grown Kevin McAllister would be today after enduring two child abandonments and harassment and attempted murder from bumbling bandits (our interpretation, not necessarily his read on Kevin’s childhood shenanigans and trauma). Disney now seems to have warmed to the idea like a cup of hot cocoa, especially thanks to the two additional names who are working with Culkin on the project: Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg. Related Stories If There’s Generative AI in ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,’ It’s Not the First Time David Fincher’s Used It Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage.

Disney’s 20th Century Studios is in early development on a sequel to “Home Alone” that would star Culkin reprising his original role and in which Rogen and Goldberg on behalf of their Point Grey banner would write and produce the film, working with Culkin on his idea, IndieWire has learned.

Things are very, very early days, and any plot details are being kept under wraps for now, and no director is attached at the moment.

Industry observers note that chris Columbus directed the original “Home Alone” and its nearly-as-loved sequel “Home Alone 2: Lost in Fresh York,” and both written by the late great John Hughes. If you can believe it, there have been six “Home Alone” movies in all, with the third one at least released in theaters and doing respectable box office numbers. The others are all TV movies or in the case of the most recent 2021 film “Home Sweet Home Alone,” a Disney+ streaming movie.

Recent findings suggest that the original two films though grossed $477 million and $358 million worldwide, respectively, and the original still gets tons of cable play and finds its way into the Nielsen streaming charts. It makes sense that a more serious sequel with Culkin back in the fold would be welcomed by audiences.

Sadly, “Home Alone” has been back on the minds of audiences of late after the recent passing of Catherine O’Hara, who played Kevin’s mom, and also Tim Curry, who had a small role as a hotel clerk in “Home Alone 2.” Joe Pesci and Daniel Stern as the Wet Bandits are still around, though Pesci has been mostly retired outside of his return in Scorsese’s “The Irishman” back in 2019 and his role in the Pete Davidson Peacock series “Bupkis” in 2023.

Culkin too has had a bit of a resurgence, making a cameo in the most recent season of “Fallout” and doing a voice in Disney’s “Zootopia 2.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Despite the controversy surrounding its launch, there is no denying that Hogwarts Legacy dominated the gaming sphere in 2023, with the Harry Potter-inspired RPG even going on to become the best-selling game of the year.

As such, it was not long before a sequel was confirmed, and over the past three years, Avalanche Software has been hard at work getting ready to send players back to Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry.

It may have been the best-selling game of 2023, but Hogwarts Legacy did not come without its downfalls, especially as it did not receive any expansions or substantial post-game content drops. As such, fans are feeling mixed over a sequel. Will it expand on the open-world and offer long-term content, or will it be much of the same?

Sources indicate that at the time of writing, Hogwarts Legacy 2 does not have a release date, or even a release window, despite previous rumors suggesting that it would coincide with the upcoming launch of the Harry Potter television show, which is set to debut on Christmas Day. However, it is unlikely that Hogwarts Legacy 2 is going to pop up over the next month, so we can safely assume that it will be 2027 at the earliest.

It was back in October that Warner Bros., the publishers behind Hogwarts Legacy, issued a statement on the game's progress, and after Paramount acquired Warner Bros. Discovery, it was confirmed that Warner Bros. Games would merge with Paramount Games Studio to create one giant gaming division.

It will be this gaming division that works on Hogwarts Legacy 2, but, as mentioned, no further information has been revealed, and fans are yet to see any gameplay or substantial updates. As such, its potential cancellation has been a subject of worry for fans, but according to a letter to shareholders discussing WB's games division, WB's strategy will be to focus on its most successful franchises, with Harry Potter being one of them. "We expect Games to more meaningfully contribute to segment profitability going forward as our pipeline expands," the statement reads, "including the second installment of Hogwarts Legacy.".

With The Game Awards taking place on December 10, we can only hope that this next major gaming event will spare a moment for Hogwarts Legacy 2, and it would be perfect timing in the lead-up to the Harry Potter television show, especially as the two projects are rumored to be working together closely. However, this is mere speculation, and for now, we will have to wait with bated breath to see what comes next for the franchise.

Back in 2023, our very own William Cennamo awarded Hogwarts Legacy an almost perfect 9/10, with his review reading:.

Hogwarts Legacy is a wonderful game filled to the brim with adventures to be had, activities to engage in, and secrets to be found. The school and the surrounding areas have been recreated beautifully, and players will easily lose hours lost in the whimsical splendor of this wizarding world.

Breaking: How a Filipino Facial Expression in ‘Forgotten Island’ Became a Universal Symbol of Representation

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (935 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Indiewire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that as soon as the first clips from DreamWorks’ latest animated film, “Forgotten Island,” started popping up online, there was one specific shot that caught on fire online — the lip pointing.
  • In a recent development, “That moment had been in the script since the first draft, because we wanted to put in as much as we can from our personal experience with Filipino culture,” director Joel Crawford told IndieWire.
  • In a recent development, the lip pointing may not happen in a pivotal scene, or be key for a character, but it became a sort of symbol for the film’s approach to representation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that as soon as the first clips from DreamWorks’ latest animated film, “Forgotten Island,” started popping up online, there was one specific shot that caught on fire online — the lip pointing. It happens at a goodbye party for Raissa Molina (Liza Soberano), who is heading to Caltech. Her best friend Jo (H.E.R.) is late to the party and asks around to see where Raissa is, when an older woman points with her lips in the right direction. It’s a small moment, a visual gag that can easily go over the audience’s heads amidst all the other jokes in the sequence. But audiences familiar with Filipino culture immediately caught on to it, as did Latino fans and many others who recognize that gesture as the most potent and accurate way to point at something. Related Stories If There’s Generative AI in ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,’ It’s Not the First Time David Fincher’s Used It Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage.

In a recent development, “That moment had been in the script since the first draft, because we wanted to put in as much as we can from our personal experience with Filipino culture,” director Joel Crawford told IndieWire. “Growing up around Filipinos, the lip point was something that was so specific and unique to me, so it’s beautiful that it transcends into other cultures. Adding that felt like a celebration of it, but also something that makes characters feel real. And in adding that specificity about the culture, it ends up being the most universal aspect of the movie because it invites everyone in.”.

In a recent development, the lip pointing may not happen in a pivotal scene, or be key for a character, but it became a sort of symbol for the film’s approach to representation. Later in the film, Jo does the lip pointing because an animator thought it would be a good idea to reprise it, after learning about its place in the culture. Indeed, in addition to having an authentically Filipino cast and a cultural consultant to really capture Filipino culture, the animation team found their own ways of homaging or capturing aspects of Filipino culture to bring to the movie.

When creating the character of Jo, the animation team based a lot of her hand expressions on Filipino skater Margie Didal and her own hand gestures, while the villainous Manananggal’s movements were created by the animation team watching choreography done by Filipino-American dancer Phil Tayag, who brought a pop locking influence to the vampire-like creature.

“When we first approached DreamWorks and Universal with this story, it was important to everybody that we got every detail of this story and this culture right,” director Januel Mercado noted. “.

After challenging what was thought possible with DreamWorks animated films in “Puss in Boots: The Last Wish,” Crawford and Mercado push the studio’s visuals forward with “Forgotten Island.” With most of the story taking place on the island of Nakali, which is populated by all sorts of mythical creatures, to really capture the fantastical possibilities of this world, the movie’s visuals go wild, taking inspiration from 1990s Filipino art as well as anime from that time period.

Industry observers note that for Crawford, the major lesson learned from “The Last Wish” was that you could take big swings in the animation style and the visuals, but you could also do specific things in the story with those visuals. Indeed, when it came to “Forgotten Island,” the idea of memories and friendship became not only central to the story of Jo and Raissa, but also to the eclectic visual styles represented in the movie.

“The idea became that we could push the animation styles to represent the different ways people recall memories,” Crawford explained. “We didn’t need to be limited by Western CG-style animation, but actually bring in some of our own nostalgia into it and make sure it fit the characters. When Raww tries to explain what happened when he met Jo and Raissa, he sees himself as way cooler than he is, so he sees himself as Goku or Guile from ‘Street Fighter,’ the animation going 2D in an action-heavy tone. But when we meet Mermahn, he is very shallow and narcissistic, and we felt his glamorous point of view fit the aesthetic of ‘Sailor Moon’ with the silly kind of heart-shaped lens flare.”.

Still, just because you can go Super Saiyan doesn’t mean you let go of reality. Instead, the directors worked with the head of cinematography, Scott Cullen, to make sure the film had a live-action look to it. The idea was to capture the nostalgia of growing up, while being able to feel the camera in the space the action takes place in, as if it was a physical set.

“Joel and I really wanted to make sure you feel like live-action, you feel the cameras there, and the way the light interacts with the lens is reminiscent of tangible photos we grew up taking, where you don’t know how they’ll develop,” Mercado stated. “ We wanted to add imperfections, and to have interaction of weather on the camera, like condensation of rain and droplets on the camera.”.

This all added to making “Forgotten Island” look like a part of the evolution of DreamWorks Animation, while standing out as something entirely fresh and unique. As Crawford stated, the studio doesn’t really have a specific house style like other big studios. “Every movie requires innovation and pushing boundaries and finding solutions,” he added.

8 Thrillers That Become Masterpieces in the Last 30 Minutes

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1374 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Collider

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Audiences seek movies as a temporary escape from reality, yet they challenge their minds and send a tingle down their spines.
  • In a recent development, some great thrillers start off strong but end with a whimper.
  • Sources indicate that directed by David Fincher and written by Gillian Flynn, Gone Girl became the definitive domestic psychological thriller.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Audiences seek movies as a temporary escape from reality, yet they challenge their minds and send a tingle down their spines. A good thriller triggers a cinematic fight-or-flight from the safety of your seat. They get to play along, becoming active participants as they try to outsmart the plot, crack the mystery, or guess the villain's motives before the reveal.

In a recent development, some great thrillers start off strong but end with a whimper. Then there are those that become legendary masterpieces within the final 30 minutes. From shocking twists you never saw coming to terrifying revelations that reshape the entire narrative, these 10 thriller films leave a lasting impression long after the final credits roll.

Sources indicate that directed by David Fincher and written by Gillian Flynn, Gone Girl became the definitive domestic psychological thriller. The story follows Nick Dunne (Ben Affleck) as he becomes the prime suspect in the sudden disappearance of his wife, Amy (Rosamund Pike), on their fifth wedding anniversary. As the police and media circus close in, a series of dark twists reveals that neither spouse is who they appear to be, exposing a deeply toxic and manipulative marriage.

Rather than ending with a neat resolution, the climax traps the characters in a dark, satirical commentary on modern marriage and media manipulation. Amy’s return home isn't a relief; it is a life sentence for Nick. By using her pregnancy to lock him into the marriage, Amy ensures total control, turning the happy ending into a satire. Gone Girl's final minutes expose their marriage as a performance, with both partners actively playing a role for public consumption, while Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross' score provides a false sense of calm.

It has been revealed that david Lynch's masterpiece Mulholland Drive is a gem from the start of the 21st century. The surreal thriller follows an aspiring actress, Betty (Naomi Watts), who helps an amnesiac woman, Rita (Laura Harring), piece together her identity after a car crash in Los Angeles. The story fractures into a dark, dreamlike puzzle that blurs the line between Hollywood fantasy and a tragic, guilt-ridden reality.

Industry observers note that in the final 30 minutes, Lynch transforms the movie from a strange neo-noir mystery into a devastating psychological portrait, turning a surreal thriller into a raw, heartbreaking tragedy about loneliness and self-destruction. The pastel glamour is ripped away to reveal the raw, grim reality of Diane Selwyn, a depressed, failed actress consumed by jealousy, unrequited love, and crushing guilt. Lynch reframes the entire movie as a study of how people use romantic illusions, denial, and fantasy to escape personal failure and moral decay.

According to recent reports, directed and co-written by Park Chan-wook, the South Korean action thriller Oldboy follows Oh Dae-su (Choi Min-sik), who, after being mysteriously kidnapped and imprisoned in a single room for 15 years, is suddenly released and given five days to track down his captor and uncover the motive behind his torment. His quest for vengeance leads him down a dark path of shocking revelations and devastating secrets.

A truly diabolical story, Oldboy transforms a brutal revenge thriller into an epic tragedy, shifting the story from physical violence to total psychological devastation. Dae-su fights through conspiracies and brutal hand-to-hand corridors, expecting a typical action-hero resolution: the hero kills the villain and wins. Instead, we have something far more twisting and crueler. In the final snowy sequence, the lingering, ambiguous look on the protagonist's face highlights that trauma cannot simply be excised; instead, it's something one must learn to accept or else be consumed by it.

Recent findings suggest that in Prisoners, directed by Denis Villeneuve, the story follows Keller Dover (Hugh Jackman) as he desperately searches for his young daughter and her friend after they go missing on Thanksgiving. When Detective Loki (Jake Gyllenhaal) releases the prime suspect, Alex Jones (Paul Dano), for lack of evidence, Dover takes matters into his own hands, pushing moral boundaries as a dedicated detective races against time to solve the mystery.

Recent findings suggest that the grim, gripping drama unravels as the complex moral framework builds to an intense, clock-ticking climax that recontextualizes everything that came before. After a series of wrong choices, Keller is trapped in the secret pit—the very place his daughter was kept, forced to face the literal and spiritual hole he dug for himself. Loki stands in the freezing cold, hearing the faint sound of Anna’s red whistle from the ground, leaving Keller’s rescue uncertain. With a perfectly ambiguous ending, we are left to decide whether he deserves salvation after the atrocities he committed.​​​​​​​.

Few films elicit guttural reactions quite like Se7en. Directed by David Fincher, the psychological crime drama follows two homicide detectives, William Somerset (Morgan Freeman), a veteran nearing retirement, and David Mills (Brad Pitt), his upcoming, hot-headed partner, as they track a meticulous serial killer (Kevin Spacey), who uses the seven deadly sins as motifs for his gruesome murders.

Se7en becomes an exceptionally dark police procedural by subverting classic Hollywood tropes, shifting power psychologically, and delivering a devastatingly bleak moral conclusion. John Doe turns himself in, halting the “catch the killer” momentum. Thrust into a bright, vast, and barren desert landscape under harsh daylight, the protagonists are exposed as Doe dominates the action. The movie ends with the antagonist successfully completing his horrific masterpiece, leaving the audience with an overwhelming sense of dread.

Scorsese’s crime thriller The Departed follows Billy Costigan Jr. (DiCaprio), an undercover cop who infiltrates an Irish gang, and Colin Sullivan (Matt Damon), a mole within the police department who secretly works for the gang's kingpin. Both sides eventually realize a traitor lurks in their ranks, sparking a deadly, high-stakes race for each man to uncover the other's identity before his own is exposed.

In a recent development, in the final thirty minutes, The Departed delivers a relentless, breathless cascade of subversion, consequences, and brutal payoffs. Right when audiences expect a traditional cinematic confrontation between Costigan and Sullivan, the movie pulls the rug out. Sergeant Dignam (Mark Wahlberg) acts as a silent instrument of pure karma, delivering a deeply satisfying yet bleakly cynical conclusion. The final, poetic shot of a literal rat scurrying across Sullivan's balcony acts as punctuation: corruption is foundational, the system is deeply broken, and the cycle of duplicity survives long after the players are dead.​​​​​​​.

Industry observers note that the Prestige may be one of Christopher Nolan's most quintessential films. Set in 19th-century London, the story centers on two rival stage magicians, Robert Angier (Jackman) and Alfred Borden (Christian Bale), who engage in a bitter, obsessive feud to create the ultimate illusion. Their fierce competition escalates into a dangerous game of sabotage and deceit, costing them everything they hold dear.

According to recent reports, established as a magic trick, the film’s final act executes a perfect structural "Prestige"—the final stage of a magic trick where everything hidden is dramatically revealed. The opening monologue by Cutter (Michael Caine) explaining the Pledge, the Turn, and the Prestige is the blueprint for the entire film. Ultimately, as they try to destroy each other, Borden loses his brother and the woman he loved, while Angier loses his humanity entirely. The Prestige is a brilliant revenge thriller with an unforgettable gut-punch of an ending.

Directed by Bryan Singer, The Usual Suspects follows five criminals who meet during a routine police lineup and blueprint a heist, only to be blackmailed by a mysterious, legendary crime lord named Keyser Söze. The entire story is told through the interrogation and flashbacks of the sole survivor of a subsequent, bloody boat explosion, Verbal Kint (Spacey).

Sources indicate that the final revelation remains one of cinema's greatest endings, reconfiguring the thriller into a masterclass in psychological manipulation and the malleability of truth. The final sequence reveals that Verbal fabricated the entire story on the spot using random objects sitting on Kujan's office bulletin board and desk. As Verbal walks out of the precinct, drops his limp, and lights a cigarette, the film cuts back through the previous 90 minutes. Every little aspect here is designed to mislead. Verbal played the part so effectively that the hunter sat across from the devil the whole time without ever noticing.

This was not just a flash in the pan, but a real talent with a seemingly boundless number of ideas and movies he wanted to make. His next film, “Anything but Ghosts,” was already in the can by the “Obsession” premiere, a yet-to-be-declared third film is in the works, while potential franchises (“Texas Chainsaw Massacre” and “Obsession,” Barker sees the One Wish Willow story device having “Knives Out” anthology-like potential) linger in the background. Related Stories Director Brian Duffield Had to Find a New Form of Visual Storytelling for ‘Whalefall’ How ‘Paper Tiger’ Evolved When Jeremy Strong and Anne Hathaway Couldn’t Reprise Their ‘Armageddon Time’ Roles.

Which is why it’s interesting that Hollywood’s hottest new director took time out from editing (he’s cutting “Ghosts” himself) and writing (“I have my next thing that I’m working on — I’m really excited about it, and nobody knows anything about it, which is super exciting”), and an unexpected Oscar campaign (“Obsession” is a legit contender for Best Picture, Actress, and Original Screenplay nominations), to make a 5-minute short film, “Mama Bear.” On this week’s episode of the Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast, Barker talked about how the success of “Obsession” interrupted his established flow of churning out short-form content for his popular YouTube channel.

In a recent development, “I have two or three short films where I’m like, ‘Oh man, this all took off really quickly, and I have this short film idea I’ve been dying to do,” mentioned Barker on Toolkit. “I actually have no time to do those short films, and then justifying if it be would be worth my time to do them when I need to be writing this, I need to be editing this, and I need to be doing press for this.”.

It’s less about Barker’s desire to scratch the itch of the shorts he never got to make, but more about a hesitancy to step away completely from the iterative process by which he learned his craft — justifying the brief time he took off to make “Mama Bear” because he felt the need to sketch.

It has been revealed that “It’s fun to have that playground because the features are bigger stakes,” said Barker. “We were like, ‘Okay, this is a short film: We can do weird stuff. Let’s come up with crazy rules that don’t make sense, and experiment.’”.

According to recent reports, barker and his “Mama Bear” cinematographer — his young brother Riley, who worked on the “Obsession” camera department — created different rules for the camera, as Curry is still trying to hone his discipline for storytelling within longer takes. Not only would they shoot a narrow 4:3 aspect ratio, but the Barker brothers denied themselves the ability to move the camera left, right, up, down, or dolly in.

“I do have a lot to learn,” mentioned Barker of making “Mama Bear.” “It’s so funny because I was having dinner and I told someone, ‘Oh, I’d love to shadow on Ari Aster’s set.’ And someone was like, ‘Well, you’re Curry Barker, what are you going to shadow for?’”.

His 2026 meteoric rise has allowed Barker to collect a group of more experienced peers he views as mentors — including Aster, Bill Hader, Zach Cregger, and Rian Johnson — and successful producers, like Jason Blum, investing in his career, but he believes there’s a misconception of what comes along with “making it.”.

“People think that once you’re in this club, you’re in the club, and everyone talks to everyone. But no — you’re in a bubble, and I want to know how Zach Cregger writes his outline. I want to watch him do it,” said Barker. “You’re all alone. Your process is your own, and you figure this stuff out on your own. Once you get into this league, there’s no one telling you, ‘Well, actually you do it like this, this, and this.’ It’s whatever you learned all along your journey; that’s your process.”.

One of the most impressive things about the self-taught Barker’s journey is how quickly he turned himself into a successful actor/writer/director/editor. In 2018, when Barker left Alabama to come to Los Angeles to pursue a career in movies, he saw himself as an actor. Despite all the story scenarios dancing around his head, the idea that he would become a screenwriter was laughable.

Recent findings suggest that “I never would’ve thought I was a screenwriter. I didn’t make great grades. I made Cs and Ds, and I wasn’t the best in English class,” said Barker, who naively assumed professional writers were the kids who won spelling bees: “I just thought to be respected as a writer you have to be that.” Barker credits taking screenwriter Aaron Sorkin’s MasterClass as what opened his eyes. “It was the first time I thought, ‘I can do this, too.’ It’s really just about being creative and cracking a story, and there are rules, there’s structure.”.

Industry observers note that directing organically grew out of Barker pulling together collaborators to shoot sketches and shorts for him to act in. Barker, half-joking, likes to say he realized one day that what he was doing was directing, and that he both enjoyed “telling people what to do” and had a knack for it.

According to recent reports, what Barker accomplishes in a single shot — establishing a tonal balance that teeters between horror and comedy, combining blocking and camera movement to edit within the frame — is remarkably sophisticated. But Barker, who studies and strives for what masters like Kiyoshi Kurosawa can accomplish, quickly says he fell short in “Obsession.”.

In a recent development, “Things that you might think we pulled off [with longer takes in ‘Obsession’], we reshot,” said Barker, who on the podcast described in detail a key early scene between Bear (Michael Johnston) and Nikki (Inde Navarrette) in the bedroom that had to be reshot because the action took too long to unfold. “I think Ari [Aster] said once that if you realize you needed to give this information in four seconds, but then it took 25 seconds, you’re stuck with 25 seconds.”.

Curry Barker, the editor, is Curry Barker, the director’s harshest critic, giving him a bird’s-eye view of what he believes is the director’s inability to envision the required pacing of how a scene will play on screen, even if it might feel unnaturally fast on set.

Industry observers note that “Every single oner that I’ve shot in my career has been a problem in the edit,” noted Barker. “I think there’s two ways to fail at something. You can either fail, realize that it didn’t work, get scared of it, and then be like, ‘Well, in my last film I did a bunch of oners and then it killed me in the edit, so I’m not going to do that anymore.’ Or you can fail, realize how you did it wrong, and try to get better at that for the next time.”.

As Barker discussed at the Future of Filmmaking Summit last month, that iterative process is key to how he got where he is, and it’s a mindset he clearly hasn’t given up. When asked how “Obsession” would have been different if he had more money, Barker doesn’t talk about locations, sets, special or visual effects, or scenes he envisioned that he couldn’t pull off — in terms of scale, he likes both writing and directing within set limitations.

“I would’ve reshot everything,” Barker answered without hesitation. “If I was finishing the edit before we got into TIFF, and you were like, ‘Dude, this is really good, we really love this movie, we think it has potential, but we want to give you $10 million to reshoot the whole thing, I would be like, ‘Deal.’ I would take it.”.

According to recent reports, “I think it’s so funny to look back and think about that now,” Barker catches himself, knowing he’s talking about a film that broke the box office and catapulted his career. “Now I wouldn’t change anything because I would be too scared to touch it.”.

Tech Report: Apple among the companies facing pressure from US senators over ‘nudify’ apps [U: Apple, TTP respond]

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1506 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the Guardian reports that three US senators have sent letters to the CEOs of Apple, Google, and Meta, demanding answers about their failure to prevent access to AI-powered ‘nudify’ apps.
  • Last month, Apple updated its App Store rules in an attempt to crack down on apps that enable owners to generate nonconsensual nude images.
  • According to the updated rules, apps that allow users to create AI-generated content must include safeguards against abuse, including tools to filter objectionable material, report offensive content, and block abusive users.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the Guardian reports that three US senators have sent letters to the CEOs of Apple, Google, and Meta, demanding answers about their failure to prevent access to AI-powered ‘nudify’ apps. Here are the details.

Last month, Apple updated its App Store rules in an attempt to crack down on apps that enable owners to generate nonconsensual nude images.

According to the updated rules, apps that allow users to create AI-generated content must include safeguards against abuse, including tools to filter objectionable material, report offensive content, and block abusive users.

Apple also warns that apps used primarily for pornographic content or the objectification of real people may be removed from the App Store without notice.

While definitely well-intended, Apple’s changes came amid growing reports of AI-powered nudify apps, which easily allow users to generate nonconsensual intimate images.

Two months before these changes, Apple removed an app that allowed owners to create pornographic deepfakes of real people after WIRED reached out for comment, which in turn came one month after San Francisco City Attorney David Chiu demanded that Apple and Google remove several nudify apps from their app stores.

Apple also removed several apps following investigations by the Tech Transparency Project (TTP), which published reports in January and April revealing that such apps were widely available on the App Store, sometimes even appearing in sponsored search results.

Throughout these investigations, Apple has maintained that nudify apps have always been prohibited under its App Review Guidelines, and that it proactively rejects and removes apps that violate its policies, including those flagged through user reports.

Apple, of course, is not alone in this challenge, with Google facing similar criticism over their availability on the Play Store, and Meta coming under scrutiny for allowing developers to advertise these apps on Facebook and Instagram, as highlighted in the WIRED report mentioned above.

Which brings us to today’s report from The Guardian.

According to The Guardian’s exclusive report, “three Senate Democrats sent letters to tech CEOs saying safeguards against nudification apps are insufficient on their platforms.”.

Sources indicate that A trio of US Senators say Apple and Google are failing to effectively detect and remove apps that can be used to generate nonconsensual nude or pornographic imagery. They also say Meta is continuing to profit off of ads for these so-called nudification apps that “victimize women and girls worldwide”.

The senators, namely Ron Wyden of Oregon, Ed Markey of Massachusetts, and Ben Luján of Latest Mexico, claim that in addition to failing to remove these apps, the companies may actually be profiting from their distribution and promotion.

Commenting on the letter, both Google and Meta said they prohibit such apps or their promotion and work to detect and remove violations from their platforms, broadly echoing what Apple has repeatedly stated when reached for comment in the past over these same problems.

However, Wyden’s office argues that simply reaffirming, or in Apple’s case, updating these policies, means little if the companies continue to struggle to enforce them.

Industry observers note that keith Chu, the chief communications adviser and deputy policy director to Wyden, said that clarifying policies is not the same thing as enforcing them. Despite the companies reaffirming the prohibition of these apps, they continue to proliferate across Apple and Google app stores or be promoted in ads on Meta platforms, he added.

In its latest investigation, published just last month, TTP found 135 apps capable of generating nude or pornographic imagery on the App Store and the Play Store, using accounts registered to 13-year-old boys.

Additionally, researchers found that even accounts configured with parental controls were able to download these apps without requiring parental approval.

Despite Apple and Google removing the apps identified in the investigation, The Guardian noted that these apps continued to work on devices where they had already been installed.

Now, Senator Wyden warns that Congress may need to step in if the companies fail to do a better job of cracking down on these apps.

To read The Guardian’s full report, follow this link.

Sources indicate that patch, 8:40 p.m. ET: In a statement to 9to5Mac, Apple said:.

“We designed the App Store to be a safe and trusted place for users. A number of the apps in the TTP report are mainstream photo and video editing tools with legitimate, widely used functionality, and do not have nudification or deepfake capabilities. We prohibit nudify apps on the App Store, and remove developers who add capabilities like it after the App Review process — a malicious tactic known as bait-and-switch. We previously removed 28 of the apps referenced in this report before it was shared with us and have taken action on the remaining apps found to violate our rules. The report also relies on testing from older software that does not reflect current Apple safety features, including expanded protections for teens and parental controls in Screen Time that give families the ability to block kids and teens from downloading apps rated above their age.”.

Expanding on the safety features mentioned in its statement, Apple noted that teens aged 13 through 17 now have certain protections enabled by default, including web content filters, even if their parents haven’t configured any restrictions, and pointed to ⁠this support article for more information.

The firm added that children under 13 are required to use Child Accounts, and that the report relied on its previous 17+ age rating system, which was replaced last year with a more granular system that includes 13+, 16+, and 18+ ratings.

Just curious. Why doesn't someone from Apple try out the app before approving it, rather than approving it and waiting until people complain? I know there are many thousands of apps on the App store. But given that Apple makes money off most of these apps, it could surely afford to hire a staff charged with reviewing submitted apps to ensure compliance with the App store's guidelines and requirements before making them available in the App store. What am I missing here?

Apple also noted that in its report, TTP counted apps depicting people in swimwear or lingerie, which the tech giant mentioned does not constitute nudification or, in itself, violate its guidelines.

As for parental controls, Apple explained that, although apps that exceed a child’s configured age restrictions won’t appear in curated App Store sections, they can still be found through search, allowing children to request permission to download them through Ask to Buy. Without parental approval, the download remains blocked.

Industry observers note that apple added that Ask to Buy is supposed to require parental approval even for purchases made using gift card balances, including subscriptions. The company noted that if a purchase didn’t trigger an approval request, that would be unexpected behavior, and that it is investigating further.

Industry observers note that upgrade, November 19, 4:00 p.m. ET: In response to Apple’s statement, TTP director Katie Paul reached out to 9to5Mac with the following comment:.

In a recent development, apple’s statement on nudify apps sidesteps crucial complications and leaves out key context. The company states it prohibits nudify apps but doesn’t address how its age rating system for apps contributes to the problem. TTP has shown how Apple relies on information provided by app developers to set age ratings—a self-reporting system that allows many nudify and pornographic apps to be misleadingly labeled a suitable for minors. Apple also continues to talk about removing nudify apps from the App Store, without mentioning that apps that are “removed” continue to be fully functional on people’s phones.

According to recent reports, there are many questions about Apple’s policy on nudify apps that the statement fails to address. Apple has adopted a limited definition of “nudify.” The company defines nudify apps as capable of showing someone naked, not stripping them down to a bikini or lingerie. But the company also notes it bans “creepy” and “nonconsensual intimate imagery.” What if an app is used to depict a woman in a bikini without her consent? We have asked Apple to clarify that and have not heard back.

As for Apple’s comment that TTP relied on “older software,” that may refer to the fact that Apple rolled out fresh child safety features in the fall. Our research was conducted in summer 2026. But many of Apple’s new features pertain to parent-supervised accounts on Apple, which have to be set up by a parent. Apple relies entirely on parents to go out of their way to locate and enable these settings. This raises obvious questions about how many people actually do this.

How World-Class Filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev Came Back to Life for ‘Minotaur’

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1281 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Indiewire

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • [Editor’s note: This interview was originally published during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival.
  • Industry observers note that world-class Russian filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev (“Leviathan”) returned to the Croisette this year in Cannes competition with “Minotaur,” having recovered from a near-fatal illness.
  • When he left the hospital in Germany in 2022, as he told me while at Cannes this year, he was in a wheelchair.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

[Editor’s note: This interview was originally published during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. MUBI will release “Minotaur” in theaters on Friday, November 20.].

Industry observers note that world-class Russian filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev (“Leviathan”) returned to the Croisette this year in Cannes competition with “Minotaur,” having recovered from a near-fatal illness. After contracting a severe case of COVID in 2021, he reacted badly to the Sputnik vaccine and was put into a medically induced coma for 14 days. When he came out of it, his arms and legs were paralyzed due to Guillain-Barré Syndrome. He lay flat on his back for a year.

When he left the hospital in Germany in 2022, as he told me while at Cannes this year, he was in a wheelchair. While he states he hasn’t watched TV for 20 years now, “I watched a lot of films online,” he said through an interpreter on the roof of the Palais. “I read some things. I did not know if I would ever be able to walk again, to live again as a normal person. I have still now some consequences. I’m not at my best. I have regained completely the motion of my hands, but I have still a bit of a difficulty walking.” Related Stories If There’s Generative AI in ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,’ It’s Not the First Time David Fincher’s Used It Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage.

But he did manage to shoot his sixth feature film last year, but not in Russia. After nine months of waiting, in the spring of 2023, he let go of one expensive project (“Jupiter”) for which he couldn’t seem to raise funding. “I stated, ‘Let’s put it on ice, we’ll come back to it later. I don’t want to sit and wait for years and years for you to find the money. I want to make a film now.'”.

So instead the filmmaker focused on a parallel project he had also been developing, an adaptation of Claude Chabrol’s 1969 thriller “The Unfaithful Wife,” starring Stéphane Audran as a well-heeled wife cheating on her husband, which was later remade as “Unfaithful” with Richard Gere and Diane Lane. The result, “Minotaur,” is the “Leviathan” Oscar nominee’s first film in nearly a decade, since 2017’s “Loveless.”.

At the same time that the filmmaker was coping with his illness, four years ago, at the start of the Ukraine war, he made the decision to leave Russia and move to Paris. Going home would mean the risk of being considered a traitor or an enemy of the state in Russia. “It might result in us becoming what is called foreign agents; it’s a hard thing,” he said. “Maybe this will happen, maybe not. Let’s not be too pessimistic, but mostly all independent journalists are saying that their oppressions are going to get even harsher, and that I think we have decades ahead of us before things get better.”.

His 16-year-old had been studying at a French high school in Moscow before the war. “His French was pretty good,” said Zvyagintsev. “So it was an obvious choice. And also, my wife [has been] in love with France for a long time, she has been learning French for many years. So it was a choice, also for both of them, and for their future.”.

It has been revealed that how’s his French? “Zero,” he said. “The other reason for me was that France is the homeland to cinema; that’s where cinema was born, and also there are so many cinephiles among spectators. Also here in France, directors have the final cut. In the states, it’s much harder to get in a position where you are not censored; it’s not a producer or someone who decides instead of you.”.

The filmmaker set about creating believable Russian locations in Riga, Latvia, which still resembles its neighbor country. “The dormitory suburbs around Riga look exactly like Russian dormitory suburbs,” remarked Zvyagintsev. “A Russian eye would not be able to distinguish between Russia and Latvia in this instance. As for interiors, Anton’s flat was constructed as a set, so it’s a constructed set, and the villa where the main characters live is a contemporary building, a very modern one, and you could find something exactly like this anywhere.”.

When it came to finding his cast, the casting director put out a call for Russian characters of a certain age. “Every actor from anywhere who is interested in working with you, they will send you a video presentation,” remarked Zvyagintsev. “They can be from Argentina, London, Moscow, Paris, wherever. You send them a scene they have to play, and they make a self-tape for you on their iPhone. Before, I despised self-tapes, but it’s convenient, because now with everybody scattered around the world, it’s the only way for us to work. We could not possibly pay for all the people I wanted to check to come to Riga to make a real-life casting. There were people also from Riga who do speak Russian.”.

One serious issue for Russian actors still living in Russia was the possible repercussions of participating in a Zvyagintsev project. “I would talk to them about the script and show them parts of the script, so that they know what they’re getting involved in, because, of course, they were at risk of getting blacklisted,” he said. “Most of them, with heartache, refused to take part in the film, but there was one who accepted, and I’m still completely amazed at his courage. It’s the main part, the main character, [actor] Dmitriy Mazurov. I said to him, ‘Are you sure you want to film with me?’ And he said, ‘If I’m not doing this part, I don’t know what I’m doing in acting.'”.

Of course, the filmmaker took a different approach to the Chabrol story. “In the first minute, the story is completely revealed,” he stated. “We understand that she is being unfaithful, so then all the film is about observing him, observing her, trying to understand, hesitating, and trying to guess what is going on, and while he observes, the spectator starts doing it along with him. And after the murder, actually, he goes back to this position where he’s mostly observing her reaction to the disappearance of a lover, yeah, and she knows what’s going on, and again it’s about observation.”.

According to recent reports, the filmmaker loved one bravura sequence that is 20 minutes long without any dialogue at all. “The sequence after the murder, it’s 20 minutes, even a little bit more, with not one subtitle, so you only observe his actions, and there are no words: it’s extremely cinematic in its essence.”.

And Zvyagintsev added many telling details from the real world, from corruption to the war. “The Chabrol film is much more classical,” he stated. “It follows a pattern: he killed, then he’s discovered, and then he will be punished. And I wanted to break up this classical structure and to invent something different based on our Russian realities.”.

In a recent development, was shooting the movie a physical challenge? “When you are full of inspiration, when you are searching constantly for solutions, the light, the sets, the performance of the actors, you don’t feel fatigued in the same way,” he said. “There is such a joy in making the film that is, in your head, real. I think it’s the best drug there is.”.

Next up, he will try and resuscitate “Jupiter.” ” I have met some producers who are interested in it,” he stated, “so hopefully we will be able to get it moving again.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every once in a while, Instagram rolls out an enhancement that addresses one of its consumers’ most longstanding requests. Today is one of those days.

As spotted by The Verge, Instagram head Adam Mosseri confirmed today that the app will finally let users edit a Story after publishing.

This means customers will be able to add stickers and drawings, fix typos or adjust text, and even change the music without having to delete the Story and publish it again, which would mean losing any views it had already received.

The catch is that consumers will only have 15 minutes after publishing a Story to make changes by tapping the ellipsis button at the bottom of the screen, and then selecting “Edit story.”.

Here’s Mosseri’s post announcing the news:.

A post shared by Adam Mosseri (@mosseri).

Today’s update is the latest in a series of changes Instagram has made this year to address longstanding user requests.

Recent findings suggest that back in March, the app introduced the ability to reorder photos and videos in a carousel after publishing. In April, it added an option to edit comments (also within 15 minutes of posting), and in June, it began letting consumers manually rearrange posts on their profile grid.

More recently, Instagram also brought its free Edits video editor to the Mac, with multi-track editing, advanced color grading tools, and 4K exports.

The 10 Best Open Endings in Film History, Ranked

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3017 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Collider

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the wonder of the movies is how they make us feel long after the final credits roll.
  • In a recent development, from characters running off in a latest direction to the spinning top that still has audiences debating today, these open endings shape the entire film, sometimes reframing everything that came before.
  • It has been revealed that in Martin Scorsese’s neo-noir psychological thriller Shutter Island, U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the wonder of the movies is how they make us feel long after the final credits roll. No matter the genre, a great film that has a brilliant ending tends to be remembered for generations. Now, a great ending doesn’t always mean that it’s tied up neatly in a bow. Sometimes an open-ended conclusion is just as impactful as one that has a definitive answer. While some brilliant films have open endings, the ten on this list are among the best in film history.

In a recent development, from characters running off in a latest direction to the spinning top that still has audiences debating today, these open endings shape the entire film, sometimes reframing everything that came before. These stories that blur reality and illusion force audiences to confront their own desire for neat closure. How many of these monumental conclusions left your jaw on the floor or left you with an array of emotions?

It has been revealed that in Martin Scorsese’s neo-noir psychological thriller Shutter Island, U.S. Marshal Teddy Daniels (Leonardo DiCaprio) and his partner Chuck Aule (Mark Ruffalo) travel to a remote psychiatric facility for the criminally insane on Shutter Island to investigate the mysterious disappearance of a patient. As a massive storm cuts them off from the mainland, Teddy uncovers dark secrets about the hospital's experimental treatments while struggling with his own haunting past and deteriorating grip on reality. By the end of the film, audiences are taken for a ride when it’s revealed that Teddy is actually Andrew Laeddis, a long-term patient at Ashecliffe Hospital who murdered his wife, Dolores (Michelle Williams), after she drowned their three children. He created the persona to cope with the trauma and guilt. After briefly accepting the truth at the lighthouse, Andrew sits outside with Dr. Sheehan (Ruffalo) and slips back into calling him "Chuck," talking as if they need to escape the island. The final line of the film, as orderlies approach to take him away for a lobotomy, Andrew asks Dr. Sheehan: "Which would be worse: to live as a monster, or to die as a good man?".

According to recent reports, the film’s ending stands out because it turns a psychological twist into a tragic moral choice. Rather than ending on a simple shock, its final exchange leaves room for debate over whether Andrew Laeddis/Teddy Daniels has relapsed into madness or is choosing a lobotomy to escape unbearable guilt. While Dennis Lehane’s book leans more clearly toward a relapse into delusion, Scorsese’s film leaves Andrew’s true state of mind more open to interpretation. Knowing the twist forces a second look at the clues, flashbacks, and performances throughout the movie. While other conclusions sparked more debate, Shutter Island made both sides feel their point was the ultimate conclusion. Was it a conscious decision? Is it a calculated choice to fake a relapse? Could it genuinely be ambiguous between insanity and manipulation? That’s the brilliance of the film’s ending.

Industry observers note that david Lynch’s defining film of the 21st century is Mulholland Drive. In this surreal mystery, a bright-eyed aspiring actress named Betty Elms (Naomi Watts) arrives in Los Angeles and teams up with Rita (Laura Harring), an amnesiac woman who survived a violent car crash, to uncover her true identity. As they follow clues through a shadowy Hollywood filled with underworld interference and a mysterious blue box, the narrative abruptly fractures, revealing a tragic, guilt-ridden reality behind their glamorous illusions. After a massive twist is revealed, the film ends with Diane Selwyn, the real identity behind the earlier dream persona Betty Elms, dying by suicide in her apartment after a blue key confirms the hitman she hired has murdered her former lover, Camila Rhodes, the real-life inspiration for Rita. Following her death, the film cuts to surreal, overlapping imagery of Los Angeles and a blue-haired woman in the theater whispering "Silencio.”.

Sources indicate that lynch left the film's exact meaning open to interpretation. It turns a traditional mystery into a psychological mirror that rewards repeated viewings. Instead of tying up loose ends, the final stretch fractures the earlier story and leaves viewers to piece together illusion, guilt, and desire. The shift from Betty Elms’s optimistic Hollywood adventure to Diane Selwyn’s bleak reality reframes what came before as a wish-fulfillment dream or nightmare. Because Lynch never locks in on a single literal explanation, the boundary between waking life, memory, and delusion stays alive. The film treats ambiguity as art, not a riddle. By letting the glamorous fairy tale collapse into rejection, obsession, and tragedy, the ending exposes the harsher side of ambition in Los Angeles. Of course, with much of his work, opinions are mixed, with some praising his conceptual, norm-defying storytelling and others viewing it as self-indulgent. Regardless, the ending operates as if that final piece is a stellar jigsaw puzzle. ​​​​​​​.

Industry observers note that even romantic comedies can have an open ending. Such is the case in Sofia Coppola’s stellar Lost in Translation. In the film, fading American movie star Bob Harris (Bill Murray) and neglected young newlywed Charlotte (Scarlett Johansson) cross paths at a luxury hotel in Tokyo as they both struggle with insomnia and personal disillusionment. Despite their age gap, the two lonely strangers form a deep, unconventional bond as they explore the foreign city together, finding brief solace from their isolating marriages and cultural displacement. At the end of the film, Bob spots Charlotte in a crowded Tokyo street while riding in his car to the airport, stops to catch up with her, hugs her, and whispers something inaudible in her ear. Charlotte replies softly, “okay,” kisses her, and departs as both walk away smiling.

So, what’s behind their glamorous illusions whisper? Coppola has noted that the whispered line was unscripted and left unvoiced, so the moment stays private between the characters and open to viewers. By keeping Bob’s whisper inaudible to the audience, the film preserves a private moment strictly between Bob and Charlotte. Instead of a tidy romantic cliché or a permanent life overhaul, the ending reflects how fleeting, melancholic connections in transit can quietly shift how two people see themselves going forward. The ending invites personal projection about longing, closure, and human connection. It’s the perfect ending because the mood, silence, and shared isolation carry more weight than traditional plot twists, making an ambiguous parting feel earned. ​​​​​​​.

One of the greatest classic romantic comedies still today is The Graduate. Directed by Mike Nichols, the film follows recent college graduate Benjamin Braddock (Dustin Hoffman) as he returns to his parents' California home and is seduced into a secret affair by Mrs. Robinson (Anne Bancroft), the older married wife of his father's business partner (Murray Hamilton). Things turn chaotic when Benjamin genuinely falls in love with Mrs. Robinson's daughter, Elaine (Katharine Ross), forcing him to navigate a messy love triangle and confront generational expectations. In a dramatic conclusion, Benjamin crashes Elaine’s wedding to Carl Smith (Brian Avery) in Santa Barbara, fending off the guests with a large cross, and fleeing with Elaine on a city bus. After initial smiles of triumph, their expressions fade into uncertainty and quiet dread as the reality of their impulsive escape sets in.

The open ending of The Graduate is widely praised because it subverts the traditional romantic "happily ever after" and captures the sudden, quiet reality after a major act of rebellion. Their initial triumph and adrenaline fade into silence and uncertainty. Rather than giving Benjamin a neat transformation, the lingering shot on the bus highlights his continuing lack of direction and raises a "what now?" question once the rebellion ends. Nichols let the camera keep rolling past the expected celebratory beat, forcing audiences to reconcile with the less-than-perfect punchline. From a grander macro lens, by trading tidy Hollywood closure for ambiguity and psychological realism, the finale helped usher in the Upcoming Hollywood era. ​​​​​​​.

Sources indicate that though it may be strikingly different than Bret Easton Ellis’ masterpiece novel, American Psycho is a pitch-perfect horror comedy. In the Mary Harron-directed film, Patrick Bateman (Christian Bale) is a wealthy and narcissistic Wall Street investment banker who hides his psychopathic nature behind a superficial, status-obsessed exterior. As his violent impulses escalate into a string of brutal murders against colleagues and strangers, his sanity unravels, and his confessions go ignored in a hollow society indifferent to his crimes. By the bitter end, Patrick breaks down, leaves a frantic voicemail confessing to dozens of murders, including Paul Allen (Jared Leto), to his lawyer Harold Carnes (Stephen Bogaert), and then discovers no one believes him or cares. When he visits Paul Allen’s apartment to clean up the bodies, a real estate agent, Mrs. Wolfe (Patricia Gage), is showing the empty, freshly painted unit and orders him to leave. At a restaurant with colleagues, Bateman confronts Harold about the confession. Harold mistakes him for someone else, laughs the message off as a joke, and says he recently had dinner with Paul Allen in London. Bateman returns to his superficial peer group, realizing in a final voice-over that his confession means nothing, and he will never face punishment or true recognition.

Recent findings suggest that so what does it all mean? It’s not an exit but an existential metaphorical trap. It turns Patrick’s unreliability into a sharp critique of 1980s consumerism and elite indifference, leaving viewers to debate whether his crimes were real or imagined. In a status-obsessed world where everyone looks and acts alike, nobody pays close enough attention for accountability to matter. Bateman wants recognition, even as a monster, yet the world around him remains indifferent and unbothered. Because the ending refuses to lock in one literal answer, viewers keep re-evaluating every clue, from Bateman's shifting mask to whether the real-estate cover-up protected property values or exposed his psychosis. ​​​​​​​.

Industry observers note that one of the most influential sci-fi thrillers of all time is Blade Runner. Directed by Ridley Scott, the film, set in a dystopian 2019 Los Angeles, follows retired cop Rick Deckard (Harrison Ford) as he is forced back into duty to hunt down and "retire" four rogue replicants, bioengineered humanoids who have escaped off-world slave labor to seek out their creator and extend their four-year lifespans. As Deckard pursues the fugitives and falls for an advanced replicant named Rachael (Sean Young), the neo-noir thriller explores deep philosophical questions about memory, empathy, and what truly defines humanity. At the end of the film, replicant leader Roy Batty (Rutger Hauer) saves Deckard from falling off a rooftop, delivers his famous "tears in rain" monologue reflecting on his fading memories, and dies as a white dove flies away. Deckard then returns to his apartment, finds the replicant Rachael, and leaves with her.

Sources indicate that with two variations on the ending that evoke different feelings, the film turns its central mystery into an active question for the viewer rather than a solved puzzle. By ending on a quiet, unresolved note instead of a neat wrap-up, the film forces viewers to weigh what makes someone human: memory, empathy, or manufactured design. The ambiguity makes viewers rethink Deckard’s actions and his growing connection to Rachael and the replicants. Though the theatrical release added a studio-mandated drive through sunny mountains and narration that spelled things out. Cutting that return to a cleaner, open finish preserves the film's bleak, reflective tone. And we like that version much better!​​​​​​​.

Recent findings suggest that if there’s one thing that No Country for Old Men’s got, it’s true grit! In Joel and Ethan Coen’s magnum opus, set in the 1980s West Texas, welder Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin) takes $2 million from a botched drug deal and is relentlessly hunted by hitman Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem). Meanwhile, aging Sheriff Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones) investigates the violence while struggling to understand a brutal world outpacing traditional law and order. What may come as a shock, No Country for Old Men ends without a traditional showdown. Moss dies off-screen, Anton Chigurh survives a car crash after killing Carla Jean Moss (Kelly Macdonald), and Sheriff Bell retires to share two dreams about his father before the film cuts to black.

In a recent development, the film ends in masterpiece fashion by shifting the focus from thriller plot mechanics to existential reflection. Bell’s quiet monologue recounting two dreams to his wife, closing on the line, "And then I woke up,” is as The Wizard of Oz as it can get. Although the cat-and-mouse chase drives the action, the story's emotional weight belongs to Sheriff Bell confronting aging, retirement, and a changing, more brutal world he feels outmatched by. Bell's dreams leave no neat moral answer, ending instead as he wakes up to reality. The abrupt, elliptical finish follows Cormac McCarthy’s 2005 novel, turning a crime thriller into a somber meditation on time, fate, and mortality. Whether the closure feels too artsy for such a raw thriller, its ending is truly a genuinely raw conclusion because life is simply uncertain. ​​​​​​​.

It has been revealed that one of the greatest and enduring sci-fi classics is Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind. Directed by Michel Gondry and written by Charlie Kaufman, the romantic drama documents the aftermath of a painful breakup, where Clementine Kruczynski (Kate Winslet) undergoes a medical procedure to erase her memories of Joel Barish (Jim Carrey), prompting heartbroken Joel to get the same treatment. As his memories fade, Joel realizes he still loves her and tries to hide her inside his mind to save their relationship from being forgotten. The film concludes in bittersweet fashion as Joel and Clementine reunite after erasing each other from their memories, discover the bitter truth of their past relationship on recorded tapes, and still choose to try again. Despite knowing the risks and potential heartbreak, they agree to give their relationship another chance, ending on a quiet "okay" as they run and laugh in the snow.

According to recent reports, rather than erasing pain to stay safe, the ending suggests that real connection requires accepting flaws and the risk of future hurt. Viewers read the final moments differently—some see a hopeful fresh start with eyes open, while others worry the couple is repeating a familiar cycle. Perhaps it depends on where your heart is when you watch. It forces audiences to confront an honest, recurring human choice: whether to love again, knowing pain is likely. Kaufman's writing and Gondry's direction blend melancholy, surrealism, and warmth without forcing a neat "happily ever after". Early ideas leaned more heavily toward a grim, inescapable cycle, whereas the finished scene leaves room for agency and connection. If you’re a cynic or a lover of love, Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind will no doubt task you with examining your own love choices from there on out. ​​​​​​​.

Industry observers note that hands down, the greatest sci-fi film of all time is the prolific 2001: A Space Odyssey. Directed by Stanley Kubrick, it follows humanity's evolutionary leaps triggered by mysterious black monoliths, from prehistoric apes learning to use tools to a voyage toward Jupiter where the sentient supercomputer HAL 9000 malfunctions. After confronting HAL, the surviving astronaut travels beyond space and time to undergo a transformative shift into the next stage of human existence. To finish the film, astronaut Dr. Dave Bowman (Keir Dullea) survives a showdown with the rogue computer HAL 9000, travels through a cosmic light vortex near Jupiter, ages rapidly in a surreal bedroom, and is reborn as a glowing fetus, the "Star Child,” floating near Earth.

Kubrick left the ending open to interpretation rather than spelling out a single literal explanation. Analyzing it, the monoliths are seen as tools or catalysts from an advanced intelligence that push human evolution forward—first nudging early hominids toward tool use and finally elevating Bowman into a higher stage of existence. By refusing to lock onto one literal explanation, the finale invites ongoing debate and personal meaning that remains a masterful timeless conclusion. It’s a mirror for the viewer as the ambiguity shifts the focus from chasing external answers to reflecting on human nature, technology, and what lies beyond the known. The film is framed as an evolutionary leap. It’s a powerfully surreal and richly philosophical conclusion that is utterly flawless. ​​​​​​​.

In a recent development, yes, we’re still debating Inception’s ending and, chances are, it’s never ever going to stop. In Christopher Nolan’s masterclass in filmmaking, Dom Cobb (Leonardo DiCaprio) is a skilled thief who steals valuable secrets by infiltrating his targets' subconscious minds while they dream. Offered a chance to clear his criminal record and return to his children, Cobb assembles a team of specialists to attempt the impossible reverse heist: planting an original idea into a business rival's mind while navigating a multi-layered dream world haunted by projections of his deceased wife, Mal (Marion Cotillard). The film ends on a profoundly ambiguous note as Dom returns home to his children after completing the dream heist, spinning his metal top totem before walking away from it to greet them. The camera lingers on the top as it begins to wobble, then cuts to black just before revealing whether it falls or keeps spinning.

Recent findings suggest that with a brilliant plot twist that lingers beyond the final frame, it serves as one last monumental character breakthrough. Throughout the film, Cobb’s fixation on proving reality and escaping guilt drives his pain. Walking away from the spinning top before seeing it fall shows he chooses his children and his present life over needing absolute proof. Cobb’s indifference to whether he is dreaming or awake underscores the film's philosophical focus on personal reality over objective truth. Nolan’s design makes the ambiguity meaningful rather than frustrating, though those in the frustration camp, I see you. I feel you. I am you. Like the team planting an idea in Robert Fischer’s (Cillian Murphy) mind, the final cut plants a lingering question in the audience’s mind. Even after Nolan shared his thoughts on the scene, audiences remained free to interpret Cobb’s final moment on their own terms.

Since the launch of Assassin's Creed in 2007, the stealth-action series from Ubisoft has become one of the cornerstones of gaming, and with fourteen mainline entries now under its belt, it is safe to say that it is here to stay.

Taking players across the globe, and exploring multiple eras, movements, and cultures, Assassin's Creed has been the best history teacher we could have had, and to celebrate the franchise approaching its 20th anniversary, Assassin's Creed: Echoes of the Past is set to stun us all when it arrives this December.

Recent findings suggest that courtesy of the artist collective Les 7 Doigts, Heredis: Echoes of the Past is a live show that takes fans to the Ubisoft universe with an experience that combines both theater and circus. Oh, and of course, there will also be plenty of parkour.

It has been revealed that whilst a preview will be held on 3 December 2026, at the Maisonneuve Theater in Montreal, several performances will be scheduled between January 21 and February 7, 2027, and so you have plenty of time to grab your tickets. So, what can you expect?

A troop of acrobats will take to the stage to perform some incredible stunts, with the show itself expected to last two hours. However, the storyline will focus on a young man called Naël who, after receiving a letter on his 25th birthday, will find his destiny changed forever. As such, he will have to embark on a journey to discover the mystery behind his father's appearance, an event that he refuses to accept.

Featuring an original Assassin's Creed storyline, Heredis: Echoes of the Past will see Naël join the HEREDIS program, and through this, he will be able to travel through many historical eras which echo the ones we all know and love from the Assassin's Creed franchise so far. Not only that, but with the stage show being officially supported by Ubisoft, you can expect a truly spectacular experience with the creator's stamp of approval.

It has been revealed that despite featuring nods to the games, such as in the historical periods that are covered, it will not focus on any of the games. As such, even those unfamiliar with the franchise will be able to go and watch. However, the catch here is that, unless you can make the Montreal preview, you will need to head to the Casino de Paris, France.

Industry observers note that over on r/assassinscreed, fans discussed the upcoming stage show, and took to the comments to share their thoughts. One user shared, "One of the theater companies I work with presented one of 7Fingers’ indicates a year or so before I started working there, and they were pretty well-attended shows. We are thinking of bringing them back to present another of their works, hopefully in the next few years. I really hope 7Fingers is able to bring Heredis to more than just Canada and France!" Another shared, "This actually sounds incredible to be honest.".

So, if you find yourself in Canada or France and just so happen to be an Assassin's Creed fan, make sure to check out Heredis: Echoes of the Past and partake in an original experience you will never forget.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that in a latest interview with Billboard’s On the Record with Kristin Robinson, Apple Music’s Zane Lowe discussed the early days of Apple Music Radio and revealed just how many people tune in each month. Here are the details.

Apple is rarely terribly specific about how many people use its services, including how many tune in to its radio stations.

In 2019, for instance, Eddy Cue said Beats 1 (now Apple Music 1) had ‘tens of millions of listeners,’ but Apple has rarely provided more specific figures since.

Apple Music’s Zane Lowe, however, has now offered a more concrete figure, revealing that the service reaches over 50 million unique listeners every month:.

It has been revealed that we were never, you know, delusional enough to assume we were going to get a huge audience overnight. We’d have to build it like anyone else would have to build anything. But we’ve just got to a point in our 11 years on where we now, overall, reach over 50 million unique listeners a month, which is a really large number for us, and it’s growing exponentially and really fast.

The revelation came in a wide-ranging interview published today with Billboard’s On the Record with Kristin Robinson, where Lowe discussed Apple Music Radio’s early struggles, its approach to supporting emerging artists, and why human curation remains central to the service.

When discussing the early days at Apple Music, Lowe recalled:.

When we started the radio here, I didn’t have access or opportunity with a lot of the artists that I built relationships with from the BBC because we were unproven. And I came over here thinking, “Well, I’ve got Jimmy Iovine over here, and I’ve got Apple over here and I feel unstoppable, and who’s not going to want to come and launch this thing with us?” But it was kind of crickets… As upsetting as that was at the time, two good things came out of it. Number one, it snapped me back into the reality force field of building something from scratch. And number two, it made us focus really clearly and in a massive way on new and emerging artists.

He also mentioned some of the first artists Apple Music Radio supported, including Billie Eilish with “Ocean Eyes,” Khalid with American Teen, and Bryson Tiller with his first song.

At the time, Lowe noted, these artists were just getting started, and supporting emerging talent became a defining part of Apple Music Radio’s approach, one that continues to this day:.

The really cool number is on our radio network. We played — this year alone — over 6,500 individual artists, which is not a commercial radio model. [Other radio networks’] playlists are very small, and the amount of plays is very great. Our playlist is gigantic. We play a lot of different artists, and over half of those 6,500 artists we’ve played in one year are new or emerging. So, think about 3,300 artists, roughly, getting played, who may be on their first song, their first EP, their first album…It’s proof of concept. It’s great.

Still on the subject of the early days at Apple Music, Lowe said “it was very clear [from the start] that that was very important to everybody who was responsible for bringing Apple Music to life,” adding that “serving artists and the artistic community in a way that is of most value and of most service” still drives “a lot of the decision-making” at the platform.

When the conversation turned to Apple Music’s recent rebranding, which introduced a upcoming logo physically created using sound waves from a composition by Fred again.., Lowe said he couldn’t speak to the decisions behind it, but stressed the human element and the creative process that went into it:.

We could have created that in a way that could utilize all of the tech available. We could type that into a prompt. But at the end of the day, seeing how it’s made is so much more additionally inspiring than just seeing it. It speaks to, I think, what we try to do here, which is, we love the process of what we do, and the result is a byproduct of getting to do it and loving to do it.

The glitch of algorithms also came up when Lowe discussed Apple Music’s approach to music discovery, with the executive emphasizing the importance of human curation over automated recommendations:.

In a recent development, well, we don’t want to say that too loudly, because someone could be like, “Wait a minute, we could cut costs here? Man, how did we not think of that!” Look, I mean, jokes aside, we’ve been incredibly fortunate, and I’ve been incredibly fortunate to take that step from the BBC into a firm and to work with people that value exactly what it is you’re describing: this idea of place and this experience of sharing things with each other, and how meaningful it is when someone shares a record with you and it comes with context. It’s a gift….

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, even six decades into his Hollywood career, Steven Spielberg is still synonymous with a brand of movie magic and spectacle that very few can rival. And when he decides to direct a new popcorn blockbuster like “Disclosure Day,” you know you’re in for a few dazzling sequences.

One of the most exciting moments in the film comes when a train collides into a car with stars Josh O’Connor and Emily Blunt close at hand. The sequence tested every department, from camera and production design to visual effects. And during IndieWire’s recent Craft Roundtables, VFX Supervisor Matthew Butler explained the unique challenge of incorporating subtle VFX work into a scene where so much happens in camera. Related Stories If There’s Generative AI in ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,’ It’s Not the First Time David Fincher’s Used It Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage.

It has been revealed that “With Steven, he wants everything to be as practical as it can be,” Butler noted. “We had a real train. A real train, a real car attached to that train, it was being dragged on a real track. That actually did happen.”.

But while Spielberg’s preferences were clear, Butler clarified that blockbusters on this scale rarely come down to a binary choice between practical effects and VFX. The biggest scenes often contain elements of both, as the pairing between in-camera human acting and cutting edge post-production is what leads to movie magic.

“When you combine some of the live action blue screen work, clearly that’s your lead actor and actress there, and your stunt work where it’s like ‘Oh my God, that looks really real’ and the stuff that you just can’t do that’s just too dangerous … that’s where visual effects came in,” he stated. “But I wouldn’t say it was a visual effects sequence. It was a sequence that contained all of those, and it came together in the right way.”.

More coverage from IndieWire’s Craft Roundtables will be published here over the coming weeks.
