Six Things You Should Do Now to Optimize Your Setup for GTA 6

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1143 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that you’re almost ready for Grand Theft Auto VI.
  • According to Rockstar, you’ll need up to 212GB of storage space.
  • Alternatively, it’s pretty easy to add more storage (if you can afford it).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that you’re almost ready for Grand Theft Auto VI. You’ve preloaded the game on your console, you’ve taken the next month off work, and you’ve locked your phone in a Faraday cage and set it adrift at sea. You’re prepared to lock in, and you haven’t forgotten a thing…right? Well, just to make sure, here are the most crucial tips to optimize your setup before you fire up the most anticipated game of the decade.

GTA 6 is absurdly large. According to Rockstar, you’ll need up to 212GB of storage space. For high-end consoles like the PS5 Pro, that’s more than 10% of the available storage space, and close to half the space on the more budget-conscious Xbox Series S. There’s a good chance you’ll have to delete something to make room.

Alternatively, it’s pretty easy to add more storage (if you can afford it). External SSDs are probably the cheapest route, though you’ll want to make sure to use a high-speed USB cable to connect it. It’s even worth shopping around for alternate models of SSD. For example, at the time of writing, the popular 2TB WD_BLACK external drive was close to $200, but the exact same drive in pink was $132.

Sources indicate that you can also directly upgrade the storage of your console with expansion drives. The Xbox Series X|S supports proprietary expansion cards, while the PS5 and PS5 Pro can accept most M.2 internal SSDs. These will generally be faster, since they plug directly into the console via higher-speed connections than a drive hooked up via USB.

Sources indicate that let’s face it: Half the fun of any sandbox game is the weird, unique stuff that happens to only you. So you’re probably going to be hitting that “record recent gameplay” button more often than usual. While you’re cleaning up your storage space (or adding more), make sure to account for all the video clips you might want to save.

Recent findings suggest that file size of video clips depends on a lot of factors, but 4K recordings can generally take up to 0.5GB per minute of footage. You can cut that down by saving footage in 1080p instead, but either way you’ll want to leave a little extra space.

Game footage is also a pretty good place to look if you need to make room on your console and don’t want to delete any games. Be honest with yourself: You don’t need all those clips from Horizon Forbidden West you saved four years ago. Dive into the settings on your console and find the biggest media files you forgot you even had on there.

According to Rockstar, GTA 6 will be targeting 30fps across consoles at launch, which is pretty low as modern AAA games go. Part of the reason for that is all the processing power going to rendering a complex environment, but it also means you won’t need a fancy high frame rate TV or monitor any time soon to get the most out of it. Still, it couldn’t hurt to check a few settings on your display.

First, make sure you’re using a higher refresh rate than 30Hz. While the game is targeting 30fps, it is technically capable of more, so if your console can keep up, you don’t want to accidentally bottleneck your frames. This setting will vary by device, so check the manual that came with your screen.

Sources indicate that also, make sure you have HDR enabled on your hardware. There’s a good chance this is already turned on for your TV, but sometimes other devices can switch display modes if they only support SDR. The game will help you calibrate your HDR settings for GTA 6 specifically when you launch it, but only if it detects HDR compatibility in the first place.

Sources indicate that if you’re planning to buy a console specifically for GTA 6, this might be one of those rare instances where a PS5 Pro really is worth the upgrade. According to Rockstar, certain features like ray-traced shadows will only be available on the Pro version of Sony’s console.

Recent findings suggest that more importantly, the PS5 Pro version supports PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (or PSSR), which upscales lower-resolution images to get better detail and higher frame rates out of the same hardware. Given that GTA 6 is already starting at a meager target of 30fps on most consoles, anything that can give your frame rate a boost is probably going to feel like a welcome improvement over the baseline.

I’ll tell you a secret as someone who’s spent a lot of time testing different game controllers: Most of the time, you really don’t need an expensive “elite” controller. Most of the time. I don’t buy into the idea that a taller control stick is going to make you an esports athlete. It can be nice to have, but it’s not a game changer. What does matter is customizing your controls, especially for long gaming sessions.

The DualSense Edge wireless controller is a favorite of mine, mainly because of the rear paddles and adjustable triggers. The former lets you map any button to a rear lever that you can access with your fingers underneath the controller, which can often ease some of the wrist strain of awkward button combos. And the adjustable triggers let you activate the buttons with less motion, again reducing repetitive stress.

Sources indicate that the Xbox Elite Series 2 controller has similar features for the Xbox, as well as custom caps for the D-pad. Both consoles’ versions of pro controllers are more expensive than the standard ones, but if you’re planning to game for many hours, it can be worth it to get a controller that’s more comfortable for you.

If you have an Xbox One, you don’t necessarily have to upgrade your console to play GTA 6, but you might want to take a look at your network. GTA 6 will be available on Xbox Cloud Gaming on day one, and you’ll be able to stream the game to an Xbox One console (as long as you purchase Cloud playtime as well or get some with your Game Pass subscription). This is the only way to play on a console older than the current generation, so if you don’t want to shell out for latest hardware, this might be your best bet.

In a recent development, xbox recommends a minimum of a 20Mbps connection to run cloud gaming, but more is obviously better. If you can connect your console to a wired Ethernet connection, that would be better and provide more stability. If you can’t connect a cable, then at least make sure you’re well within range of your wifi router, and try to limit any other bandwidth-hogging applications on the network while you’re playing.

In a recent development, looks like Hollywood could be heading into the new year with relief on a national level. The push to pass a federal film and television tax credit by the end of 2026 picked up momentum on Friday at a White House press conference, where President Trump said his administration was actively negotiating the measure and predicted it would pass.

“It’s running its way through Congress, and it has unbelievable support,” Trump said. He singled out Senator Adam Schiff, the California Democrat who introduced the bill with Republican Senator Tim Scott of South Carolina back in September, and said, “I tell you what, Adam Schiff said, ‘Wow, we love that bill.’ Adam Schiff said that.” Related Stories Box Office: ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Debuts to Mighty $120 Million, Reviving Lionsgate’s Most Important Franchise Box Office: A24’s ‘You Can See Everything’ Crosses $100 Million Globally.

According to recent reports, trump mentioned Georgia and Latest Jersey by name as states with good tax credits for film and TV production, but argued that those incentives alone would not bring enough production work back from overseas. With a federal credit, he said, “Hollywood would open again.”.

Trump said his administration was also negotiating whether to extend the measure to benefit movie theaters, but said the matter was unsettled. He first publicly called for a federal production incentive in August after meeting with actor Jon Voight: one of three industry “special ambassadors” he appointed early last year.

The bill’s sponsors revealed more than 60 newly introduced House cosponsors and four new Senate cosponsors on Thursday morning — with lawmakers from both parties signing on in both chambers. The following day, Trump himself brought up the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act in response to a question about whether he could work with Democrats. Calling the bill “very bipartisan,” he said, “I can tell you right now it’s going to happen.”.

Trump gave no timetable, though earlier this week, Representative Linda Sánchez, one of the bill’s House sponsors from California, called for Congress to pass it before 2027 so productions could qualify for benefits on the first of the year.

“Members of both parties have watched jobs in their districts move overseas,” she stated in a release from Schiff’s office sent to the press. “Momentum is on our side, and we need to strike while the iron is hot by passing this bill before the end of the year.”.

According to recent reports, A floor vote has yet to be unveiled, but multiple sources told IndieWire the measure would move faster if attached to a stopgap government funding bill. If passed and approved, the federal initiative would give qualifying film and TV productions a 20 percent credit on labor expenses for American workers. The credit could reach 30 percent for productions that qualify for bonuses.

According to recent reports, for crews accustomed to watching projects follow tax breaks to Canada or the U.K., the proposal would give producers a clear financial incentive to keep that work here for them in the U.S. The bill’s new Senate cosponsors include Republicans Katie Britt of Alabama and Thom Tillis of North Carolina — as well as Democrats Chris Coons of Delaware and Dick Durbin of Illinois.

The AFL-CIO and the American Hotel & Lodging Association also endorsed the bill, joining a coalition that already included IATSE, SAG-AFTRA, the Directors Guild of America, and the Motion Picture Association.

“Given the support from Republicans and Democrats in both chambers and the president, we can get this legislation across the finish line,” Schiff said.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yellowstone might have made Westerns cool again, but it’s not the only series that depicts the atrocities committed in the name of claiming American soil. Like Taylor Sheridan's landmark Western, Netflix’s American Primeval revolves around the fight for Native land. But instead of greedy corporations, the conflict involves Mormon militias, Indigenous communities, and white settlers all caught in the middle.

While men are often the ones framing these narratives, American Primeval indicates a different side of these conflicts, particularly through the women pulled into a world that disregards their value. Yellowstone might have shocked viewers with its relentless violence, but it doesn’t come close to American Primeval. The best part is that the miniseries only needs six episodes to expose the truth of America's colonial past, giving its female characters room to tell stories that Westerns have often left on the sidelines.

According to recent reports, set during the 1857 Utah War, American Primeval reimagines the Mormon Church’s expansion under Brigham Young (Kim Coates), rooted in deep religious fanaticism and historical violence committed in the name of faith. Young’s campaign to take control of Fort Bridger puts him in conflict with the U.S. Army officer Captain Edmund Dellinger (Lucas Neff), the fort’s owner Jim Bridger (Shea Whigham), and Red Feather (Derek Hinkey), the leader of a renegade group of Crow warriors known as the Wolf Clan.

It has been revealed that at the center of the miniseries are mother and son Sara Rowell (Betty Gilpin) and Devin Rowell (Preston Mota), who have come a long way from Missouri to Fort Bridger, Wyoming, with the intention of reaching Devin’s father in Crooks Springs, Utah. However, getting there is easier mentioned than done. With the treacherous terrain, bounty hunters scattered across the region, and wildlife that could kill them in an instant, their chances of making it are slim to none — and that's before they have to contend with the conflict brewing around Fort Bridger. Fortunately, the reluctant mountain man Isaac Reed (Taylor Kitsch) is willing to join Sara and Devin on their journey, but even that doesn't guarantee survival.

Sources indicate that there’s no doubt that Yellowstone doesn’t shy away from violence. The series already has plenty of stomach-churning moments: a charging bull let loose inside a bar, Beth Dutton (Kelly Reilly) assaulted in her own office, and the controversial Monica (Kelsey Asbille) storyline, in which she puts herself in danger while trying to lure a predator. However, American Primeval arguably takes things much further, largely because of its historical setting. Unlike the more modern world of Yellowstone, where the Duttons still have to contend with law enforcement, government officials, and legal bureaucracy, the Utah Territory depicted in American Primeval is a largely lawless frontier where formal authority has little control over the men fighting for power and land.

In American Primeval, violence is normalized, with little regard for human life or legal consequences. Public hangings, the abduction of women, and the slaughter of entire groups of settlers are all part of the brutal reality of the frontier. The series takes things even further with its bloody depictions of clashes between opposing groups, including a fictionalized portrayal of the Mountain Meadows Massacre of September 1857. In this world, there’s no telling when someone might fire the first arrow or when a seemingly ordinary verbal confrontation could end with someone getting stabbed. Whether they're battling for control, to settle scores, or simply to defend themselves, nearly everyone resorts to violence to survive.

In a recent development, four icons and four completely different ways of walking into trouble. This is the one you would have been out there, why it fits, and what it would have cost you.

You have never explained yourself and you have never needed to, because people work out fairly quickly that you are the most capable person in the room without you ever having to mention it.

You are the funniest person in most rooms and the most loyal person in all of them, and you would be genuinely insulted if somebody suggested those two things were in any tension.

You never wanted this job, and you took it anyway because the alternative was standing there watching somebody less careful do it badly, which is the most Western reason there has ever been.

Nobody has ever successfully talked you out of something you had already decided was right, and a long line of grown adults has found that out the hard way.

It has been revealed that american Primeval focuses on three women whose lives are upended by violence. From different societal, cultural, and religious backgrounds, each faces the limited choices available to women on the frontier. Sara is a mother fleeing her past to protect her disabled son; Abish (Saura Lightfoot-Leon) is a Mormon wife questioning religious expectations after falling into the hands of the Shoshone; and Two Moons (Shawnee Pourier) is a mute Shoshone woman escaping her village after killing her rapist.

Recent findings suggest that yellowstone depicts its female characters in fairly rigid roles throughout its five seasons. In contrast, American Primeval gives its women more room to evolve in just six tight episodes. Initially appearing helpless, they're forced out of their comfort zones to protect themselves and others, adapting to circumstances they never imagined facing. With its complex history, religious conflicts, and women doing whatever it takes, American Primeval shows there's more to these stories than bloodbaths and conquest, offering a more complex and haunting portrait of the country's violent past than Yellowstone ever explores.

American Primeval is a Netflix limited series that follows the lives of several men and women in the middle of the expansion of the American West. Social dynamics clash as men and women battle for a piece of the fresh world against rivals and each other.

#74107. HBO's 9-Part Thriller Masterpiece Has Earned Its Status As A Modern Classic

HBO's 9-Part Thriller Masterpiece Has Earned Its Status As A Modern Classic

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (935 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Screenrant

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There was a time when superhero TV shows were synonymous with colorful costumes, campy action, and plots that focused much more on outlandish spectacle than delivering anything grounded or relatable.
  • Recent findings suggest that that approach to small-screen superhero stories feels familiar in the 2020s, but this definitely wasn’t always the case.
  • Set in Tulsa 34 years after the attack on New York in Alan Moore’s original story, Watchmen introduces viewers to detective Angela Abar (Regina King) as she investigates a white supremacist group.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There was a time when superhero TV shows were synonymous with colorful costumes, campy action, and plots that focused much more on outlandish spectacle than delivering anything grounded or relatable. The genre has, thankfully, developed a grittier and more realistic edge in the age of streaming. Modern superhero series like The Penguin, Daredevil: Born Again, and Lanterns have ditched the obsession with superpowered spectacle to instead focus on the injustices and inequality that lead to heroes taking up their mantles in the first place.

Recent findings suggest that that approach to small-screen superhero stories feels familiar in the 2020s, but this definitely wasn’t always the case. The prestige superhero series model didn’t come out of nowhere, either. There’s a show that paved the way for contemporary hits that give the genre its current level of dramatic clout and mainstream respect among those who’d once never have given a superhero story a chance. That series is 2019’s Watchmen, HBO’s sequel miniseries to Alan Moore’s groundbreaking graphic novel.

Set in Tulsa 34 years after the attack on New York in Alan Moore’s original story, Watchmen introduces viewers to detective Angela Abar (Regina King) as she investigates a white supremacist group. The case draws her into the lives of the original Watchmen vigilantes while continuing the graphic novel’s questioning of whether wearing a mask and calling oneself a hero is enough to make it true. While it may not be a superhero household name, shows like The Penguin, Lanterns, and Daredevil: Born Again may not ever have existed without HBO’s Watchmen to pave the way.

According to recent reports, while there were several grittier superhero shows arriving around the same time as Watchmen, such as The Boys in the same year or the Netflix-Marvel shows that began with Daredevil in 2015, none of them felt like they changed the game in quite the same way as HBO’s miniseries. For years, the selling points of pretty much every superhero TV show were its hero, its villain, and the prospect of seeing them fight. Watchmen bucked this trend in a way few, if any, series had before.

Recent findings suggest that rather than focusing on setting up a hero-villain showdown, HBO’s Watchmen built itself around a mystery. It didn’t feel like a superhero show. It felt like a detective show that just so happened to have superheroes in it. What’s more, these “heroes” are far from morally good. Watchmen presents its masked vigilantes not as saviors, but as ordinary people with their own ideological agendas. It’s an approach that put a fresh spin on the familiar tropes of the genre. For example, secret identities shift from being a way for heroes to protect their loved ones to a way to use anonymity to negate accountability.

Recent findings suggest that opening with the 1921 Tulsa Race Massacre also gave Watchmen a sense of history and political relevance that superhero TV series rarely attempted at the time. By the time the action reaches 2019, generations have grown up with different ideas about what a hero is and who deserves their protection. Who counts as a hero and a villain depends on perspective, with those that society labels as the former often working to hold up corrupt institutions and protect a societal status quo that perpetuates inequality.

In a recent development, that shift from the traditional hero-vs-villain setup to a politically charged mystery narrative won Watchmen no shortage of acclaim, including 11 Primetime Emmy wins. At the time, a superhero series receiving this much critical praise was basically unheard of. It was a true turning point for the genre on the small screen. Many gritty and grounded superhero TV reveals have followed in the years since, but none have made as much of an impact on the genre itself quite like Watchmen.

While Watchmen is celebrated today and was far from a ratings flop when it aired in 2019, it didn’t perform as well as it could have done given just how good it is. The reasons why are obvious, too. While it’s an incredible piece of television in its own right, early discussions about Watchmen were defined not by its merits, but by its relation to the source material. Alan Moore’s Watchmen comics are among the most beloved of all time. As is often the case with such highly regarded properties, HBO’s adaptation became defined by the divisive and often toxic responses of the existing fandom.

Even the announcement that HBO was creating a sequel to Watchmen was met with immediate and disproportionately vocal backlash. Many fans of the original graphic novel wanted Alan Moore’s story to stand alone. This wasn’t just down to longtime fans wanting the existing canon and timeline to remain untouched, either. There were also some particularly toxic and abhorrent reactions to racism becoming central to HBO’s story too. For casual viewers who weren’t at all familiar with the Watchmen comic, the discussions surrounding the 2019 miniseries made it seem like a hotbed of controversy that it simply wasn’t worth wading into.

This is an incredible shame, because Watchmen is an incredibly solid thriller that even viewers completely unaware of Alan Moore’s original graphic novel are bound to appreciate. It’s not just a game-changing superhero TV series, it’s a rich mystery story that uses its genre as a tool to explore some incredibly poignant themes and topics. While it’s impossible to say for certain, it feels likely that Watchmen would today be much more widely discussed if its legacy wasn't defined by the polarizing pop-culture discourse that surrounded it when it arrived in 2019.

It has been revealed that black Friday is usually a great time to grab a newly introduced e-reader, but the ongoing RAM crisis has made that a question mark this year: Amazon recently raised the prices of all its Kindles by around $50 and refreshed the entire lineup, which means your odds of grabbing one at a big discount are low. But you aren't totally out of luck: If you haven't noticed, micro-e-readers—I'm talking credit card-sized, with screens that measure around four inches—are all the rage in 2026, and right now, you can pick up one of them for around $55.

Sources indicate that if you too can see the appeal of carrying all of your books with you on a device so small you'll forget it's even in your pocket, it's a great time to jump in: The recently released Xteink X4 Classic is at the moment 38% off for Black Friday, bringing it down to $54.87, a record-low price. Meanwhile, the smaller X3 is $55.72, or 19% off. Both are available in either "mist grey" or "space black." The discounts should last through the end of Cyber Monday on Nov. 30.

Xteink is a Chinese startup that shook up the e-reading world last year with the launch of the X4, a super bare-bones device that made up for its lack of features and usability with a cheap sub-$70 price point. Since then, a huge online community of fans has formed, sharing tips on Reddit and even coming together to crowdsource an alternate operating system that fixed a lot of early problems. Xteink quickly followed up the X4 with a slate of other devices, including the 3.7-inch X3 and the X4 Pro, which adds a front light and touchscreen (at the cost of screen clarity and two physical buttons).

In a recent development, the X4 Classic and the X3 improve on the original X4 with quality-of-life upgrades like a larger battery, relocated page-turn buttons, a real-time clock, and a tilt-to-turn-page feature. They're also lighter and thinner than the X4, though there is a trade-off involved: They drop the USB-C charging port in favor of magnetic pogo pins that require a separate adapter (included).

These upgrades also increased the cost: The X4 Classic typically retails for $89, $20 more than the discontinued X4 and only $10 less than the X4 Pro, while the X3 debuted at $79. But right now, the X4 Classic is just under $55, or around 38% off, and the X3 is about a dollar more. Either is a great option for those who prioritize crisp, readable text above the conveniences of a built-in light or touchscreen, as those add extra layers between the inner screen and outer glass. It's also important to understand what you're getting into: These devices support only e-books without Digital Rights Management (DRM), which means you can't use it to read your existing library of Kindle books. On the plus side, there's no longer a need to worry about flashing new firmware if you don't want to, as the native version has been totally overhauled and is now one of your best options (though the new firmware, called "Licorice," isn't available on the X3 quite yet).

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The uproar over the alleged use of generative AI imagery in “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” has taken a familiar path. Early responses to the Netflix film penned by Quentin Tarantino and directed by David Fincher have pointed out egregious examples of generative video artifacts sticking out in key flashback moments in the film — including one shot from the trailer where it certainly looks like a video AI program rendered a wagon the wrong way around.

It has been revealed that the criticism is of the use of generative AI in principle as a fundamental betrayal of the creative process — but it’s also of Fincher, as a director who, historically, has been meticulous with the level of detail and intention in every single shot of his films. In the early responses to Fincher’s latest, there’s been a lot of surprise and disappointment about this particular filmmaker being caught up in an AI controversy. Related Stories Box Office: ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Debuts to Mighty $120 Million, Reviving Lionsgate’s Most Important Franchise Box Office: A24’s ‘You Can See Everything’ Crosses $100 Million Globally.

At first blush, his approach seems at odds with using generative AI video, which relies on regurgitated (and, it bears repeating every time, stolen) data. But Fincher has defended his use of AI to the LA Times as a way to continue to innovate on an art form that is, after all, just over a hundred years old.

It has been revealed that that defense really shouldn’t be surprising, given Fincher’s history with AI specifically. Although he’s been critical of generative tools in the past, Fincher admitted to using them (never publicly disclosing which) in the 4K remaster of “Se7en,” which the director described as a process of needing to remake the negative in order to battle the ravages of time (and the thousands of tiny scratches that would show up in 4K). “If you could see a 30-year-old negative and what it looks like even when immaculately stored — it was an enormous amount of fixing, just digs and scratches and cinch,” he told EW at the time.

Sources indicate that that kind of image restoration technology was around long, long before the Anthropic IPO failed to save the stock market, but its level of precision has increased enormously in the past year. There were also sequences in the stored “Se7en,” though, where generative tech filled in gaps from the original. For one example, Fincher talked about a moment where a camera pan overshot the mark and changedh a shot. The performance had been good enough to use a technically flawed take — and, combined wit an unused take, allowed software to generate the missing information and restore the intended image.

Industry observers note that “It ends up being the most thrillingly stupid fix in the world because if you see it, we didn’t do our jobs. And you probably won’t see it. You probably won’t be aware that it’s happened. But you look at it, and you just think to yourself, ‘It’s so nice that we can fix that kind of stuff today,'” Fincher told Collider about that moment in “Se7en.”.

By Fincher’s own lights, then, the problem with AI in “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is that people are painfully aware of it. AI critics might make a distinction between video restoration tools that work on existing projects and those tools being used because they can more swiftly and cheaply generate originals that would’ve otherwise needed to be crafted by human hands. Having something AI-generated isn’t necessarily better than nothing when it comes to art, and choosing to AI-generate a Western chase sequence inside of, say, 10 seconds isn’t a solution to all.

Sources indicate that still, Fincher knows what he’s doing. This past week, he emphasized to the LA Times that he’s not a Luddite when it comes to film: “We’re talking about a thing that’s a hundred years old, and everyone’s going, ‘Stop. Pencils down. No more iterating. It’s not necessary to have at your fingertips the ability to change the color of that person’s eyes.’ Well, it exists. Should we not use it?”.

The answer is an emphatic “No!” to some And they can certainly be mad, or disappointed, or disheartened about Fincher’s decision to use AI tools. The one thing they shouldn’t be is surprised.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, “You Can See Everything,” an unconventional documentary about Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes in exile, has crossed $100 million at the global box office. Its success extends a hot streak for A24, the indie studio behind last summer’s blockbuster “Backrooms” as well as arthouse hits such as “The Drama” and “Primetime.”.

“You Can See Everything” now ranks as the eighth-highest grossing non-music documentary, moving ahead of “Deep Sea 3D,” and the second-highest grossing non-music and non-nature documentary, behind Michael Moore’s “Fahrenheit 9/11.” It’s unlikely to surpass Moore’s anti-Bush jeremiad, which grossed an astonishing $222.4 million when it opened in the height of a fiercely contested presidential election. Related Stories If There’s Generative AI in ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,’ It’s Not the First Time David Fincher’s Used It Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage.

Those aren’t the only benchmarks with which to measure “You Can See Everything’s” impact. It is now the seventh-highest grossing film in the history of A24, coming in behind “Materialists,” which earned $105.6 million globally. On a domestic basis, “You Can See Everything” is A24’s third-highest grossing film, ranking just behind “Backrooms” ($197.5 million) and “Marty Supreme” ($96 million). It should easily surpass “Marty Supreme” and that film had Timothée Chalamet and a boatload of Oscar noms behind it.

Tom Hanks’ Heart-Breaking Drama Is Still His Greatest Movie 33 Years Later

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that tom Hanks is viewed by many audiences as a comforting figure in culture – Mr.
  • Sources indicate that set in the titular city, Hanks plays Andrew Beckett, a successful lawyer who finds himself fired from his firm after his employers find out that he is both gay and has contracted the AIDS virus.
  • Industry observers note that loosely based on the stories of real-life lawyers, the film earned Tom Hanks his first Oscar for Best Actor, while Bruce Springsteen won Best Original Song for his haunting theme “Streets of Philadelphia.” For Washington, it was another classic performance, one that addressed the ignorance toward HIV/AIDS and the gay community at the time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that tom Hanks is viewed by many audiences as a comforting figure in culture – Mr. Rogers, Santa, Woody, and Walt Disney have all been brought to life by his singular warmth and charm. However, the movie that first propelled him to dramatic actor status is one that remains his best and riskiest bet. The 1993 Oscar-winning drama Philadelphia took an urgent subject for the time and gave it a human perspective, proving that then-comedy star Hanks could also deliver a heart-breaking performance while sharing the screen with a heavyweight like co-star Denzel Washington. Over three decades later, it remains his finest acting moment.

Sources indicate that set in the titular city, Hanks plays Andrew Beckett, a successful lawyer who finds himself fired from his firm after his employers find out that he is both gay and has contracted the AIDS virus. Determined to sue them for discrimination, he approaches personal injury lawyer Joe Miller (Washington) to represent him. Joe initially refuses due to homophobic preconceptions, but has a change of heart once he sees what Andrew is up against. The pair fight against bigotry and Andrew’s worsening health in an attempt to find justice.

Industry observers note that loosely based on the stories of real-life lawyers, the film earned Tom Hanks his first Oscar for Best Actor, while Bruce Springsteen won Best Original Song for his haunting theme “Streets of Philadelphia.” For Washington, it was another classic performance, one that addressed the ignorance toward HIV/AIDS and the gay community at the time. For Hanks, it kicked off a decade of prestige performances that would make him a Hollywood legend.

There’s no doubt that Hanks was a star by the time he took on the role of Andrew Beckett. For much of the 1980s, he had been the lead in a number of box office hits, primarily in the comedy genre. Substantial, Turner & Hooch, The ‘Burbs, Splash, and A League of Their Own had cemented him in the minds of audiences as someone who was adept at making you laugh. But in Philadelphia, he proved he could also make you sob.

Industry observers note that as Beckett, he is strong, principled, but also vulnerable. He knows there is nothing wrong with who he is, despite the prejudice he faces, but at the same time, knows he is facing a disease that, in that moment, meant he did not have much time to make his case. Hanks committed to the part fully, losing 35 pounds for the role and acknowledging that his likable presence made people face their own preconceptions. In a 2022 interview with The Upcoming York Times, he mentioned: “One of the reasons people weren't afraid of that movie is that I was playing a gay man.”.

According to recent reports, given the attitudes at the time, it was a risk to his crowd-pleasing reputation. However, the movie was a deeply emotional, human journey spearheaded by his earnest portrayal. Any gamble he took paid off, as the Oscar win confirmed he could make a dramatic hit as well as a comedy. In the following years, he doubled down on that reputation, starring in classics like Apollo 13, Saving Private Ryan, and The Green Mile before the 1990s were over.

Some of the exposition in director Jonathan Demme’s film may seem simplistic while watching over three decades later, as so much more progress has been made with societal attitudes as well as the treatment of HIV/AIDS. However, context is key in understanding how impactful the movie had been in spreading mainstream awareness of these issues. 1993 was the peak of the HIV/AIDS epidemic, with millions dying of the disease by the end of the decade. Parallel to this was a cultural rift, where false information about the virus had given the public an inaccurate picture.

While it did not address the political complications that activists felt needed highlighting, what it did was take people outside the crisis and make them see a human instead of a headline. This was a major Hollywood picture talking about subjects for the first time that were uncomfortable, but important, and only great art can do that. By focusing on one man’s struggle, it was easier to put yourself in his shoes and see it as a global struggle.33 years later, Philadelphia is a landmark moment in Hollywood history, creating discourse off-screen and launching one of the industry's finest stars on it. It's arguable that the first step toward Tom Hanks producing numerous classics of the '90s and beyond begins by taking a risk that shows how good he can be.

Internationally, “Sunrise on the Reaping” earned $105 million from 84 territories, pushing its worldwide box office gross to $225 million.

It has been revealed that lionsgate is distributing the $150 million production, as it has the previous films. The studio recently mounted something of a comeback under Adam Fogelson, who replaced Joe Drake as the motion picture chief in 2024. Lionsgate was on its back foot at the time, having released flops like “Borderlands” and the reboot of “The Crow.” In recent months, its fortunes have shifted thanks to blockbusters like “Michael” and hits such as “The Housemaid” and “The Long Walk.” A revived “Hunger Games” franchise is critical, as it gives Lionsgate another pillar for its slate.

But “The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes” success threatened to overshadow “I Play Rocky.” The Amazon MGM Studios release earned $9.3 million after expanding from 29 locations to 2,477 theaters. It’s playing like gangbusters, earning an A+ CinemaScore, a rare distinction that puts it in the tech giant of “Top Gun: Maverick” and “The Avengers.” The word-of-mouth is clearly excellent, which could help it build momentum over the holidays. It’s also worth noting that “I Play Rocky” is catering to older moviegoers who take their time getting around to seeing things. Even if it starts to fade, “I Play Rocky” is a relatively economical bet. It cost in the $30 million range to produce and has earned $10.4 million since it debuted.

Then there’s “Ebenezer.” The Johnny Depp revival isn’t as glorious as his most diehard fans may have hoped. The Christmas story fell roughly 60 percent in its second weekend, earning $7.7 million to bring its domestic total to $32.5 million. But Paramount didn’t spend lavishly to make the film. It only cost $38 million to remind Depp’s Scrooge of the Christmas spirit. “Ebenezer” has also earned $45.9 million internationally, bringing its global total to a respectable $78.4 million.

Industry observers note that among the newcomers, Sumerian Pictures released “Josephine,” a family drama with Gemma Chan and Channing Tatum,” on four screens in New York and Los Angeles this weekend, grossing an estimated $84,200 for a per-screen average of $21,050. The film earned raves at Sundance where it premiered and Sumerian bought it. “Elsinore,” a drama about Ian Charleson’s final stage performance, opened with $240,000 from six locations in New York and Los Angeles for a per-theater average of $40,000. Focus Features is distributing the film, which has earned Oscar buzz for Andrew Scott. Lastly, Janus Films and Criterion debuted Paul Thomas Anderson’s concert film “Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall” in three locations, where it earned $162,000 for $54,000 per-screen average. The film is only showing in 35mm, which limits the number of screenings available to cinephiles and PTA completists.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Amazon's Black Friday sale kicked off today, which means it's a good time to score some of the year's best prices on e-readers. Timing your purchase is now a bigger deal than ever (so to speak), as Amazon recently raised the price of basically every Kindle by $50 or more due to the ongoing RAM crisis.

Recent findings suggest that because of this, the prices aren't nearly as low as they were last year, but now is still the time to get a decent discount on a Kindle Paperwhite or Colorsoft—but if you'd rather read differently, you can also save big on a few worthy Kindle alternatives. Here are your e-reader best bets in the lead-up to Black Friday and Cyber Monday.

The Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition is the best e-reader for most people. An upgraded version of the basic Kindle, the Paperwhite adds a larger screen, temperature-adjustable lighting, water resistance, and better battery life—and if you opt for the Signature Edition, you also get double the storage and no lock screen ads. Earlier this year, it jumped in price to $250, even before the tech giant introduced a upcoming model—but you can get the 2024 model for $179.99, 28% off the new list price.

If you want a great Kindle but you don't care about paying extra for more storage or getting rid of lock screen ads, the non-Signature Edition of the Kindle Paperwhite is also a great buy right now. The 2024 model has been discounted to $129.99 from the list price of $199.99. It's available in standard black, Jade, or Raspberry colors.

If you don't need the bells and whistles of the Paperwhite, you can also pick up the standard Kindle. It's still a very capable device, with good lighting, 16GB of onboard storage, and the ability to hook up your Bluetooth speakers to listen to Audible audiobooks. The standard Kindle, which now retails for $150, is marked down to $119.99, making it the cheapest Kindle option. Though I think it makes more sense to spend $10 more on the Signature Edition, this is the way to go if you want the cute Matcha color.

According to recent reports, if you like to read comics or you just appreciate looking at your book covers in full color, the 2024 Kindle Colorsoft is also at a strong 41% discount for Black Friday, bringing it down to around $170. For $10 less than the Paperwhite Signature edition, you get all the same perks (including an ad-free experience) and a color e-ink screen that's great for reading magazines, graphic novels, and manga. Color e-ink isn't for everyone, but if it's for you, the Colorsoft has the best color screen on the market. For an extra $10, the Colorsoft Kids Edition adds a case, a yearlong subscription to Kindle Kids+, and an extended warranty.

Sources indicate that if you're looking for a combination e-reader and e-notebook, the Kindle Scribe is a great option. With a larger screen than Amazon's other e-readers, it offers all the benefits of the Paperwhite but adds support for the excellent Premium Pen stylus, allowing you to take notes in your Amazon e-books or create handwritten documents that you can later convert to text using the onboard AI tools. The 32GB black-and-white version of the Kindle Scribe is currently $349.99, while the Colorsoft version will run you $449.99. Both of these are the newest models, released in 2025.

The upcoming Kindle Scribe Colorsoft has all the same great features of the black-and-white version discussed above, but adds a full-color e-ink display. Combined with the large 11-inch screen, this makes it a great device for reading comics or magazine articles as they were meant to be read, or marking up PDFs using the included Premium Pen. This device usually costs a hefty $630, but the current Black Friday sale cuts $180 off of that price.

If you want to step outside of the Amazon ecosystem, the Kobo Libra Colour is a good bet. Discounted $30 to $229.99 at Best Buy, it's currently pricier than the Kindle Colorsoft, but you get a bit more for your money. While most of the specs are similar (they both use the same Kaleido 3 screen and offer 32GB of storage), the Kobo supports a stylus, so you can jot down notes in your books or keep a digital journal. It also has physical page-turn buttons, which the Colorsoft lacks.

It has been revealed that if you don't want to be tied to the Amazon ecosystem and/or you're looking for a device that's a bit more portable, consider the Viwoods AiPaper Reader, right now marked down to $200, its lowest price ever. It's got a 6.13-inch screen, so it's the same size and shape as your phone, and it has a crisp e-ink screen with a strong (if not temperature-adjustable) front light and 128GB of onboard storage. The best part is, it runs on an open Android system, so you can install multiple reading apps, including Kindle, Nook, Kobo, and Libby, and keep all of your books in one place. (Check out my review of the Viwoods AiPaper Reader for more—it's a nifty little device.).

In a recent development, if you don't have a large Kindle library, you're moderately tech-savvy, and you praise portability above all else, I can't recommend Xteink's line of e-readers more highly. The 4.3-inch Xteink X4 Classic is at its lowest price ever, coming in at just under $55, around $34 off the list price. Meanwhile, the smaller 3.7-inch Xteink X3 is about a dollar more; that's a less-generous 19% discount. I own both, and while the Classic is definitely worth the current sale price, I actually prefer the form factor of the smaller X3 (at the moment $55.72), which is about the size of a library card.

If you're feeling tentative about trusting a seemingly no-name Chinese tech brand, read more about the devices in my review, or listen to the collected wisdom of the tens of thousands of people in the bustling r/xteink Reddit group.

Sources indicate that in short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

No. If you find the product you're looking for with a major discount right now, get it. It's not likely to drop any lower, but it could always run out of stock. Take advantage of price matching or guarantees instead of waiting. Remember, you can always return products later if you change your mind. For the majority of products, the deal from Black Friday will be the same one on Cyber Monday.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Meta employees have expressed concerns about what appear to be major privacy breaches when using Muse, currently the second most popular free iPhone app in the App Store with over 10 million downloads.

This includes again accessing end-to-end encrypted messaging without permission, and sharing what may be the bank balances of another Muse user ….

Siri AI was not the only AI app to launch back in September; Meta’s Muse AI app was released the same month, with the company describing it as “your personal AI agent that gets things done across every part of life.”.

According to recent reports, muse initially launched as an iPhone app, with Mac and iPad apps following shortly afterwards. It immediately moved to the top of the US App Store charts, overtaking ChatGPT. It quickly exceeded 5 million downloads following a major advertising push by Meta, and that number has since doubled.

It wasn’t long before major privacy concerns were raised. Tech writer Jason Aten reported that the Mac app accessed his messages despite him explicitly refusing permission. The app then lied to him about how it had achieved this. Meta described this as a bug.

Security researcher Patrick Wardle also discovered a zero-day vulnerability that could allow an attacker to hijack dictated prompts, directing them instead to their own server.

I remarked at the time that I would absolutely not be one of the millions of people using the app, and the wisdom of that decision has now been underlined by a fresh report.

Reuters now reports Meta employees discussing further breaches. This includes another example of accessing encrypted messages without permission.

An employee using Muse on her personal phone reported it had surprised her with a reminder to respond to a message from her sister on Signal, an end-to-end encrypted messaging service popular with privacy advocates that competes with Meta’s WhatsApp.

In a recent development, “This seems like an extreme privacy violation. I definitely did not grant it access to other apps, or recall being asked about this,” the employee said in her post.

The report indicates this appears to have been done by capturing push notifications. However, this was what the app claimed had happened in the earlier case, and it turned out not to be true. The AI Now Institute was able to replicate the problem of Muse accessing Signal messages without permission.

Another employee reported receiving unsolicited bank balances that they say appeared to be those of another Muse user.

Muse had randomly added an extra message to its regular chats about fishing-related weather and tide information, saying: “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.”.

“I have never shared my bank account with Muse and never discussed any banking topic with Muse. I’m afraid it’s sending other’s bank info to me,” the staffer wrote in his post.

Sources indicate that meta told Reuters that these were “isolated incidents” and suggested that the bank balances may have been AI hallucinations rather than leaked information. Update: Meta has now told us that the balances were definitely hallucinations.

Recent findings suggest that "AI Agent" = Malware. There are an expanding number of "I told it not to do that" cases.

The instructions (prompt) you give the agent are a tiny fraction of the total prompt context the agent uses, and Meta/Grok/etc. is not going to let you see that context. Agents harvesting your data (ex. see full disk access) and sending it to the mothership is just another revenue/training stream. Even if you are paying you are still the product.

In a recent development, meta has taken problem with the messaging claims. It indicates that access to either notifications or messaging must be explicitly granted.

Sources indicate that with Android, owners have the option to grant apps notification access, which allows apps to see notifications as they’re received. This is something users need to opt in to and is not specific to Muse. With Mac, to allow Muse to work on your behalf, you not only need to click allow for accessibility and screen recording, but after that it takes you to a settings screen where you once again need to confirm and turn this on.

The organization also implies that the experience of employees may relate to internal versions of Muse.

Employees have access to different versions of Muse than the public, so they’re often reviewing features, functionality, and behavior not available elsewhere.

I can only repeat my previous take on Muse: Nope.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Rian Johnson isn’t writing a Star Wars movie, but he isn’t ruling one out, either.
  • Responding to a question from IndieWire during an in-conversation event at the 23rd Marrakech International Film Festival, the writer/director of “Star Wars: The Last Jedi” was clear that his next project lies elsewhere: “I’m already writing the next thing I’m going to do, and it’s not a Star Wars thing, or in that genre,” he said.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rian Johnson isn’t writing a Star Wars movie, but he isn’t ruling one out, either.

Responding to a question from IndieWire during an in-conversation event at the 23rd Marrakech International Film Festival, the writer/director of “Star Wars: The Last Jedi” was clear that his next project lies elsewhere: “I’m already writing the next thing I’m going to do, and it’s not a Star Wars thing, or in that genre,” he said.

“I’m very much enjoying just making my own stuff, but I mean, if the opportunity presented itself,” Johnson remarked, nodding. “It’s a world I deeply love. It’s also a group of people I love.”.

“I love Star Wars more now than I ever have,” he added. “And it’s exciting to me that there are a lot of different voices now taking cracks at it.” The timing is hard to ignore. Related Stories Box Office: ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Debuts to Mighty $120 Million, Reviving Lionsgate’s Most Key Franchise Box Office: A24’s ‘You Can See Everything’ Crosses $100 Million Globally.

Johnson’s remarks land just as Lucasfilm appears to be turning back toward the corner of the saga he helped shape. Polygon reported that two long-gestating features, “Star Wars: Upcoming Jedi Order” and an untitled film from Dave Filoni, are still listed as in development by Production Weekly, despite months of silence and the soft box office performance of “The Mandalorian & Grogu.”.

“Fresh Jedi Order” would theoretically bring back actress Daisy Ridley as Rey roughly 15 years after “The Rise of Skywalker,” rebuilding the Jedi Order that “The Last Jedi” so memorably called into question. Sharmeen Obaid-Chinoy is attached to direct, with George Nolfi now writing after earlier drafts from Damon Lindelof and Justin Britt-Gibson, and a stint by Bond 26 screenwriter Steven Knight. The film was pulled from its December 17, 2027 release date in May 2025. Meanwhile, “Star Wars: Starfighter,” the Shawn Levy-directed film starring Ryan Gosling and set five years after “The Rise of Skywalker,” remains the only Star Wars feature with a firm date: May 28, 2027.

In 2017, the year “The Last Jedi” hit theaters, Lucasfilm confirmed that Johnson would create a latest Star Wars trilogy. Those films have yet to materialize, but Johnson had warm words for Filoni, who took on the role of Lucasfilm’s president and chief creative officer in January: “Dave Filoni I got to know while making ‘The Last Jedi’, and he’s a wonderful guy who really has the spirit of Star Wars in him,” he mentioned. “All the Lucasfilm folks are awesome.”.

Later, answering questions from the audience, Johnson described “The Last Jedi” as “the most joyful process of any movie I’ve ever made”, despite the challenge of stepping from his own original films into what he called a contested mythology.

Sources indicate that “I’m a huge, huge fan of George Lucas, and I’ve read a lot about when he was writing the original Star Wars, how personal it was for him,” Johnson continued. “I think especially with something that has a deep cultural impact, and that belongs to everybody, that makes it even more vital… to make sure it’s coming from a personal perspective and something that’s deeply on fire inside you, as opposed to thinking, ‘what’s gonna please this person and this person and this person’. That leads to homogeneity, to repeating yourself and to something that feels dead on screen.”.

As a middle chapter, “The Last Jedi” drew directly on Johnson’s childhood experience of “The Empire Strikes Back,” though not as something to copy. “I didn’t want to imitate ‘The Empire Strikes Back’,” Johnson noted. “What I wanted to get to was the heart of what that movie has, which is this center part of life where your job is to fail, and your job is to learn from that and to get up and keep moving forward.”.

He drew a distinction between a film having a moral compass and having a moral. The compass, he remarked, “comes from the entire mass of every single creative decision made by the writer, or director, or whole team.”.

According to recent reports, johnson also reflected on the only two composers he has worked with. His cousin Nathan Johnson has scored his films since the pair started making movies together at age ten: “Nathan is the first person to read the script; he’s on set for the entire shoot so it’s very much a collaboration.”.

Sources indicate that john Williams, he said, is also “a miracle of a human being”, and working with him was the opposite experience. “You give him the movie and then the first time I hear any music is when we’re on the scoring stage, and there are 200 musicians playing it.”.

If Johnson does return to Star Wars, it seems he won’t be thinking about franchise strategy. “For me it’s not about thinking about IP, it’s about stories,” he noted. “I deeply believe the only way to actually make a movie that matters and is worth something is to have your eyes nowhere else except on making that movie. What is the story we’re telling? Why are we telling it? Why do we care about it?”.

“Outside of that bubble,” Johnson added, “I’ll leave it to the executives.”.

With those executives now steering Star Wars back toward Rey and the post-“Rise of Skywalker” era, the bubble may be closer to his than it has been in years.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that rebooting familiar properties as prestige TV indicates has become a staple of the streaming era, but few platforms have developed a knack for it quite like Prime Video. From The Tick and Reacher to Carrie, A League of Their Own, and Jack Ryan, Amazon has repeatedly turned established IPs into fresh-feeling modern series. These shows cover wildly different genres, but they all manage to successfully walk the fine line between nostalgic appeal and original storytelling.

Prime Video is showing no signs of slowing down when it comes to investing in modern reinventions of established franchises, either. Its upcoming slate includes projects like a live-action Tomb Raider series and Blade Runner 2099. However, one of its most exciting upcoming small-screen revivals is bringing back a sci-fi property that’s spent over a decade dormant. Once among the genre’s most recognizable names, RoboCop has had a rocky history over the last few decades, but Prime Video recognizes the enormous potential that still exists in its central concept and is creating a TV series to prove it.

In a recent development, beginning with Paul Verhoeven’s classic 1987 movie, the core of the RoboCop franchise is the story of murdered Detroit police officer Alex Murphy (set to be played by Dan Stevens, who is resurrected as a cyborg by the corrupt corporation Omni Consumer Products. The original film spawned sequels, animated and live-action TV shows, and a 2014 reboot. However, none of the later installments managed to capture the success of the original. Prime Video’s upcoming series is the latest attempt to give the franchise a new project worthy of its enduring legacy, and, with the right creative approach, it could finally make RoboCop a household name once again.

There’s definitely a lot of excitement surrounding Prime Video’s upcoming RoboCop TV series. While the RoboCop name doesn’t hold the weight it did decades ago, there’s a lot of nostalgic fondness both for its story and iconic imagery. However, nostalgia and audience familiarity alone doesn’t guarantee success. This is especially true for RoboCop, as there have been two attempts to bring the franchise to the small-screen in live-action before, and neither can really be considered a success.

Recent findings suggest that the first attempt was 1994’s RoboCop: The Series. This original RoboCop TV show softened the violence of the first two movies in an attempt to appeal to a broader audience, and it definitely didn’t work. A key part of the appeal of RoboCop as a character is both the brutality of his methods and the borderline body-horror of the way he’s created. Remove that from the equation and there’s little to separate Alex Murphy from the dozens of other sci-fi cyborg heroes out there.

Recent findings suggest that the 2001 miniseries RoboCop: Prime Directive moved back toward adult territory, but restoring bloodshed could only achieve so much. Yes, it had the violence of the 1987 RoboCop movie, but it lacked the deeper themes that gave its visceral moments weight. It felt very much like an “if you build it, they will come” attempt to cash in on the RoboCop name without actually understanding why fans love it. Alex Murphy’s cyborg body is definitely iconic, but simply putting RoboCop on the small-screen isn’t enough.

However, neither series failed because RoboCop won’t work on television. With the right approach, it definitely can, which is why the timing feels right for the upcoming Prime Video revival. Unlike the landscape of the 1990s and very early 2000s, today's studios seem to understand the importance of the stories and themes that support the sci-fi spectacle and visceral violence of classic cinematic franchises. The chances that Prime Video’s RoboCop will misunderstand the appeal of the source material like the 1994 and 2001 attempts feel very slim. The central premise of RoboCop has always felt like it has great TV show potential, and the upcoming Prime series may be the project that finally unlocks it.

Any established franchise usually guarantees some attention when a streamer announces a revival. However, few properties feel like they deserve a high-quality return quite like RoboCop. The original 1987 movie is still considered a highpoint for sci-fi movies, with its initial success spawning two sequel films, a reboot, animated and live-action TV show attempts, video games, and plenty of merchandise. It’s an enormously recognizable franchise, but one that still feels like it’s living in the shadow of its first entry.

Nearly 40 years later, Paul Verhoeven’s RoboCop film remains celebrated as a sci-fi achievement thanks to the remarkable balancing act it pulls off. The action is brutal, the corporate satire is viciously funny, and Murphy’s struggle to reclaim his identity gives the spectacle a hugely relatable emotional center. Every element reinforces the others, turning a potentially ridiculous premise into an unforgettable sci-fi tragedy.

Recent findings suggest that roboCop’s dystopian cyberpunk setting has also aged uncomfortably well. The idea that law enforcement and government institutions really serve corporate interests feels even more poignant now than it did in the 1980s. This is especially true today when surveillance, automation, and technology companies’ influence are common concerns. RoboCop may not be the household name of, say, Star Wars or Star Trek, but it’s still a hugely crucial and influential science fiction story. The 1987 movie still holds up as a piece of cinema, and the core concept of its story still feels relevant.

Sources indicate that with this in mind, it seems clear why Prime Video is determined to recreate RoboCop for modern audiences as a prestige TV show. If the revival can recreate the original’s combination of savage humor, awareness of social challenges, and genuine tragedy at the heart of Alex Murphy’s latest life, the new RoboCop series can be every bit as successful as the 1987 film. The potential is already there, all that Prime Video needs to do is stick the landing.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the definition of a cult superhero film, Francis Lawrence and Keanu Reeves' 2005 DC adaptation, Constantine, has developed a second life among devotees of its star and '90s-gothic style — and an upcoming sequel is among the most anticipated in recent superhero memory. Constantine did well at the box office, but seemed to drop off the cultural map after leaving theaters, despite its status as probably the single most visually striking comic book film ever made. Lawrence used it as his calling card for a variety of huge Hollywood projects (ranging from The Hunger Games to Stephen King's The Long Walk), but nothing ever approached his work with DC Comics' John Constantine for sheer visual spectacle.

In a recent development, while many critics at the time dinged the film for its plotting and heavy reliance on visual effects, earning it a 46% Rotten Tomatoes rating, the story is quite different among cinephiles on Letterboxd, where an impressive 40% of viewers rated it at four stars or above. Reeves and Lawrence are on the same page as the film's fans, and have talked for years about sequel ideas — including some in which they'd swing for the fences in terms of the R-rating. Fans of DC Comics or supernaturally-tinged noir who missed out on Constantine for the past 21 years owe it to themselves to check the film out on HBO Max today.

According to recent reports, constantine begins like a stylistic cross between an Indiana Jones film and The Exorcist ... then proceeds into demonic film noir before ending up entirely its own thing: a confident, hyper-stylized superhero saga begging for sequels. Lawrence embraces a '90s comic book-goth aesthetic without fear of goofiness, bathing exteriors and interiors alike in Se7en-esque greens, yellows, and browns while every angle that can be canted or birds-eyed tends to be so. Demons and angels alike walk the Earth: demons in the form of winged abominations that burst into embers when hit with holy light, and angels in the otherworldly Tilda Swinton, who gives her all in the role of Gabriel.

There's a priest besieged by demonic forces until he drinks himself to death, and is then cradled by an enraged and grieving celestial liquor store owner. The film even features a demonic nightclub, reminiscent of the one in Blade, in which patrons literally cannibalize victims on tables and turn white wine into blood. And this is all before Constantine descends into hell itself, which is envisioned as Los Angeles frozen mid-atomic blast, while thousands of sinners and demons alike writhe just beneath the blown-out surface. It's all bold and beautifully visualized, and should still be catnip to genre enthusiasts today.

Sources indicate that and character actor Peter Stormare's single, five-minute scene as Satan himself, should be the stuff of legend. Barefoot, dripping tar, and dressed in a crisp, white suit, Stormare's Satan makes an incredible first impression. Stormare lays on the tics, like inhuman gulping, licking various objects, and twitching with the sheer ecstasy of being evil. This sequence, as Satan tries to take Constantine's soul, elevates an already terrific picture into something genuinely special.

Recent findings suggest that despite Francis Lawrence's obvious dexterity with visual spectacle and design, Constantine wouldn't work quite as beautifully without its star. Reeves was already an icon upon its 2005 release from The Matrix trilogy, but he'd yet to don the iconic suit and pistols of John Wick. Still, he brings an unmistakable Wick energy to Constantine, constantly issuing patented, angry Reeves "Yeahs" to demons and angels alike, furiously lighting up at every opportunity, and eventually flipping off the devil.

Industry observers note that reeves manages to bring real pathos with precious little facial work to scenes in which oily black tumors are pulled from his chest, and in which he slices his own wrists in a bid to save a single doomed woman's life. Watching Constantine today, especially with the hindsight of the John Wick films, it's clear as day that sequels are warranted. Although it's been a long road, Reeves and Lawrence have thankfully confirmed that one is finally on its way.

It has been revealed that the 2005 Constantine remains a visual masterpiece, and one of the coolest superhero movies ever made. It also stands as a striking reminder of what comic book films could have been over the last two decades, particularly given the run of CGI slop-laden, televisual-looking features we've gotten as of late. Anyone who missed out on its demonic charms the first time should catch it now on HBO Max.

The SE 3 does just about everything you'd expect an Apple Watch to do. It, of course, has a heart rate sensor to keep tabs on your pulse, including high and low heart rate alerts; the ability to track dozens of different workouts and exercise types (including swimming, thanks to the device's water resistance); a sleep tracker with daily analyses available in the Health app; notification forwarding to check in on your alerts without opening your iPhone; and the ability to send and receive text messages.

In a recent development, it comes in two sizes (40mm and 44mm) depending on how large or small you prefer your watch. No matter which model you get, the watch comes with the S10 chip, Apple's last-generation watch processor. While it isn't as fast as the current S11 chip, the S10 is more than capable of running watchOS 27. Apple indicates the SE 3 can run for up to 18 hours on a single charge, and up to 32 hours in Low Power Mode, with fast charging from 0% to 80% in 45 minutes.

It has been revealed that the majority of the features missing from the SE 3 aren't essential. Apple's other watches have things like bigger, brighter displays, additional health tracking tools like hypertension alerts and an ECG sensor, longer battery life, and Audio Intelligence—the latter of which might be a benefit to miss, depending on who you are.

Industry observers note that if your giftee wants or needs any of those additional features, Series 12 or Ultra 4 might be a better choice. But for anyone who wants the essential Apple Watch experience, the SE 3 is simply the best-value watch Apple sells right now—especially at this discount. It has been revealed that in light of growing pushback from owners who want more control over how AI is integrated into their apps (if at all), Canva is introducing upcoming settings that let them hide generative AI features and see less AI-generated content. Here are the details.

Canva today declared upcoming controls that will let Free and Pro users choose whether to see generative AI features across the app, as well as how much AI-generated content appears in search results and in recommendations for templates and design elements.

The company notes that both controls are available at no additional cost and can be turned on or off at any time.

According to Canva, “the future of creativity isn’t a choice between AI and no AI.” For this reason, it is introducing the following controls:.

The organization notes that, while it knows that there is an ongoing debate between owners with opposing views on whether AI has a place in creative work, it thinks “both views are valid”:.

“It’s not our place to tell anyone how to create, so today we’re launching two newly introduced controls that put that decision firmly with our community […].”.

Importantly, the firm noted that select features that use AI without generating newly introduced content will remain available even when generative AI features are turned off:.

“Some of Canva’s everyday editing tools use AI to make simple tasks faster, without generating anything fresh. Background Remover, one of Canva’s most popular tools, lifts a subject cleanly out of a photo in a single click, and Magic Grab lets creators select an object in an image and move it somewhere else in the design. Both remain available when the generative AI switch is off, because they work only with what’s already in a design.”.

Canva added that these tools also won’t add an AI label to a design’s metadata, since that label is reserved for AI-generated content.

As for the tech giant’s design content library, Canva noted that while “a small portion of the library is AI-generated content made by Canva, including some abstract backgrounds and illustrated graphics,” its community has told it “they want an easier way to find design assets made by real people, so the content control reduces the number of AI-generated templates and elements that appear in search results and recommendations.”.

With today’s announcement, Canva is essentially expanding on the AI permissions already available to administrators of Business, Enterprise, Teams, and Education accounts, which let organizations control how their teams use AI.

To learn more about today’s announcement, follow this link.

Tech Report: Why Black Friday and Cyber Monday Are Bad Days to Impulse Buy Electronics

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1127 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Black Friday sales officially start Friday, November 28, and run through Cyber Monday, November 30, 2026, and Lifehacker is sharing the best sales based on product reviews and comparisons before it's over.
  • It's Cyber Monday, and Lifehacker is sharing the best sales based on product reviews and comparisons before the sales are over.
  • Some Cyber Monday deals are still live, and Lifehacker is sharing the best sales based on product reviews and comparisons before the sales are over.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Black Friday sales officially start Friday, November 28, and run through Cyber Monday, November 30, 2026, and Lifehacker is sharing the best sales based on product reviews and comparisons before it's over.

It's Cyber Monday, and Lifehacker is sharing the best sales based on product reviews and comparisons before the sales are over.

Some Cyber Monday deals are still live, and Lifehacker is sharing the best sales based on product reviews and comparisons before the sales are over.

Follow our live blog to stay up-to-date on the best sales we find.

Browse our editors’ picks for a curated list of our favorite sales on laptops, fitness tech, appliances, and more.

Sales are accurate at the time of publication, but prices and inventory are always subject to change.

Not every Black Friday or Cyber Monday deal is as sweet as it seems. With electronics and tech in particular, you could be buying last year's model that has actually been on sale since the summer—and was maybe a better price a few months ago. Here’s how to avoid impulse buying a misleading Black Friday “deal” and make sure you’re getting the best bang for your buck.

When you see products like food, clothes, or home goods with a substantial "Black Friday" or "Cyber Monday" tag slapped on them, it's probably safe to take advantage of that deal. Chances are it's the same exact product you'd find on other days of the year. The same can’t be noted for a TV, laptop, and other tech deals, where the product itself is constantly being upgraded.

Because tech is always evolving, and retailers want to move inventory before latest models come out, electronics are especially susceptible to a practice known as "price anchoring." That's when retailers mark up prices in the weeks leading up to Black Friday, before "slashing" those prices back down, giving the appearance of a deal that isn't really a deal at all. Still, when you see that marked-up number, aka the "price anchor," you might get tricked into thinking you're saving money when you're not. There's also the false sense of urgency that gets created. It's second nature to assume that anything labeled "deal" won’t last long—even when this so-called deal price has actually been going on since the summer.

Price anchoring isn't even unique to Black Friday. The nonprofit Consumers’ Checkbook tracked prices at 25 major retailers over 33 weeks in 2022 and found that more than half the items tracked were offered at false discounts every week or almost every week. Less common, but also worth noting, is a known practice of "derivative" or retailer-exclusive models produced specifically for the holiday shopping season. These versions often feature cheaper components, fewer features, or lower specifications than their regular counterparts. A 55-inch TV from a reputable brand might look identical to the year-round model, but it could have a lower refresh rate, inferior panel technology, or fewer HDMI ports.

Recent findings suggest that in the same vein, that "amazing deal" on a laptop might come with last year's processor, or a smartphone that's about to be replaced. The issue isn't that the tech is an older model, but again, it's that it probably has been at this low a price, or lower, since the summer. Alternatively, some deeply discounted electronics are refurbished units or open-box returns that have been repackaged. Again, while this isn't necessarily a bad thing, impulse buyers may not fully realize what they're buying.

Sources indicate that the key phrasing here is impulse buying. Events like Black Friday are psychologically engineered to trigger impulse purchases. Limited-time offers, countdown clocks, and "while supplies last" warnings create artificial urgency. When you're caught up in the moment, it's easy to convince yourself you need a latest tablet, smartwatch, or gaming console, even if you hadn't considered buying one before.

Industry observers note that to avoid a low-key scam, do your research. The easiest way to tell that you’re getting the correct product is by checking the model or serial number. And with online shopping, finding and double-checking those numbers is quick and easy. In addition, don't just compare prices—compare specs. Look at processor speeds, RAM, storage capacity, screen resolution, refresh rates, and connectivity options. A $300 laptop isn't a deal if a slightly more expensive model offers significantly better performance that will last longer.

It has been revealed that if you do see a deal that catches your eye, it could pay to wait. Cyber Monday, post-Christmas sales, and even January clearances often feature electronics deals that rival or beat Black Friday prices, all without the famous chaos and pressure. Then again, you risk more “out-of-stock” results if you wait, so the risk is up to you, depending on the popularity of the item you’re eyeing (and how badly you want it).

The bottom line: Don’t fall victim to a falsely advertised lower-quality product, and do a little research to find actually good deals ahead of time.

According to recent reports, yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

Industry News: Todd Boehly Dissects How How Daniel Katz’s Trading Desk Acumen Fed Into A24 Success: “Very Few Entertainment People Understand Math”
